title: The Penguin Who Made Everyone Laugh
paragraphs: Few kinds of television have reached as many people as nature documentaries. When the crew of one [[epic|L7-0363]] series set out to film life near the South Pole, they spent almost three years in some of the coldest places on Earth. For every minute that viewers finally saw, hours of [[footage|L7-0416]] were collected. Snow storms sometimes kept the crew inside for days. The team lived in a small hut [[adjacent|L7-0013]] to a colony of penguins, and every morning they checked the weather before deciding whether it was safe to go outside.

One scene quickly became [[iconic|L7-1227]]. A young penguin tried to climb a steep slope of ice, slid back down again and again, and finally walked away with a look of pure determination. Online, people found the clip [[hilarious|L7-1221]], and it was shared so widely that it was seen [[nationwide|L7-0660]] within days. The director, however, was [[seemingly|L7-1229]] less amused. "That penguin was fighting for its life," she said. "We can smile at it, but we should also learn from it."

The series was a great success. [[Ratings|L7-1222]] were high, and the [[earnings|L7-1220]] from selling the show to other countries paid for the crew's next project. [[Reportedly|L7-0849]], thousands of students wrote to the team to ask how they could become scientists or filmmakers. Some critics say that such popularity is a [[testament|L7-1060]] to people's growing love of nature, and many teachers now use the series in their classrooms.

Yet the filmmakers know that the polar regions are not gentle places. For the penguins, the ice is both a [[haven|L7-0472]] from land animals and a home that is slowly growing warmer. The crew hopes that every viewer who laughs at the little penguin will also remember how fragile its world is. As the director put it, a good film should make people smile first and then make them think.
zh: 很少有哪一種電視節目能像自然紀錄片一樣觸及這麼多人。某部史詩般的系列影集的劇組前往南極附近拍攝生態時，在地球上一些最寒冷的地方待了將近三年。觀眾最後看到的每一分鐘，背後都蒐集了好幾個小時的影片素材。暴風雪有時會把劇組成員困在屋內好幾天。團隊住在緊鄰一個企鵝群聚地的小木屋裡，每天早上都要先查看天氣，再決定出門是否安全。
有一幕很快成了經典畫面。一隻幼小的企鵝想爬上陡峭的冰坡，卻一次又一次滑下來，最後帶著一臉純粹的決心走開了。在網路上，大家覺得這段影片爆笑無比，轉傳的範圍之廣，讓它在幾天內傳遍全國。然而導演看起來似乎沒那麼覺得好笑。「那隻企鵝是在為生存而奮鬥，」她說，「我們可以對牠微笑，但也應該從牠身上學到東西。」
這部影集大獲成功。收視率很高，把節目賣到其他國家賺得的收入，也支付了劇組下一個計畫的經費。據報導，有數千名學生寫信給團隊，詢問要如何才能成為科學家或電影人。有些評論者說，這樣的人氣證明了人們對大自然的喜愛與日俱增，而許多老師現在也把這部影集用在課堂上。
然而，電影人明白，極地並不是溫和的地方。對企鵝而言，冰既是躲避陸上動物的避風港，也是一個正慢慢變暖的家。劇組希望，每一位被那隻小企鵝逗笑的觀眾，也會想起牠的世界有多麼脆弱。正如導演所說，一部好電影應該先讓人微笑，再讓人思考。

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How penguins learn to climb ice and snow
The making and effects of a popular polar documentary
Why the South Pole is getting warmer every year
How students can become professional filmmakers
questions.explain: 全文談一部極地紀錄片的拍攝過程（第一段）、爆紅的片段（第二段）、成功與影響（第三段）以及背後的環境提醒（第四段），故選 (B)。(A) 只是其中一幕的內容；(C) 只在最後一段提到變暖，並非全文主旨。

questions.evidence: The team lived in a small hut adjacent to a colony of penguins, and every morning they checked the weather before deciding whether it was safe to go outside.

questions.stem: The word "iconic" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to ______.

questions.explain: 那一幕在幾天內傳遍全國，成為大家都記得的畫面，iconic 就是「代表性的、人人認得的」，故選 (A)。(C) 只說明剛拍好，無法解釋它為何傳遍全國。

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the director's feeling toward the penguin clip?
options: She was angry at the people who shared it.
She wished she had never filmed it.
She wanted viewers to take the penguin's struggle seriously.

questions.explain: 導演說企鵝是在為生存奮鬥，我們可以微笑但也應該學習，可見她希望觀眾認真看待牠的掙扎，故選 (C)。(A) 她沒有生氣，只是補充看法；(D) 她看起來並不覺得好笑。
questions.evidence: That penguin was fighting for its life

vocab.stem: The company had to pay a large fine for a serious ______ of safety rules.
vocab.explain: 公司因為嚴重「違反」安全規定而被罰款，breach of rules 為常見搭配，故選 breach。haven（避風港）、hub（中心）、tier（層級）都不能與 of safety rules 搭配表示違規。

vocab.stem: The new train station is a busy transport ______ where many bus and rail lines meet.
vocab.explain: 許多公車與鐵路路線交會的車站是交通「樞紐」，故選 hub。其他選項無法與 transport 構成合理搭配。

title: Who Decides What You Watch?
paragraphs: Every time you open a video app, a computer program chooses what you will see. This program is called an [[algorithm|L7-1238]], and it has become an [[integral|L7-0537]] part of daily life for millions of people [[nationwide|L7-0660]]. It works by following a set of rules, and the people who build it decide the [[parameters|L7-1239]], such as how long you watched a clip or whether you pressed the like button.

At first, the idea may sound [[creepy|L7-1235]]. How can a machine know what you enjoy? In fact, it does not understand you at all. It simply collects data from millions of users and looks for patterns. If people who watch cooking clips also tend to watch gardening clips, the program will guess that you want more gardening. Researchers who studied the [[aggregate|L7-0026]] behavior of users published their [[findings|L7-1219]] last year. To describe a typical viewer, they used the [[median|L7-1234]], which is the middle number when all the numbers are lined up from smallest to largest.

Experts have mixed feelings about this technology. Some praise it because it helps small creators reach new audiences. Others worry that a [[spike|L7-0969]] in popularity can be made by a program rather than by real interest. [[Hype|L7-1237]] is easy to build when a clip appears on thousands of screens in a single hour, and only a few creators ever reach the top [[tier|L7-1225]]. Computers think in a [[binary|L7-1242]] world of zeros and ones, but human taste is far more complex. Our tastes are not [[static|L7-0985]]; they change as we grow, and no program can see the whole picture.

[[Nonetheless|L7-1236]], the technology is here to stay. To [[offset|L7-0689]] the risks, some companies now let users clear their history or choose what the program may use. A video with high [[ratings|L7-1222]] is not always a good one, so the best advice for young people is simple. Enjoy what the program offers, but now and then search for something it would never have chosen for you. That small choice reminds you that you, not the machine, are in charge.
zh: 每次你打開影片應用程式，電腦程式就會替你選出你將看到的內容。這種程式叫做演算法，它已成為全國數百萬人日常生活中不可或缺的一部分。它依照一組規則運作，而設計它的人會決定各項參數，例如你看了一段影片多久，或者你有沒有按下喜歡鍵。
乍聽之下，這個概念可能令人毛骨悚然。機器怎麼會知道你喜歡什麼？事實上，它根本不了解你。它只是從數百萬名使用者身上蒐集資料，並尋找其中的規律。如果看烹飪影片的人也常看園藝影片，程式就會猜想你想看更多園藝內容。研究人員研究了使用者的整體行為，並在去年發表了研究結果。為了描述典型的觀眾，他們使用了中位數，也就是把所有數字由小到大排列後，位於正中間的那個數。
專家對這項技術抱持複雜的心情。有些人稱讚它，因為它能幫助小型創作者接觸新觀眾。另一些人則擔心，人氣的暴增可能是由程式製造出來的，而不是出於真正的興趣。當一段影片在一小時內出現在數千個螢幕上，炒作就很容易形成，而只有少數創作者能登上最頂層。電腦是在由 0 和 1 組成的二元世界裡思考，但人類的喜好複雜得多。我們的喜好不是一成不變的；它們會隨著我們成長而改變，沒有任何程式能看見全貌。
儘管如此，這項技術仍會繼續存在。為了抵銷風險，有些公司現在讓使用者清除自己的觀看紀錄，或選擇程式可以使用哪些資料。評分很高的影片未必是好影片，所以給年輕人最好的建議很簡單：享受程式提供的內容，但偶爾也去找找它絕不會替你挑選的東西。這個小小的選擇會提醒你，掌控一切的是你，而不是機器。

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How video programs choose content and why we should think carefully about them
Why computers can understand human feelings better than people can
How small creators can become famous in a single hour
Why young people should stop watching online videos
questions.explain: 全文介紹推薦程式如何依據資料挑選影片（一、二段），專家的看法（三段），以及我們應有的態度（四段），故選 (A)。(B) 第二段明說機器根本不了解你；(D) 作者並未要求停止觀看。
questions.evidence: Experts have mixed feelings about this technology.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, how does the program guess what you like?
options: It reads the messages you send to friends.
It asks you to fill in a long form.
It looks for patterns in data from millions of users.
It copies the videos your family watches.
questions.explain: 第二段說程式只是從數百萬使用者身上蒐集資料並尋找規律，故選 (C)。(A)(B)(D) 文中皆未提到。
questions.evidence: It simply collects data from millions of users and looks for patterns.

questions.stem: The word "static" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 作者說我們的喜好不是 static，而是「會隨著成長而改變」，所以 static 是「不變的」，故選 (B)。
questions.evidence: Our tastes are not static; they change as we grow, and no program can see the whole picture.

questions.stem: Which best describes the writer's attitude toward recommendation programs?
options: Balanced, with a reminder to stay in control
questions.explain: 作者既說明它的運作，也提到優缺點，最後建議享受但也要主動尋找新事物，是持平並提醒自己掌控的態度，故選 (D)。(A) 作者並未強烈反對，還說這項技術會繼續存在。
questions.evidence: That small choice reminds you that you, not the machine, are in charge.

vocab.stem: Climbing the world's highest mountain without any extra oxygen is an amazing ______.
vocab.explain: 不靠額外氧氣登上世界最高峰是令人驚嘆的「壯舉」，故選 feat。其他選項放進句中語意都不通。

vocab.stem: The earthquake was so strong that its ______ was felt in cities hundreds of kilometers away.
vocab.explain: 地震強到數百公里外的城市都感覺得到，指的是地震的「規模／震級」，故選 magnitude。

title: The Engineer Who Taught Drones to Rescue
paragraphs: When Nina Chen was a child, she loved to build model planes from paper and wood. Her father often helped her, and the two of them worked until dark. Her teacher noticed that she was always more interested in how a plane flew than in how it looked. Years later, as a young engineer, she saw the [[aftermath|L7-0024]] of a strong earthquake on the news. Rescue workers could not reach many villages because the [[terrain|L7-1056]] was steep and the roads were broken. Nina decided that a flying machine might do what trucks could not.

She began to design a small [[aerial|L7-0020]] vehicle that could carry food and medicine. Her team used a computer [[simulation|L7-0942]] to test hundreds of designs before building a single one. They looked for the [[optimal|L7-1247]] balance between weight and strength, and they studied wind [[velocity|L7-1164]] in the mountains. One early model fell into a river, [[albeit|L7-1253]] without causing any harm, and the team laughed, took notes, and tried again.

Soon the drone carried a small computer [[embedded|L7-1256]] in its body, a [[thermal|L7-1063]] camera, and an [[algorithm|L7-1238]] that could find people hidden under fallen buildings. The [[footage|L7-0416]] it sent back showed rescuers where to dig, and the strength of its signal told them the [[proximity|L7-0793]] of a person in need. [[Humanitarian|L7-0499]] groups asked to test it, and in its first real mission it helped a rescue team find several families who had been trapped for two days.

At a technology [[showcase|L7-1252]], Nina told the crowd that machines are only tools. Her real hope was [[advocacy|L7-1254]]: she wanted every country to prepare before disaster strikes, not after. Today her work is [[arguably|L7-1255]] one of the most meaningful uses of drone technology, and her students often ask how she stayed hopeful after so many failures. Her answer is short. A failure is just data waiting to be understood.
zh: 妮娜·陳小時候喜歡用紙和木頭做飛機模型。她的父親常常幫她，兩人總是一起忙到天黑。她的老師注意到，比起飛機好不好看，她總是對飛機如何飛行更感興趣。多年後，身為年輕工程師的她，在新聞上看到一場強震的災後景象。救難人員無法抵達許多村莊，因為地形陡峭，道路又被震斷。妮娜決定，也許飛行機器能做到卡車做不到的事。
她開始設計一種能運送食物與藥品的小型空中載具。她的團隊先用電腦模擬測試了數百種設計，才真正做出一架。他們尋找重量與強度之間的最佳平衡，也研究山區的風速。有一架早期的原型機掉進了河裡，不過沒有造成任何傷害，團隊大笑一陣，做好紀錄，然後再試一次。
不久，這架無人機的機身裡裝了一台嵌入式的小電腦、一台熱像儀，以及一套能找出被困在倒塌建築下的人的演算法。它傳回的影像告訴救難人員該往哪裡挖，而訊號的強弱則讓他們知道需要幫助的人離得有多近。人道救援組織請求測試它，而在第一次真正的任務中，它協助救難隊找到了好幾戶被困了兩天的家庭。
在一場科技展示會上，妮娜告訴群眾，機器只是工具。她真正的期望是倡導：她希望每個國家都能在災難發生之前就做好準備，而不是在之後。如今，她的成果可以說是無人機技術最有意義的運用之一，而她的學生常常問她，歷經這麼多次失敗後，她是怎麼保持希望的。她的回答很簡短：失敗只是等著被理解的資料。

questions.stem: The word "albeit" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to ______.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from Nina's final answer about her attitude toward failure?

She sees failures as chances to learn.
She thinks failures show that a plan is hopeless.

questions.evidence: A failure is just data waiting to be understood.

title: The Carrots Nobody Wanted
paragraphs: The [[genesis|L7-1264]] of Lisa's [[startup|L7-1272]] was a bag of carrots. While visiting a farm, she saw workers throwing away crates of vegetables because they were bent or too small. The carrots tasted perfect, yet supermarkets would not buy them. "Nobody wants a strange-looking carrot," the farmer told her with a sigh. Lisa thought otherwise.

She began to sell boxes of these "ugly" vegetables directly to families at a lower price. Her business was a small [[niche|L7-1265]] at first, but her [[proposition|L7-0787]] was simple: the same taste, less waste, and a better price. Many customers liked the idea, and her website became a [[gateway|L7-1270]] for people who had never thought about food waste before. There was little [[hype|L7-1237]] in her advertising. She just showed pictures of the vegetables and let people decide.

Success brought new problems. Keeping vegetables fresh as they moved from farms to homes required careful [[logistics|L7-1261]], and Lisa had to learn quickly about trucks, storage, and timing. She also had to change her [[mindset|L7-1262]]. At the beginning she thought of herself as a friend of farmers; later she saw that she was running a real company. A business [[guru|L7-1275]] who visited her school told her to listen more than she talked, and she [[wholly|L7-1273]] agreed. She now reads every complaint herself and uses what she learns to [[leverage|L7-1257]] better service for her customers.

Today, Lisa dreams of [[autonomous|L7-0077]] trucks that will deliver her boxes without a driver. Critics say the idea helps with only a small part of a very large problem, and they may be right. Even so, the [[saga|L7-1260]] of the ugly carrot has changed how many families think about food. Her [[earnings|L7-1220]] are modest, but she says that the most important number is the amount of food saved. For her, success is not only about the [[optimal|L7-1247]] price. It is about making sure good food ends up on a table instead of in the trash.
zh: 莉莎的新創公司，起源於一袋胡蘿蔔。有一次參觀農場時，她看到工人把一箱箱蔬菜丟掉，因為它們彎曲或太小。這些胡蘿蔔嚐起來很完美，超市卻不肯收。「沒有人想要長得奇怪的胡蘿蔔，」農夫嘆著氣對她說。莉莎卻不這麼想。
她開始以較低的價格，把這些「醜」蔬菜整箱直接賣給家庭。她的事業起初只是一個小眾市場，但她的主張很簡單：一樣的好味道、更少的浪費、更好的價格。許多顧客喜歡這個想法，而她的網站也成為讓從未想過食物浪費問題的人踏入這個議題的入口。她的廣告幾乎沒有炒作，只是展示蔬菜的照片，讓大家自己決定。
成功帶來了新的問題。要讓蔬菜從農場到家庭的過程中保持新鮮，需要周密的物流規劃，莉莎得很快學會卡車、倉儲與時間安排。她也得改變自己的心態。一開始，她把自己看成農夫的朋友；後來她明白，自己經營的是一間真正的公司。一位到她學校演講的商業大師告訴她，要多聽少說，她完全同意。她現在親自閱讀每一則客訴，並運用所學為顧客提供更好的服務。
如今，莉莎夢想有一天無人駕駛的卡車能不需司機就把她的箱子送出去。批評者說，這個想法只能解決一個龐大問題中的一小部分，他們或許是對的。即便如此，醜胡蘿蔔的故事已經改變了許多家庭看待食物的方式。她的收入不高，但她說最重要的數字是被救下來的食物量。對她而言，成功不只是最理想的價格，更是要確保好食物最後是出現在餐桌上，而不是垃圾桶裡。

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How farmers can grow bigger carrots
How a young woman built a business that sells imperfect vegetables

title: Why Sleeping Beats Cramming
paragraphs: Many students believe that the best way to prepare for an exam is to stay up all night. Sleep experts disagree. In their view, sleep is the [[foremost|L7-0418]] tool for learning, and giving it up is like throwing away half of your study time. A tired brain cannot store new facts well, so [[retention|L7-0862]] drops sharply after a night without rest.

How do researchers know this? Their [[methodology|L7-1277]] is usually simple. They ask one group of volunteers to learn a list of words and then sleep normally, while another group stays awake. The next day, both groups are tested. The [[findings|L7-1219]] are [[predominantly|L7-0769]] the same: those who slept remember more. Some studies use special [[apparatus|L7-0054]], such as sensors on the head, to watch the brain at work. During deep sleep, the brain seems to move new memories from a short-term [[buffer|L7-0148]] to a more permanent place, a little like saving a file on a computer.

Sleep matters for the body as well. Poor sleep affects [[metabolism|L7-1284]], the process by which the body turns food into energy. People who sleep too little often feel hungry and choose sugary snacks, and researchers have linked this habit to [[obesity|L7-1279]]. Because short sleep is now so [[prevalent|L7-0775]] among teenagers, many doctors have called it a serious health problem. [[Nonetheless|L7-1236]], not everyone takes it seriously, and for many young people the idea of an early night has little [[traction|L7-1287]].

What can students do? Experts suggest a few simple habits. Go to bed at the same time each night, keep screens away from the bed, and avoid heavy meals late in the evening. A change in [[mindset|L7-1262]] also helps. Rather than seeing sleep as lost time, think of it as the [[optimal|L7-1247]] way to prepare your brain. A good night's sleep may not feel like [[bliss|L7-1283]] when the alarm clock rings, but your test results may thank you.
zh: 許多學生認為，準備考試最好的方法就是熬夜。睡眠專家並不同意。在他們看來，睡眠是學習最重要的工具，放棄睡眠就像把一半的讀書時間丟掉。疲倦的大腦無法好好儲存新知識，所以一夜沒睡後，記憶的保留會大幅下降。
研究人員是怎麼知道的？他們的研究方法通常很簡單。他們請一組志願者背一份單字表，然後正常睡覺，另一組則保持清醒。隔天，兩組都接受測驗。結果大多相同：睡過覺的人記得比較多。有些研究會使用特殊儀器，例如貼在頭上的感應器，來觀察大腦的運作。在深層睡眠中，大腦似乎會把新的記憶從短期的緩衝區移到較持久的地方，有點像是把檔案存進電腦裡。
睡眠對身體也很重要。睡眠不足會影響新陳代謝，也就是身體把食物轉換成能量的過程。睡得太少的人常常覺得餓，並選擇含糖的零食，研究人員已將這個習慣與肥胖連結起來。由於睡眠不足在青少年之間如此普遍，許多醫生把它稱為嚴重的健康問題。儘管如此，並非每個人都認真看待它，對許多年輕人而言，早點睡這個想法並沒有多少說服力。
學生可以怎麼做？專家提出幾個簡單的習慣。每晚在同一時間上床，不要把螢幕放在床邊，並避免晚上太晚吃大餐。心態的改變也有幫助。不要把睡眠當成浪費的時間，而是把它想成讓大腦做好準備的最佳方式。鬧鐘響起時，一夜好眠或許不會讓你覺得幸福至極，但你的考試成績可能會感謝你。

vocab.explain: 咳嗽、呼吸困難是「呼吸系統」的問題，故選 respiratory。maternal（母親的）、righteous（正義的）、prevalent（盛行的）都不能形容 problem 並符合咳嗽的情境。

title: The Machine That Changed How Ideas Travel
paragraphs: Before the 1450s, books in Europe were copied by hand, and a single volume could take months to finish. Even skilled workers made mistakes, and no two copies were exactly alike. Only wealthy families, schools, and the Church could afford them, so reading belonged to a small [[elite|L7-0346]]. Then a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg, working in the German city of Mainz, built a printing press that used small metal letters which could be moved and used again. The [[genesis|L7-1264]] of modern publishing had arrived.

The new machine spread quickly. Within a few decades, presses were working in many cities, and printers traveled from town to town, carrying their skills and their tools. Venice became a [[hub|L7-1232]] of the book trade. Prices fell, and ordinary merchants and craftsmen could buy their first books. A busy [[marketplace|L7-1276]] of ideas had opened. Scholars of the [[renaissance|L7-0842]] used it to share their work far beyond the [[vicinity|L7-1171]] of their own universities.

Printing also changed how knowledge looked. A copied drawing often became less accurate each time it was copied, but a printed picture could be identical in every book. In 1543, a book on human [[anatomy|L7-1246]] by Andreas Vesalius appeared with remarkably detailed [[imagery|L7-1271]] of the body, and doctors across Europe could study the same pictures. New ideas gained [[traction|L7-1287]] faster than ever before, and cheap pamphlets became [[prevalent|L7-0775]] in city streets.

Not everyone welcomed this freedom. Rulers and city officials feared that unwelcome opinions would spread, so many issued a [[decree|L7-0281]] that books had to be approved before sale. Such [[censorship|L7-1263]] was hard to enforce, because a banned book could be printed again in another town. Writers also found clever ways to speak. A [[critique|L7-1268]] of those in power might appear as a [[parody|L7-1285]], a funny imitation that made readers laugh while it made them think.

In the [[aftermath|L7-0024]] of Gutenberg's invention, literacy slowly rose, schools multiplied, and newspapers appeared. Ideas that once took years to cross a continent now crossed it in months. Today we scroll through endless screens, yet the basic questions remain the same as in 1450. Who decides what may be said, and who is able to hear it?
zh: 1450 年代以前，歐洲的書都是手抄的，一本書可能要花上好幾個月才能完成。即使是熟練的工人也會出錯，而且沒有兩本抄本是完全一樣的。只有富裕的家庭、學校和教會買得起書，所以閱讀屬於一小群菁英。後來，一位在德國美因茲工作的金匠約翰內斯·古騰堡，造出了一台印刷機，使用可以移動並重複使用的小金屬字母。現代出版業的起源就此出現。
這項新機器傳播得很快。短短數十年內，許多城市都有了印刷廠，印刷工人從一個城鎮走到另一個城鎮，帶著他們的技術和工具，威尼斯成為書籍貿易的樞紐。價格下降，一般商人和工匠也能買到自己的第一本書。一個熱鬧的思想市集就此展開。文藝復興時期的學者利用它，把自己的作品分享到所屬大學周邊以外的遠方。
印刷也改變了知識的樣貌。手抄的圖畫往往每抄一次就變得更不準確，但印出來的圖卻能在每一本書裡都完全相同。1543 年，安德烈亞斯·維薩里的一本人體解剖學著作問世，書中對身體的圖像描繪極為精細，歐洲各地的醫生都能研讀同樣的圖。新的想法比以往更快獲得支持，廉價的小冊子也在城市街頭變得隨處可見。
並非每個人都歡迎這樣的自由。統治者和城市官員擔心不受歡迎的意見會擴散，因此許多人頒布法令，規定書籍必須先經核准才能販售。這種審查很難徹底執行，因為被禁的書可以在另一個城鎮重新印刷。作家們也找到巧妙的發聲方式。對當權者的批評可能會以戲仿作品的形式出現，那是一種滑稽的模仿，讓讀者在發笑的同時也開始思考。
在古騰堡這項發明的餘波中，識字率慢慢提高，學校增加，報紙也出現了。過去要花上數年才能橫越一個大陸的想法，現在只需數月。今天，我們滑著無盡的螢幕，但基本的問題仍和 1450 年一樣：誰來決定什麼可以說，又有誰能夠聽見？

title: A Detective Among the Ancient Bowls
paragraphs: At the back of a quiet museum, behind a door marked "Staff Only," Dr. Huang does what some people call detective work. Her job is to answer a simple but difficult question: is this object really what it claims to be? Every year, the museum receives gifts of ancient [[artifacts|L7-1309]], from small coins to [[iconic|L7-1227]] statues, and each one must be checked before it enters the museum's [[registry|L7-1293]]. The museum is also a [[hub|L7-1232]] for researchers, so one fake could mislead scholars around the world.

Her [[methodology|L7-1277]] borrows [[forensic|L7-1300]] techniques from police laboratories. A tiny piece of paint can show how old a painting is, because some colors did not exist until a certain time. [[Quantitative|L7-0803]] tests measure the exact amount of metals in a bronze bowl, and a number that does not match the period is a warning sign. She also studies the [[spatial|L7-0966]] arrangement of the marks left by tools, because ancient workers often shaped objects in patterns that modern copies fail to follow.

But science alone is not enough. Before any test begins, Dr. Huang studies the object's [[pathway|L7-1292]] through time: who owned it, where it was found, and who sold it. Missing years in that story make her suspicious. She also reads old letters and a [[memoir|L7-1291]] written by a traveler who once visited the place where it was found. "A good story can be a [[catalyst|L7-1296]] for a good discovery," she says, "but it can also be a trap." Her [[credentials|L7-1301]] include a degree in chemistry and years of work in the field, and colleagues often ask her to check their [[findings|L7-1219]].

Why does she care so much? For Dr. Huang, truth is [[paramount|L7-1306]]. A fake object teaches visitors the wrong things about the past. She also feels a kind of [[empathy|L7-1310]] for the people who made the originals, who put their skill and hope into every bowl and sword. "When I protect an object, I protect their voice," she says. And when a rare object is shown to be real, the whole team feels the thrill of having touched history.
zh: 在一間安靜的博物館後方，一扇標著「僅限工作人員」的門後，黃博士做著有些人稱為偵探的工作。她的任務是回答一個簡單卻困難的問題：這件物品真的是它所宣稱的那樣嗎？博物館每年都會收到贈送的古代文物，從小硬幣到代表性的雕像都有，而每一件在登錄進博物館的登記簿之前，都必須先經過檢驗。博物館同時也是研究人員的中心，所以一件贗品可能會誤導全世界的學者。
她的研究方法借用了警方實驗室的鑑識技術。一小片油漆就能顯示一幅畫的年代，因為有些顏色直到某個時期才出現。定量測試能測出一只青銅碗中金屬的確切含量，而與該時代不符的數字就是警訊。她也研究工具所留下的痕跡在空間上的排列，因為古代工匠常以特定的紋理形塑器物，而現代仿品往往無法遵循。
但光靠科學還不夠。在任何測試開始之前，黃博士會先研究這件物品穿越時間的來歷：誰擁有過它、它在哪裡被發現、又是誰賣掉的。故事中缺少的年份會讓她起疑。她也會閱讀舊信件，以及一位旅人所寫的回憶錄，他曾造訪過那件物品的出土地點。「一個好故事可以成為重大發現的催化劑，」她說，「但它也可能是個陷阱。」她的資歷包括化學學位以及多年的實務經驗，同事常請她核對他們的研究結果。
她為什麼這麼在意？對黃博士來說，真相至高無上。贗品會讓參觀者學到關於過去的錯誤知識。她也對製作原件的人懷有一種同理心，他們把技藝與希望傾注在每一只碗和每一把劍上。「當我保護一件古物，我也是在保護他們的聲音，」她說。而當一件稀有的物品被證明是真品時，整個團隊都能感受到彷彿親手觸摸了歷史的興奮。

title: A Toad That Hopped Out of Control
paragraphs: In 1935, farmers in Queensland, Australia, had a problem. A kind of beetle was eating their sugar cane. Scientists suggested bringing in a large toad from South America, which was known to eat insects. About one hundred toads were released, and everyone hoped that the beetles would soon disappear. The plan failed badly. The toads could not reach the beetles, which lived high on the plants, and they began to eat almost everything else.

Today the cane toad is one of the world's best-known [[invasive|L7-1331]] animals. Because it has few natural enemies in Australia, it found a perfect [[niche|L7-1265]] in the warm, wet north, and toads are now [[prevalent|L7-0775]] in many areas. The [[fallout|L7-1330]] for local wildlife has been serious. The toad's skin contains a poison, and many native animals die after trying to eat it. These animals showed great [[vulnerability|L7-1325]] because they had never met anything like the toad before.

Scientists who study the problem face an unusual difficulty: they need a [[baseline|L7-1320]], a clear picture of what the wildlife looked like before the toads arrived. The toad's [[dietary|L7-1323]] habits make matters worse, since it eats insects, small animals, and even pet food left outside. Researchers have also noticed that the toads at the front of the [[exodus|L7-1329]] from crowded areas have longer legs and move faster than those behind them. The spread across the [[terrain|L7-1056]] is [[akin|L7-1319]] to a wave, and at the [[onset|L7-1312]] of each wet season the wave moves forward again. This [[recurring|L7-1317]] pattern makes it very hard to stop.

Some people have tried to trap the toads, and others teach native animals to avoid eating them. In the [[aftermath|L7-0024]] of the original plan, these efforts have helped in small places, but no one has found a way to remove the toad from the [[entirety|L7-1328]] of the country. Historians often [[chronicle|L7-1321]] the plan as a warning for future projects. The story is a lesson about human choices. When people move an animal from one place to another, the result may be difficult to predict, and the cost may last for generations.
zh: 1935 年，澳洲昆士蘭的農民遇到了難題。一種甲蟲正在啃食他們的甘蔗。科學家建議從南美洲引進一種大型蟾蜍，因為牠已知會吃昆蟲。大約一百隻蟾蜍被放出去，大家都希望甲蟲很快就會消失。這個計畫慘遭失敗。蟾蜍搆不到棲息在植物高處的甲蟲，於是牠們開始吃起幾乎所有其他東西。
如今，蔗蟾蜍是世界上最著名的外來入侵動物之一。由於牠在澳洲幾乎沒有天敵，便在溫暖潮濕的北部找到了完美的生存位置，現在許多地區都很常見到蟾蜍。對當地野生動物造成的後果十分嚴重。蟾蜍的皮膚含有毒素，許多本地動物在試圖吃牠之後死亡。這些動物表現出極大的脆弱，因為牠們以前從未遇過像蟾蜍這樣的東西。
研究這個問題的科學家面臨一項特殊的困難：他們需要一條基準線，也就是蟾蜍到來之前野生動物樣貌的清楚圖像。蟾蜍的飲食習慣使情況更糟，因為牠吃昆蟲、小動物，甚至連放在戶外的寵物食物也吃。研究人員還發現，從擁擠地區大批遷出的蟾蜍群中，位於最前頭的那些，腿比後面的更長，移動也更快。蟾蜍在地表上的擴散就像一道波浪，而每到雨季開始時，這道波浪就會再度向前推進。這種反覆出現的模式讓牠們很難被阻止。
有些人試著用陷阱捕捉蟾蜍，也有人教本地動物避免吃牠們。在最初那項計畫的餘波中，這些努力在小範圍內有所幫助，但沒有人找到辦法把蟾蜍從整個國家清除。歷史學家常把那項計畫記載為未來計畫的警訊。這個故事是關於人類抉擇的一課。當人們把動物從一個地方移到另一個地方，結果可能難以預料，而代價可能延續好幾個世代。

title: A Garden for Every Sense
paragraphs: On Saturday, the [[inaugural|L7-1343]] day of the Riverside Sensory Garden brought together students, teachers, and neighbors. The garden, built on an empty piece of land in the [[vicinity|L7-1171]] of the school, was designed for visitors who learn about the world through touch, smell, and sound as much as through sight. The [[turnout|L7-1339]] was higher than the organizers had expected, and the paths were full by noon.

The project began two years ago, when a group of students noticed that no [[communal|L7-0209]] space in the neighborhood was welcoming to people who are [[impaired|L7-1335]] in sight or hearing. A [[consortium|L7-0224]] of local businesses, a university, and the school's parent group agreed to work together. The [[procurement|L7-1337]] of materials took several months, because the team chose only safe and long-lasting products, such as smooth stone and soft grass. Doctors who work with children gave advice on the [[terminology|L7-1054]] used on signs, so that every label would be clear and respectful.

Each part of the garden is built around one [[sensory|L7-1338]] experience. A bed of herbs invites visitors to touch and smell the leaves. A set of metal pipes makes music when the wind blows. A wooden [[partition|L7-0720]] covered with thick panels creates a quiet area, because it helps with the [[absorption|L7-1348]] of noise from the busy road. The [[focal|L7-1342]] point of the garden is a small fountain, where the sound of falling water can be heard from every path. With the [[advent|L7-0017]] of spring, [[vibrant|L7-1347]] flowers will add color for those who can see them.

The organizers say the garden is also a [[showcase|L7-1252]] for what a community can do when people work together. Several student groups plan to continue their [[advocacy|L7-1254]] by asking other schools to build similar spaces. A [[baseline|L7-1320]] survey of visitors was taken on opening day, and a second survey will be made next year to see how the garden has changed people's lives. For now, the message of the project is simple: a good space should let everyone enjoy the world in their own way.
zh: 星期六，河岸感官花園的開幕日讓學生、老師和鄰居們齊聚一堂。這座花園建在學校附近的一塊空地上，專為那些除了視覺外，也透過觸覺、嗅覺與聲音來認識世界的訪客而設計。到場的人數比主辦單位預期的還多，中午之前步道上就已擠滿了人。
這個計畫兩年前展開，當時一群學生發現，社區裡沒有任何公共空間對視力或聽力受損的人友善。一個由當地企業、一所大學以及學校家長會組成的聯合團體同意合作。材料的採購花了好幾個月，因為團隊只選用安全又耐用的產品，例如光滑的石頭和柔軟的草皮。長期與孩童相處的醫生針對標示牌上使用的術語提供了意見，讓每一塊標籤都清楚而且帶有尊重。
花園的每個區域都圍繞著一種感官體驗打造。一片香草花圃邀請訪客觸摸並聞聞葉子。一組金屬管在風吹過時會奏出音樂。一道鋪有厚板的木製隔間牆形成了一處安靜區，因為它有助於吸收來自繁忙馬路的噪音。花園的焦點是一座小噴泉，從每一條步道都能聽見流水聲。隨著春天的到來，鮮豔的花朵將為看得見的人增添色彩。
主辦單位表示，這座花園也展示了人們齊心協力時，社區所能達成的成就。有幾個學生社團打算繼續倡導，請其他學校也興建類似的空間。開幕當天對訪客做了一份基準調查，明年還會再做第二次調查，看看這座花園如何改變了人們的生活。目前，這個計畫傳遞的訊息很簡單：好的空間應該讓每個人都能以自己的方式享受這個世界。

title: The Record That Refused to Die
paragraphs: In the early 2000s, many people thought that vinyl records were [[obsolete|L7-1362]]. Music was now stored in tiny files, and a whole library could fit into a pocket. The record, invented more than a century earlier, was [[seemingly|L7-1229]] ready for a museum. Shops closed, and factories stopped making them. Yet something surprising happened. Instead of dying, the record came back.

Why did it return? Some point to its [[tangible|L7-1357]] qualities. A record is something you can hold, with large artwork and a smooth black surface, and you must stand up to turn it over. In a world of invisible digital files, this physical experience feels special. Others say the [[novelty|L7-0681]] of a spinning disc attracts young listeners who grew up with only screens. Critics call this mere [[hype|L7-1237]]. From the [[standpoint|L7-0979]] of the listener, however, the record is less a piece of old technology than a ritual of careful listening.

Music has gone through many changes. From the [[inception|L7-1359]] of recorded sound in the 1800s, each new format has tried to replace the last. After the cassette and later the compact disc arrived, the record was pushed to the [[peripheral|L7-1354]] edges of the market, where only a few collectors still cared about it. Experts expected its [[demise|L7-0288]] to be complete by the 1990s. What they did not expect was how well it would [[withstand|L7-1201]] the age of streaming. The [[prevalence|L7-1355]] of free online music may even have helped: when everything is available instantly, some listeners want something slower.

Today the [[marketplace|L7-1276]] is not unlimited. Some experts warn that it may become [[saturated|L7-1356]] if too many companies make records at once, and there are not enough factories to meet demand. [[Nonetheless|L7-1236]], the story has a clear [[resonance|L7-0855]] for anyone who loves music. New technology does not always replace the old; sometimes it simply gives us a reason to value it again. The [[nexus|L7-1361]] between memory and sound is strong, and a spinning record, with its soft crackle, may remind listeners of something no screen can supply.
zh: 2000 年代初期，許多人認為黑膠唱片已經過時了。音樂此時存放在小小的檔案裡，一整座音樂圖書館可以放進口袋。這種在一個多世紀前發明的唱片，看似已準備好被送進博物館。商店紛紛關門，工廠也停止生產。然而，令人驚訝的事發生了。唱片沒有消失，反而捲土重來。
為什麼它會回來？有些人指出它具體可觸的特質。唱片是你能握在手裡的東西，有大幅的封面設計和光滑的黑色表面，你還得站起來把它翻面。在一個充滿看不見的數位檔案的世界裡，這種實體的體驗顯得特別。另一些人說，轉動的圓盤所帶來的新鮮感，吸引了從小只接觸螢幕的年輕聽眾。批評者則說這只是炒作。然而，從聽眾的立場來看，唱片與其說是舊科技，不如說是一種專心聆聽的儀式。
音樂經歷過許多變革。從有聲錄音在 1800 年代誕生以來，每一種新格式都試圖取代前一種。在卡式錄音帶與之後的光碟出現後，唱片被推到市場的邊緣，只剩下少數收藏家還在乎它。專家預期它到了 1990 年代就會完全消失。他們沒料到的是，它竟能如此經得起串流時代的考驗。網路免費音樂的普及，說不定還幫了忙：當一切都能立刻取得時，有些聽眾反而想要慢一點的東西。
如今的市場並非沒有上限。有些專家警告，如果太多公司同時生產唱片，市場可能會飽和，而且工廠的數量也不足以滿足需求。儘管如此，這個故事對每個熱愛音樂的人都有明顯的共鳴。新科技並不總是取代舊事物，有時它只是給了我們一個重新珍惜舊事物的理由。記憶與聲音之間的連結很強，而一張旋轉的唱片，伴隨著輕柔的雜音，可能會讓聽眾想起任何螢幕都給不了的東西。

title: Journey to the Center of the Earth
paragraphs: No one has ever traveled to the center of the Earth. The deepest hole ever drilled reaches only a tiny part of the distance, so scientists must find other ways to answer a simple [[query|L7-0812]]: what lies below our feet? One [[plausible|L7-0751]] guess would be solid rock all the way down, but [[empirical|L7-0352]] evidence shows that this is not the case.

That evidence comes mainly from earthquakes. When the ground shakes, waves travel through the planet, and sensors around the world record when they arrive. Because the instruments must ignore [[ambient|L7-1373]] noise such as traffic and wind, they are often placed deep underground. The paths of the waves are [[distorted|L7-1370]] as they pass through layers of different material, and by studying these changes scientists can draw a map of the Earth's interior. The sensors are now [[standardized|L7-1368]], so records from different countries can be compared easily. The [[findings|L7-1219]] show a thin outer crust, a thick layer called the [[mantle|L7-1377]], a liquid outer core, and a solid inner core.

The mantle is not completely still. Over millions of years its hot rock moves very slowly, like thick syrup in a warm pot, and this motion helps push the plates of the crust around. In some places, the plates pull apart and create a long valley called a [[rift|L7-1367]]. East Africa has one of the best-known examples. The [[temporal|L7-1372]] scale of these changes is hard to imagine, because they take place across millions of years. Other events are more [[periodic|L7-0733]], such as the earthquakes that return to the same region again and again.

For students, the [[conceptual|L7-1374]] challenge is to imagine something so large and slow. Computer [[simulation|L7-0942]] can help, because researchers can change [[parameters|L7-1239]] such as heat and pressure and watch what happens. A boiled egg also offers a [[tangible|L7-1357]] picture: a thin shell, a thick white, and a small yolk at the center. The comparison is not exact, but it gives a picture that is easy to remember. Scientists still have many questions, and with every new earthquake a new piece of the puzzle appears.
zh: 從來沒有人去過地球的中心。有史以來鑽得最深的洞，也只到達那段距離的一小部分，因此科學家必須找其他方法來回答一個簡單的疑問：我們腳下是什麼？一個看似合理的猜測是，一路往下都是堅硬的岩石，但實證證據顯示事實並非如此。
這些證據主要來自地震。當地面搖晃時，震波會穿過整個地球，而世界各地的感應器會記錄震波到達的時間。由於儀器必須忽略交通和風等周遭環境的噪音，它們常被安置在很深的地下。當震波穿過不同物質的地層時，它們的路徑會被扭曲，科學家藉由研究這些變化，就能畫出地球內部的地圖。如今感應器已經標準化，因此各國的紀錄可以輕易比對。研究結果顯示，地球有薄薄的外層地殼、一層厚厚的地函、液態的外核，以及固態的內核。
地函並非完全靜止。經過數百萬年，它灼熱的岩石以極緩慢的速度移動，就像在溫熱的鍋裡的濃稠糖漿，而這種運動有助於推動地殼的板塊。在某些地方，板塊彼此拉開，形成一道長長的山谷，稱為裂谷。東非就有最著名的例子之一。這些變化的時間尺度很難想像，因為它們跨越數百萬年。其他事件則比較有週期性，例如會一再回到同一地區的地震。
對學生來說，概念上的挑戰在於想像如此巨大而緩慢的事物。電腦模擬可以幫上忙，因為研究人員可以改變熱度和壓力等參數，觀察會發生什麼。水煮蛋也提供了一個具體的畫面：薄薄的蛋殼、厚厚的蛋白，以及中心的一小顆蛋黃。這個比較並不精確，但它給出了一個容易記住的畫面。科學家仍有許多疑問，而每一次新的地震，都會出現一塊新的拼圖。

title: The Last Summer of the Maple Street Pool
paragraphs: The notice on the gate was short. The old Maple Street swimming pool, it said, would close at the end of summer, and its [[demolition|L7-1375]] would begin with the [[advent|L7-0017]] of autumn. For Mr. Lin, who had spent the [[entirety|L7-1328]] of his working life there as a lifeguard, the words felt like a blow. Every morning he still unlocked the gate, checked the water, and sat in his tall white chair, though the town had cut the hours and the paint was peeling from the walls.

Word spread quickly, and the pool's regular visitors began to share stories. A woman remembered learning to swim there as a girl, as if it were a [[rite|L7-0873]] that every child in the neighborhood had to pass. A boy said he had finally jumped from the high board after three summers of being afraid. Their [[nostalgia|L7-1378]] was warm and sometimes funny. Mr. Lin began to [[chronicle|L7-1321]] these stories in a notebook, and it slowly became a kind of [[memoir|L7-1291]] of the whole neighborhood.

The notebook became a [[catalyst|L7-1296]]. A teacher suggested an exhibition of photographs and old [[artifacts|L7-1309]], such as faded swim caps, a rusty whistle, and a score board from a swimming meet. On the first day, the [[turnout|L7-1339]] surprised everyone. People of all ages filled the hall, and the room felt [[vibrant|L7-1347]] with talk and laughter. A recording of the pool's [[ambient|L7-1373]] sounds, made by a student years earlier, played softly in the background: splashing water, children's voices, and the [[recurring|L7-1317]] note of Mr. Lin's whistle. Visitors were asked to [[refrain|L7-0831]] from touching the oldest photographs, but nobody could resist the whistle.

The council did not change its decision, but it made a new promise: a smaller pool and a park would be built on the same land. Mr. Lin did not argue. He had learned something from the stories he had written down. A building might disappear, but the [[empathy|L7-1310]] people felt for one another around it would remain, and that mattered more than concrete and tile. On the final evening he locked the gate and put the key in his notebook. [[Paramount|L7-1306]] in his mind was one simple hope: that the new pool, whatever its shape, would one day hold stories of its own.
zh: 門上的告示很短。上面寫著，舊的楓樹街游泳池將在夏末關閉，拆除工程會隨著秋天的到來而展開。對林先生來說，他以救生員的身分在這裡度過了整個職業生涯，這幾句話讀來像是重重一擊。他每天早上仍然會打開大門、檢查水質，並坐上他那張高高的白色椅子，儘管鎮上已經縮減了開放時間，牆上的油漆也在剝落。
消息很快傳開，這座游泳池的常客開始分享各自的故事。一位女士回憶自己小時候在這裡學會游泳，彷彿那是附近每個孩子都得通過的儀式。一個男孩說，他在害怕了三個夏天之後，終於從跳台上跳了下去。他們的懷舊之情溫暖，有時還很有趣。林先生開始把這些故事記在筆記本裡，而這本筆記慢慢變成了整個社區的回憶錄。
這本筆記本成了一個催化劑。一位老師建議辦一場照片與舊物展覽，展出褪色的泳帽、生鏽的哨子，以及一場游泳比賽的記分板。第一天，到場的人數讓所有人都吃了一驚。各個年齡層的人擠滿了大廳，整個空間充滿了談笑聲，十分熱鬧。一段由學生多年前錄下的游泳池環境音在背景輕輕播放：潑水聲、孩子們的說話聲，以及林先生哨音一再響起的那個音符。參觀者被請求不要觸碰最老的照片，但沒有人能抗拒去碰一碰那支哨子。
議會沒有改變決定，但做出了一項新的承諾：會在同一塊土地上興建一座較小的游泳池和一座公園。林先生沒有爭辯。他從自己寫下的那些故事中學到了一些事。建築物可能消失，但人們圍繞著它對彼此所懷有的同理心會留下來，而這比水泥與磁磚更重要。最後一個夜晚，他鎖上大門，把鑰匙放進筆記本裡。在他心中最重要的是一個簡單的願望：希望新的游泳池，不論形狀如何，有一天也能擁有屬於它自己的故事。

title: The Wall Every Runner Hits
paragraphs: Ken Lin started running at the age of fifteen, and for two years his improvement seemed [[perpetual|L7-0736]]. Every month he lowered his time in the 5,000-meter race, and his coach kept a careful [[tally|L7-1031]] of the results in a small notebook. His [[trajectory|L7-1392]] pointed straight upward, so when his times stopped improving in his third year, he was shocked. He had reached a [[plateau|L7-0750]].

Almost every athlete meets this wall. Experts in [[physiology|L7-0743]], the study of how the body works, explain that the body adapts to a given amount of training. After a while, the same effort no longer produces the same gain. Researchers speak of an [[equilibrium|L7-0367]]: the body has found a balance and sees no reason to change. To grow again, a runner must provide a new challenge, such as a different distance, a hill, or a [[periodic|L7-0733]] rest week. Ken's coach first asked him to take a fresh test to set a new [[baseline|L7-1320]].

She did not ask him to run harder. Instead, she asked him to change his [[mindset|L7-1262]]. She told him to stop comparing every run to his best time and to treat each run as a [[benchmark|L7-1394]] for learning, not a score. With a new plan, a short [[stint|L7-1391]] of strength training, and more sleep, he put in his [[utmost|L7-1160]] effort in a different way. She also showed him how to find the [[optimal|L7-1247]] amount of rest. Some of his friends thought the change was strange, but his coach, an [[underrated|L7-1393]] teacher, had seen it before.

Within months, his times began to fall again. Ken is now an adult and a school coach himself, and every year on the first day of training he thanks the woman who changed his career. He tells new runners the story of his plateau as a kind of [[homage|L7-1385]] to her. [[Onwards|L7-1387]] from that day, he says, the question was no longer "How fast can I go?" but "What can I learn?"
zh: 肯·林十五歲開始跑步，頭兩年他的進步似乎永無止境。他每個月都在 5000 公尺比賽中縮短自己的成績，教練也在一本小筆記本裡仔細記錄著這些結果。他的進步軌跡一路向上，所以當他的成績在第三年停止進步時，他大吃一驚。他遇到了停滯期。
幾乎每位運動員都會碰到這道牆。研究身體如何運作的生理學專家解釋，身體會適應特定的訓練量。過了一陣子，同樣的努力不再帶來同樣的進步。研究人員談到一種均衡狀態：身體找到了平衡，認為沒有理由改變。要再進步，跑者必須提供新的挑戰，例如不同的距離、坡道，或是定期的休息週。肯的教練先請他重新做一次測驗，建立新的基準線。
她並沒有要求他更用力地跑。相反地，她請他改變心態。她請他不要再把每一次跑步都拿來與自己的最佳成績比較，而是把每一次跑步都當成學習的基準，而不是分數。在新的計畫、短期的肌力訓練以及更多睡眠之下，他以不同的方式拿出了全力。她也教他如何找到最理想的休息量。有些朋友覺得這種改變很奇怪，但他的教練是一位被低估的老師，她以前就看過這種情況。
幾個月內，他的成績又開始進步了。肯如今已是成年人，自己也成了學校教練，每年訓練的第一天，他都會感謝那位改變他職涯的女士。他向新的跑者講述自己遇到停滯期的故事，作為對她的一種致敬。他說，從那天起，問題不再是「我能跑多快？」而是「我能學到什麼？」

title: The Painter Who Collected Dreams
paragraphs: Elena Rossi was born in a small fishing town, where the sea, [[seemingly|L7-1229]] endless, was the constant [[backdrop|L7-1411]] of daily life. As a child she watched the men mend their nets and listened to the old women tell stories about sea monsters and lost ships. Years later, when she began to paint, her canvases looked like [[surreal|L7-1409]] dreams: clocks floating in the sky, fish swimming through living rooms, and houses growing from the backs of whales.

She did not become famous at once. She was twenty-five when she held her first [[exposition|L7-0379]], and only a handful of people came. But Elena was a [[prolific|L7-1400]] painter, and she continued to work every day, sometimes finishing a new canvas each week. She would [[commence|L7-0206]] each painting with a small drawing in a notebook, then enlarge it. Friends said that no two of her pictures were alike, because she hated to [[duplicate|L7-0329]] her own work. For years she was an [[underrated|L7-1393]] artist, and she told friends that she was content to wait.

Her breakthrough came when a museum asked her to design a large [[mosaic|L7-1415]] for its entrance hall. Elena used a [[multitude|L7-0654]] of tiny pieces of colored glass to create a giant eye that seemed to watch visitors as they walked in. The eye became an [[emblem|L7-1412]] of the museum and is now her most [[iconic|L7-1227]] work. Soon there was an [[influx|L7-1413]] of tourists who wanted to see it, and her paintings began to sell for large sums. In interviews she admitted that, while living in the city, old stories of the harbor filled her with [[nostalgia|L7-1378]].

Despite her success, Elena kept a quiet [[humility|L7-1404]]. When reporters asked how she explained her fame, she answered that a painter only borrows what the world has already given her. Critics tried to explain her paintings, mostly to no [[avail|L7-0078]], because she preferred to let viewers decide what they saw. Today, children in her hometown learn to paint in a small studio that carries her name, and above the door hangs a sign with her favorite advice: look at the ordinary until it becomes strange.
zh: 艾蓮娜·羅西出生在一個小漁村，那裡的海看似無邊無際，是日常生活中永遠的背景。小時候，她看漁夫們修補漁網，聽老婆婆們講述海怪與失蹤船隻的故事。多年後，當她開始作畫，她的畫布看起來就像超現實的夢境：時鐘漂浮在天空，魚兒游過客廳，房子從鯨魚的背上長出來。
她並沒有立刻成名。她二十五歲辦了第一場展覽，只有寥寥幾個人來。但艾蓮娜是一位多產的畫家，她每天持續創作，有時一週就完成一幅新畫。她總是先在筆記本裡畫一張小草圖作為開始，再把它放大。朋友們說，她沒有兩幅畫是相像的，因為她討厭複製自己的作品。多年來她是一位被低估的藝術家，她對朋友說自己很樂意等待。
她的突破來自一間博物館請她為入口大廳設計一幅大型馬賽克壁畫。艾蓮娜用了無數小片彩色玻璃，拼出一隻巨大的眼睛，彷彿在注視走進來的參觀者。這隻眼睛成了博物館的標誌，也是她現在最具代表性的作品。很快就湧入了許多想一睹它的觀光客，她的畫也開始以高價售出。在訪談中，她坦承，住在城市的那段時間，港口的老故事總讓她充滿鄉愁。
儘管成功了，艾蓮娜仍保持著一份安靜的謙遜。記者問她如何解釋自己的名氣時，她回答說，畫家只是借用世界已經給予她的東西。評論家試圖解釋她的畫，大多徒勞無功，因為她寧願讓觀眾自己決定看到了什麼。如今，她家鄉的孩子們在一間以她命名的小工作室裡學畫，門上掛著一塊寫著她最愛的建議的牌子：凝視平凡的事物，直到它變得陌生。

title: Messages in Secret
topic: 歷史・科技（密碼與加密）
paragraphs: For thousands of years, rulers and generals have depended on [[secrecy|L7-0905]] to protect their plans. A letter carried to an army might fall into enemy hands, so clever people invented ways to hide its meaning. One famous method is named after Julius Caesar, who is said to have moved every letter of his orders three places along the alphabet. Anyone who managed to [[intercept|L7-1419]] such a letter would see only nonsense.

Caesar's trick was simple to use, but it was also simple to break. Once a patient reader noticed that certain letters appeared again and again, the pattern gave the secret away. Over the centuries, codes became far more [[intricate|L7-0543]]. In the last century, some governments used machines with many wheels that could mix up a single sentence in billions of ways. Breaking those codes took teams of [[eminent|L7-1422]] mathematicians, and their work is often said to have helped end the Second World War earlier.

Today, most of us use [[encryption|L7-1423]] without ever noticing it. When you send a message on your phone or pay for a meal online, software turns your words into signs that only the person at the other end can read. You do not need to be a [[savvy|L7-1425]] computer expert to benefit, because the process happens quietly in the background. The growing [[connectivity|L7-1420]] of modern life, in which billions of devices are linked together, makes such protection more important than ever. A good [[algorithm|L7-1238]] can hide a message so well that even the fastest computers would need a great deal of time to crack it.

Still, no system is perfect, and people are often the weakest part. Banks, hospitals, and schools must [[adhere|L7-0012]] to strict [[regulatory|L7-1223]] requirements about how they store private data, and every [[stakeholder|L7-1426]], from managers to customers, shares some responsibility. Many users find it a [[hassle|L7-1418]] to remember a different password for each account, and typing long codes can feel [[repetitive|L7-1424]]. [[Nonetheless|L7-1236]], a few minutes of effort can prevent serious trouble. After all, the best lock in the world is useless if the key is left on the table.
zh: 數千年來，統治者與將領一直仰賴保密來保護他們的計畫。一封在戰場上傳遞的信可能落入敵人手中，所以聰明的人發明了隱藏訊息意義的方法。其中一個著名的方法以凱薩大帝命名，據說他會把命令中的每個字母沿著字母表往後移三格，於是 A 變成 D，B 變成 E。任何設法攔截到這種信件的人，只會看到一堆胡言亂語。
凱薩的把戲使用起來很簡單，但要破解也同樣簡單。只要有耐心的讀者注意到某些字母一再出現，這個規律就洩漏了祕密。幾個世紀以來，密碼變得複雜許多。到了二十世紀，有些政府使用裝有許多轉輪的機器，能以數十億種方式打亂一個句子。破解這些密碼需要由傑出數學家組成的團隊，一般認為他們的工作幫助第二次世界大戰提早結束。
今天，我們大多數人使用加密技術卻從未察覺。當你用手機傳訊息，或在網路上付餐費時，軟體會把你的文字變成一團雜亂，只有另一端的人才讀得懂。你不必是精通電腦的專家也能受益，因為整個過程是在背景中悄悄進行的。現代生活中連線能力日益增強，數十億個裝置彼此相連，使這種保護比以往更加重要。一個好的演算法能把訊息打亂得非常徹底，即使最快的電腦也需要極長的時間才能破解。
然而，沒有任何系統是完美的，而人往往是最脆弱的一環。銀行、醫院和學校都必須遵守嚴格的監管規定，規範它們如何儲存私人資料，而從經理到顧客，每一位利害關係人都分擔一部分責任。許多使用者覺得為每個帳號記一組不同的密碼很麻煩，輸入冗長的密碼也令人覺得單調重複。儘管如此，花幾分鐘的功夫就能避免嚴重的麻煩。畢竟，如果鑰匙就扔在桌上，世上最好的鎖也毫無用處。

title: The Long Way Home
paragraphs: Mia's trip home from her exchange year in Canada felt like an [[odyssey|L7-1435]]. First her train was late. Then her bag went missing, and finally her flight was delayed for three hours. By the time she found her seat, which was [[adjacent|L7-0013]] to a window, she was tired, hungry, and ready to sleep through the whole journey. [[Admittedly|L7-1443]], she was also a little nervous, because she had never crossed such a wide ocean by plane.

An hour after takeoff, the plane began to shake. Coffee cups rattled, and somewhere behind her a baby started to cry. Mia gripped the armrest while the captain's voice came through the speakers. She wanted a [[clarification|L7-1445]], but the message was short: the plane was passing through some [[turbulence|L7-1440]], and everyone should remain seated. Her heart raced and her hands turned cold. Mia knew that this was a normal [[physiological|L7-0742]] reaction to fear, but knowing it did not make her feel any better.

Then a flight attendant named Mr. Chen knelt beside her seat. He spoke with such calm and [[flair|L7-1451]] that Mia almost smiled. “Think of the sky as a road with a few bumps,” he said. “Rumors about flying accidents are [[rampant|L7-1437]] online, but flying is one of the safest ways to travel.” He also showed her how to breathe slowly: in for four seconds, out for six. It was a simple way to [[mitigate|L7-1453]] her fear, and within minutes her shoulders relaxed.

The [[ensuing|L7-1450]] hours passed quietly. When the plane finally landed at the busy [[hub|L7-1232]] near Taipei, Mr. Chen told her that a fastened seat belt is the best way to [[safeguard|L7-0889]] passengers during rough air. Mia thanked him and walked into the arrivals hall, where her family was waiting with a big sign. Her bag was still missing; [[nonetheless|L7-1236]], she hugged them tightly, her fear now [[seemingly|L7-1229]] a thing of the past. She had learned that fear, like turbulence, usually passes if you stay calm and keep breathing.
zh: 米亞從加拿大交換學生一年後返家的旅程，感覺就像一場漫長的冒險。先是她的火車誤點，接著行李不見了，最後她的班機又延誤了三個小時。等她找到靠窗的座位時，已經又累又餓，只想一路睡到終點。不可否認，她也有點緊張，因為她從沒搭飛機橫越過這麼寬廣的海洋。
起飛一小時後，飛機開始搖晃。咖啡杯嘎嘎作響，後方某處一個嬰兒哭了起來。機長的聲音從廣播傳來時，米亞緊緊抓住扶手。她想要更清楚的說明，但廣播很簡短：飛機正通過一些亂流，請大家留在座位上。她的心跳加速，雙手變得冰冷。米亞知道這是對恐懼的正常生理反應，但知道這點並沒有讓她好過一些。
這時，一位名叫陳先生的空服員在她座位旁蹲了下來。他說話的態度沉穩又帶點巧思，讓米亞差點笑了出來。「把天空想成一條有幾個小坑洞的路吧，」他說，「網路上關於飛行事故的謠言滿天飛，但飛行是最安全的旅行方式之一。」他還教她慢慢呼吸：吸氣四秒，吐氣六秒。這是一個減輕恐懼的簡單方法，幾分鐘內，她的肩膀就放鬆了。
接下來的幾個小時平靜地度過。飛機終於降落在台北附近那座繁忙的樞紐機場時，陳先生告訴她，繫好安全帶是在氣流不穩時保護乘客最好的方法。米亞向他道謝，走進入境大廳，家人正舉著一面大牌子在那裡等她。她的行李仍然沒找到；儘管如此，她還是緊緊擁抱了家人，恐懼似乎已成過去。她學到，恐懼就像亂流一樣，只要保持冷靜、持續呼吸，通常就會過去。

How Mia learned to stay calm during a rough flight

vocab.explain: 戴安全帽是「保護」頭部的最好方法，safeguard 可直接接受詞，故選 safeguard。replicate（複製）、retaliate（報復）不合；mitigate 是減輕影響，不接 your head。

title: The Town That Said No to Plastic
paragraphs: When the fishing town of Pine Bay announced that it would ban single-use plastic bags, many residents laughed. Some dismissed the idea as a [[hoax|L7-1456]] meant to attract news reporters, and others called it the [[quirky|L7-1457]] dream of a young mayor. Yet the [[rationale|L7-1458]] was clear. Local divers kept finding bags on the sea floor, and the marine [[fauna|L7-1468]] of the bay, from sea turtles to small fish, was in [[jeopardy|L7-1471]].

The first step was to teach people why plastic matters. Plastic never fully disappears; it breaks into tiny pieces that fish may swallow, and chemical [[residue|L7-1459]] can stay in the water for years. Volunteers visited every school and market, handing out cloth bags and explaining how each family could reduce its carbon [[footprint|L7-1469]]. At first, the results were [[mediocre|L7-1472]], and shop owners worried that customers would stay away. After a year, however, bag use had dropped sharply.

The change also had a deeper meaning. Like many small ports, Pine Bay had long suffered from a [[dependency|L7-1466]] on cheap imported goods, and its harbor was often full of garbage after storms. Now the town became a [[vanguard|L7-1461]] for others. Visitors came to study its methods, and shop owners began to sell local products instead. A community that had been [[stricken|L7-1474]] by falling income found new customers who wanted to buy from a clean and caring place. Teachers, businesses, and fishermen worked in [[tandem|L7-1460]], and each group learned from the others.

Many people now regard the day of the ban as a [[watershed|L7-1462]] in the town's history. Its story soon spread, and a [[nationwide|L7-0660]] campaign borrowed its ideas. The cloth bags cannot [[alleviate|L7-0036]] the pollution of the whole ocean, and the mayor is the first to admit it. Even so, the town's success is a [[testament|L7-1060]] to what a small community can do. Scientists who studied the bay reported encouraging [[findings|L7-1219]]: fewer bags on the sea floor and healthier fish. The town no longer looks [[seemingly|L7-1229]] foolish; it looks wise.
zh: 當漁村松灣宣布將禁用一次性塑膠袋時，許多居民都笑了。有些人把這個想法當成是為了吸引新聞記者的騙局，也有人說這是年輕市長古怪的夢想。然而，理由其實很明確。當地潛水員不斷在海底發現塑膠袋，海灣的海洋動物群，從海龜到小魚，都處於危險之中。
第一步是教大家為什麼塑膠很重要。塑膠永遠不會完全消失；它會碎成微小的碎片，魚可能會吞下去，而化學殘留物能在水中留存多年。志工拜訪了每一所學校和市場，發放布袋，並說明每個家庭如何能減少自己的碳足跡。起初成果平平，店家擔心顧客會不上門。但一年後，塑膠袋的使用量大幅下降。
這項改變也有更深的意義。像許多小港口一樣，松灣長期苦於依賴廉價的進口商品，風暴過後港口常堆滿垃圾。如今，這個小鎮成了其他地方的先鋒。訪客前來研究它的做法，店家也開始改賣在地產品。一個原本受收入下滑所苦的社區，找到了想向乾淨而用心的地方購買東西的新顧客。老師、商家和漁民攜手並進，每一方都從其他方學到東西。
許多人現在把實施禁令的那一天視為小鎮歷史上的轉折點。它的故事很快傳開，一項全國性的運動也借用了它的想法。布袋無法減輕整片海洋的汙染，市長自己就最先承認這一點。即便如此，小鎮的成功證明了一個小社區能做到什麼。研究這片海灣的科學家報告了令人鼓舞的結果：海底的塑膠袋變少了，魚也更健康。這個小鎮已不再顯得愚蠢；它看起來很有智慧。

title: Should Schools Ban Phones?
paragraphs: Few school debates are as heated as the one about smartphones. The [[proliferation|L7-1389]] of these devices over the past decade has changed how teenagers study, talk, and relax. Some schools have banned them completely, while others allow them in every class. Both sides have a [[rationale|L7-1458]] worth hearing, and a fair discussion should begin with their arguments.

Supporters of a ban point first to attention. A phone's [[perpetual|L7-0736]] stream of messages is a powerful distraction, and many students admit a [[craving|L7-1421]] to check the screen every few minutes. Teachers say that learning requires long periods of focus, and constant interruptions can be [[detrimental|L7-1428]] to it. There are also worries about the [[distortion|L7-1429]] of self-image caused by perfect-looking photographs online, and about a growing [[dependency|L7-1466]] on screens for comfort.

Opponents answer that a ban ignores the [[societal|L7-1408]] reality that phones are everywhere. A phone can be a dictionary, a calculator, and a camera for a science project. Students who learn to use these tools wisely become [[savvy|L7-1425]] adults, whereas a total ban gives them no practice. Some teachers believe that trusting students is a form of [[empowerment|L7-1449]], though it works only when the rules are clear rather than [[lax|L7-1452]].

Between these two positions lies a middle path. Schools can set clear times when phones must be put away, such as during tests, and allow them when a teacher plans an activity that needs them. Every [[stakeholder|L7-1426]], including students, parents, and teachers, should help to write the rules so that everyone understands why they exist. Such a plan may [[mitigate|L7-1453]] the worst problems without throwing away the benefits. It also lets the school change its approach when a rule does not work.

The long-term [[trajectory|L7-1392]] of technology suggests that phones are not going away. Perhaps the real question is not whether students should have them, but how we can teach students to control their phones rather than be controlled by them. A school that does this well will have done more than silence a device. It will have taught a skill that lasts for life.
zh: 很少有校園辯論像智慧型手機這個議題一樣火熱。過去十年間，這類裝置的激增改變了青少年讀書、交談和放鬆的方式。有些學校完全禁止，有些學校則允許在每堂課使用。兩方都有值得一聽的理由，一場公平的討論應該從他們的論點開始。
支持禁令的人首先指出專注力的問題。手機上源源不絕的訊息是強大的干擾，許多學生承認自己渴望每隔幾分鐘就看一次螢幕。老師說，學習需要長時間的專注，而不斷的打斷可能對學習有害。人們也擔心網路上看似完美的照片造成自我形象的扭曲，以及人們越來越依賴螢幕來尋求慰藉。
反對者回應說，禁令忽略了手機無所不在的社會現實。手機可以是字典、計算機，也可以是科學專題的相機。學會明智使用這些工具的學生，會成為精明的成年人，而全面禁止卻讓他們毫無練習的機會。有些老師認為信任學生是一種賦權，不過這只有在規則清楚、而非鬆散時才行得通。
在這兩種立場之間有一條中間路線。學校可以規定明確的時段必須收起手機，例如考試期間，並在老師設計需要手機的活動時允許使用。每一位利害關係人，包括學生、家長和老師，都應該參與制定規則，讓每個人都明白規則存在的原因。這樣的方案可能減輕最嚴重的問題，又不必丟掉好處。它也讓學校在某項規則行不通時能夠改變做法。
科技的長期發展軌跡顯示，手機不會消失。或許真正的問題不是學生該不該擁有手機，而是我們如何教學生控制手機，而不是被手機控制。一所把這件事做好的學校，做的就不只是讓一個裝置安靜下來而已。它教會的是一項受用一生的能力。

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Phones should be banned in all schools.
Phones should be allowed everywhere in school.
Both sides of the phone debate have reasons, and a balanced plan with shared rules may work best.
Teachers should use phones more than students.
questions.explain: 全文先列出支持與反對禁令的理由，再提出由各方共同制定規則的中間路線，故選 (C)。(A)(B) 都只代表其中一方，作者的態度是持平的。
questions.evidence: Between these two positions lies a middle path.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, what concern do supporters of a ban have?
options: Constant messages can distract students from learning.
Teachers do not know how to use phones.
Students have too much free time.
questions.explain: 第二段說支持禁令的人首先指出訊息不斷是強大的干擾，會妨礙專注，故選 (B)。
questions.evidence: A phone's perpetual stream of messages is a powerful distraction, and many students admit a craving to check the screen every few minutes.

questions.stem: The word "lax" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 句子說信任學生只有在規則清楚、而不是 lax 時才行得通，lax 與 clear 相對，意思是「鬆散、不嚴格」，故選 (B)。(A) 與原意相反。
questions.evidence: Some teachers believe that trusting students is a form of empowerment, though it works only when the rules are clear rather than lax.

questions.stem: In the last paragraph, "it" in "It will have taught a skill that lasts for life" refers to ______.
options: a school that teaches students to control their phones
questions.explain: 前一句主詞是 A school that does this well，所以 It 指的是「把這件事做好的學校」，也就是教學生控制手機的學校，故選 (B)。(C) 前句說學校做的「不只是讓裝置安靜下來」。
questions.evidence: It will have taught a skill that lasts for life.

vocab.stem: The ______ of streaming services in recent years has given viewers more choices than ever before.
vocab.explain: 近年串流服務「激增」，讓觀眾有更多選擇，故選 proliferation。lax（鬆散的）、flair（天分）、hoax（騙局）都不能搭配 The ... of streaming services。

vocab.stem: Students who rely too much on their phones may develop a ______ on screens that is hard to break.
vocab.explain: 對螢幕產生難以擺脫的「依賴」，故選 dependency。footprint（足跡）、residue（殘渣）、truce（休戰）都不合語意。

title: Grandma Lin's Garden
paragraphs: Lin Mei-Hua never planned to become famous, but by the age of seventy-five, her small garden had made her well known across her neighborhood. She was born in a farming village, where she learned the names of plants before she could read. Her [[ancestry|L7-1482]] was full of farmers, and she often said that soil ran through her family like a river. When she moved to the city after marriage, she missed the countryside so much that she began planting herbs in old tin cans on her balcony.

As the years passed, the cans became boxes, and the boxes became a roof garden. Grandma Lin became an [[avid|L7-1484]] gardener who got up before the sun every morning. She grew [[perennial|L7-0732]] flowers that returned each spring, as well as vegetables that her neighbors loved. Her cooking was never [[bland|L7-0108]]; she added fresh herbs to every dish. Her [[mantra|L7-1491]] was simple: “Water a little every day, and worry a little less.”

Gardening was not always easy. Weeds were a constant [[nuisance|L7-0682]], and snails ate her young lettuce. One summer, a typhoon caused [[havoc|L7-1489]] on the roof, breaking pots and tearing plants out of the soil. Only a few green [[remnants|L7-1480]] were left. Instead of giving up, Grandma Lin gathered the seeds that had [[dispersed|L7-1487]] across the roof and started again. Her [[resilient|L7-1494]] and [[seemingly|L7-1229]] endless energy encouraged the neighbors, who came to help her plant again. Because she never used harmful chemicals, she believed her vegetables were free of [[toxins|L7-1495]] and good for everyone's [[wellbeing|L7-1475]].

Today, the roof garden is shared by more than twenty families and has become a [[hub|L7-1232]] of the neighborhood. It stands as a [[testament|L7-1060]] to her patience. Children learn how seeds grow, and older residents enjoy a quiet place to talk. Grandma Lin says that a garden teaches [[decency|L7-1486]], because you must care for something before it can give anything back. Last spring, a young student asked her how to [[embark|L7-0348]] on a garden of his own. She smiled, handed him a small pot, and said, “Start with one seed. The rest will follow.”
zh: 林美華從未打算出名，但到了七十五歲，她的小花園已讓她在整個社區聞名。她出生在一個農村，在還不會讀書之前就先學會了植物的名字。她的祖先都是農夫，她常說泥土像一條河一樣流過她的家族。婚後搬到城市，她太想念鄉下，於是開始把香草種在陽台上的舊鐵罐裡。
隨著歲月流逝，鐵罐變成了木箱，木箱又變成了一座屋頂花園。林奶奶成了熱衷的園丁，每天清晨日出前就起床。她種了每年春天都會回來的多年生花卉，還有鄰居們很喜愛的蔬菜。她煮的菜從不乏味；每道菜裡她都加入新鮮香草。她的座右銘很簡單：「每天澆一點水，少擔心一點。」
園藝並不總是容易。雜草是永遠的麻煩，蝸牛還吃掉她剛長出的生菜苗。有一年夏天，颱風在屋頂上造成大破壞，打破了花盆，把植物連根拔離了土壤。只剩下少數綠色的殘存物。林奶奶沒有放棄，而是把散落在屋頂各處的種子收集起來，重新開始。她堅韌又彷彿用不完的精力鼓舞了鄰居，大家都來幫她重建。因為她從不使用有害的化學藥劑，她相信自己種的蔬菜不含毒素，對每個人的身心健康都有益。
如今，這座屋頂花園由二十多戶人家共享，已成為社區的核心。它證明了她的耐心。孩子們在這裡學習種子如何生長，年長的居民則享有一處安靜聊天的地方。林奶奶說，花園教人正派體貼，因為你必須先照顧一樣東西，它才能回報你。去年春天，一個年輕學生問她該如何開始自己的花園。她微笑著遞給他一個小花盆，說：「從一顆種子開始，其餘的自然會跟上來。」

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How a typhoon destroyed a neighborhood
How a woman's love of gardening grew into a shared community space
Why vegetables are better than flowers
How to cook with fresh herbs
questions.explain: 文章從林奶奶在陽台種香草，寫到屋頂花園，再到二十多戶共享，主旨是她的園藝如何成為社區共享的空間，故選 (B)。(A) 颱風只是第三段的一個事件。
questions.evidence: Today, the roof garden is shared by more than twenty families and has become a hub of the neighborhood.

questions.stem: What did Grandma Lin do after the typhoon damaged her garden?
options: She moved back to the village.
She collected the scattered seeds and began again.
She sold the rooftop to her neighbors.
questions.explain: 第三段說她把散落在屋頂的種子收集起來重新開始，故選 (B)。(A) 文中只提到她婚後搬到城市，並沒有說颱風後搬回村子。
questions.evidence: Instead of giving up, Grandma Lin gathered the seeds that had dispersed across the roof and started again.

questions.stem: The word "perennial" in paragraph 2 describes flowers that ______.
questions.explain: 句中說這些花 returned each spring，可知 perennial 是「多年生的」，會年年回來，故選 (C)。(B) 開花一季的是一年生植物，與 returned each spring 矛盾。
questions.evidence: She grew perennial flowers that returned each spring, as well as vegetables that her neighbors loved.

questions.stem: What is Grandma Lin's attitude toward gardening?
options: She finds it too tiring to continue.
She sees it only as a way to earn money.
She believes it must be done alone.
She sees it as patient care that teaches good values.
questions.explain: 她說花園教人正派體貼，因為你必須先付出照顧，它才會回報；顯示她把園藝視為需要耐心照顧、能培養品德的事，故選 (D)。(B) 文中從未提到賺錢。
questions.evidence: Grandma Lin says that a garden teaches decency, because you must care for something before it can give anything back.

vocab.stem: Her strong and ______ nature helped her recover quickly after the long illness.
vocab.explain: 長期生病後能很快恢復，說明她的個性「有韌性」，故選 resilient。bland（乏味的）、avid（熱衷的）、obligated（有義務的）都不能說明復原快。

vocab.stem: The old castle is now only a few ______ of walls standing in an empty field.
vocab.explain: 古堡如今只剩幾段牆「殘跡」立在空地上，故選 remnants。mantras（口號）、toxins（毒素）、nuisances（麻煩）都不合語意。

title: When Day Turns to Night
paragraphs: On rare days, the Moon passes exactly between the Earth and the Sun, and for a few minutes the middle of the day turns into night. This is a total solar eclipse, one of the most [[noteworthy|L7-1504]] events in nature. The reason we can see it at all is a remarkable accident of size and distance. The Sun is about four hundred times wider than the Moon, but it is also about four hundred times farther away. As a result, their apparent sizes nearly [[coincide|L7-0200]] in our sky, and the Moon can just cover the Sun's bright disk.

Ancient peoples watched eclipses with fear, because without [[astronomical|L7-1496]] knowledge they could not predict them. Some believed that a monster was eating the Sun. Today, scientists can calculate the exact time of an eclipse years ahead, and museums use a [[simulated|L7-1507]] sky to show how the Moon's shadow will move. Yet the shadow is small, so it crosses the surface of the Earth along a narrow path. People on this [[terrestrial|L7-1057]] globe often have to travel far to stand inside it.

During the few minutes of full darkness, the air grows cool and birds fall silent. The sky takes on a strange [[hue|L7-1501]], like a deep blue evening, and a pale glow called the corona appears around the dark disk. Observers report [[myriad|L7-1503]] small effects, from shaking shadows on the ground to the cheers of strangers. Researchers value these minutes, because the Sun's outer layers are usually hidden by its bright light. [[Findings|L7-1219]] from past eclipses have taught us a great deal about the Sun's atmosphere. The [[magnitude|L7-0613]] of the event is hard to describe in words.

Safety, however, requires a [[pragmatic|L7-1505]] attitude. Looking straight at the Sun can harm the eyes, and a single [[lapse|L7-1502]] in care is enough to cause damage. Viewers should use special eclipse glasses and follow the advice of experts. Many communities now [[commemorate|L7-0205]] great eclipses with festivals, and those who plan well can enjoy an [[optimal|L7-1247]] view. [[Nonetheless|L7-1236]], the best advice is simple: watch carefully, and never trust ordinary dark glasses.
zh: 在罕見的日子裡，月亮會正好從地球與太陽之間經過，於是白天正中央有幾分鐘變成了黑夜。這就是日全食，是自然界中最值得注意的事件之一。我們之所以能看到它，是因為大小與距離上一個了不起的巧合。太陽的寬度約為月亮的四百倍，但它也比月亮遠約四百倍。結果，兩者在我們天空中的視大小幾乎一致，月亮剛好能遮住太陽明亮的圓盤。
古代的人們帶著恐懼看待日食，因為沒有天文知識，他們無法預測它。有些人相信是怪獸在吞食太陽。如今，科學家能提前數年算出日食的確切時間，博物館也用模擬的星空來展示月影將如何移動。然而月影很小，所以它只沿著一條狹窄的路徑掠過地球表面。生活在這個地球上的人，常常得長途跋涉才能站進那道影子裡。
在日全食的那幾分鐘裡，空氣變涼，鳥兒也安靜下來。天空呈現一種奇異的色調，像深藍色的傍晚，一圈稱為日冕的淡淡光暈出現在黑色圓盤周圍。觀測者回報了無數細微的現象，從地面上晃動的影子，到陌生人的歡呼。研究人員很重視這幾分鐘，因為太陽的外層通常被它明亮的光芒所掩蓋。過去日食所得的研究結果，讓我們對太陽的大氣層了解甚多。這個事件的震撼程度很難用言語形容。
然而，安全需要務實的態度。直視太陽可能傷害眼睛，只要一次疏忽就足以造成損傷。觀賞者應使用專用的日食眼鏡，並遵循專家的建議。許多社區現在會以節慶來紀念重大的日食，而計畫周全的人就能享有最佳的視野。儘管如此，最好的建議很簡單：小心觀看，千萬別相信一般的深色眼鏡。

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How to make special glasses for children
Why the Moon is farther away than the Sun
How the Sun gives light to the Earth
How and why a total solar eclipse happens, and how to watch it safely
questions.explain: 全文先解釋日全食為何出現（大小與距離的巧合），再描述觀測與研究，最後提醒安全觀看，故選 (D)。(B) 與文中太陽比月亮遠約四百倍的說法相反。
questions.evidence: This is a total solar eclipse, one of the most noteworthy events in nature.

questions.stem: Why can the Moon just cover the Sun during an eclipse?
options: The Moon is about as big as the Sun.
The Sun is about four hundred times wider but also about four hundred times farther away.
The Moon moves faster than the Earth.
The Sun becomes smaller during an eclipse.
questions.explain: 第一段說太陽比月亮寬約四百倍，卻也遠約四百倍，所以視大小幾乎相同，月亮剛好能遮住太陽，故選 (B)。(A) 月亮其實比太陽小很多。
questions.evidence: The Sun is about four hundred times wider than the Moon, but it is also about four hundred times farther away.

questions.stem: The word "hue" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 天空像深藍色的傍晚，是在形容天空的「色調」，故選 (B) color。
questions.evidence: The sky takes on a strange hue, like a deep blue evening, and a pale glow called the corona appears around the dark disk.

questions.stem: What does the writer suggest about looking at an eclipse?
options: People should never watch an eclipse.
Careful preparation lets people enjoy it without harming their eyes.
Eclipses are dangerous only in the evening.
questions.explain: 作者提醒要用專用日食眼鏡並聽從專家建議，暗示做好準備就能安全欣賞，故選 (C)。(A) 作者明說千萬別相信一般的深色眼鏡。
questions.evidence: Viewers should use special eclipse glasses and follow the advice of experts.

vocab.stem: A single ______ in attention on the highway can lead to a serious accident.
vocab.explain: 在高速公路上一次注意力的「失誤」就可能導致嚴重事故，故選 lapse。hue（色調）、tariff（關稅）、placebo（安慰劑）都不合語意。

vocab.stem: The town will hold a parade to ______ the founding of its first school one hundred years ago.
vocab.explain: 遊行是為了「紀念」建校一百週年，故選 commemorate。confiscate（沒收）、revoke（撤銷）不合；coincide 是「同時發生」，不接受詞。

title: One Cup, Many Countries
paragraphs: Imagine a morning cup of coffee in Taipei. The beans may have grown on a mountain in Ethiopia or Colombia, been dried by a small farmer, packed in a busy port [[hub|L7-1232]], and sold to a roaster across the sea. This long chain is one example of [[globalization|L7-1532]], the process by which the economies of different countries become tied together through trade. For many customers it brings choice, since a single shop can offer flavors from a dozen countries.

But the same chain makes coffee prices very sensitive. A frost or a drought in one country can change the price in every other country, and these [[fluctuations|L7-1523]] hurt farmers most, because they cannot easily plan their income. One bad harvest can set off a [[cascade|L7-1516]] of troubles: lower income, fewer workers hired, and children leaving school. Price swings that once seemed an [[anomaly|L7-1514]] are now seen as a normal part of the trade.

The environment is affected too. Traditional farms that grow coffee under tall trees protect [[biodiversity|L7-1515]], giving homes to birds and insects. When farmers cut down the trees to grow more coffee in the sun, wildlife loses its home. Some customers now pay a higher [[tier|L7-1225]] of price for coffee grown in the shade, hoping to link fair income with a healthy forest. Yet the true story of a cup is [[elusive|L7-1521]]: it is hard for a customer to know how the beans were grown, and information is often [[diluted|L7-1520]] on the long road from farm to shop.

Opinions differ. Some experts say that trade creates opportunity, while others warn that small farmers receive too small a share. Some large companies have worked to [[consolidate|L7-0223]] their supply chains, which makes them easier to manage but harder for small farms to join. There has also been a [[convergence|L7-1529]] of tastes, and from Taipei to Sao Paulo many people now [[crave|L7-1518]] the same kinds of drinks. Many farmers say their work has an [[intrinsic|L7-0544]] value that no price can measure. [[Nonetheless|L7-1236]], what seems like a simple pleasure carries a long chain of people, and its fairness is worth thinking about.
zh: 想像一杯台北的早晨咖啡。咖啡豆可能生長在衣索比亞或哥倫比亞的山上，由小農曬乾，在繁忙的港口樞紐裝箱，再賣給海另一頭的烘豆商。這條漫長的鏈條，是全球化的一個例子，也就是各國經濟透過貿易而相互連結的過程。對許多顧客而言，它帶來了選擇，因為一家店就能提供來自十幾個國家的風味。
但同一條鏈條也讓咖啡價格異常敏感。某一國的霜害或乾旱，就能改變各地的價格，而這些波動對農民傷害最大，因為他們很難規劃自己的收入。一次歉收可能引發一連串的麻煩：收入減少、雇用的工人變少、孩子輟學。過去看似反常的價格劇烈波動，如今被視為這項貿易的正常現象。
環境也受到影響。在高大樹木下種植咖啡的傳統農場，能保護生物多樣性，為鳥類和昆蟲提供棲身之處。當農民砍掉樹木，改在陽光下種更多咖啡時，野生動物就失去了家園。有些買家現在願意以更高一級的價格購買遮蔭栽培的咖啡，希望把公平的收入與健康的森林連結起來。然而，一杯咖啡背後真正的故事難以捉摸：顧客很難得知咖啡豆是怎麼種出來的，而資訊在從農場到商店的漫長路途中常被沖淡。
意見不一。有些專家說貿易創造了機會，也有人警告小農分到的份額太少。一些大型買家努力整合他們的供應鏈，使其更容易管理，卻也讓小農更難加入。口味也出現了趨同，從台北到聖保羅，許多人現在渴望同樣種類的飲料。許多農民說，他們的工作有著任何價格都無法完全衡量的內在價值。儘管如此，看似簡單的享受，背後卻連著一條由許多人組成的長鏈，而這條鏈是否公平，值得我們思考。

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: A cup of coffee connects many people and places, and global trade brings both benefits and problems.
Coffee tastes best when it is grown in Ethiopia.
Farmers should stop growing coffee under trees.

title: Behind the Museum Walls
paragraphs: Visitors to a museum see beautiful objects on quiet walls, but they rarely meet the person who chose them. This person is the [[curator|L7-1427]], and her job is to [[curate|L7-1554]] an exhibition: to select, arrange, and explain works so that a story appears. For a show on the history of photography, Ms. Huang once spent two years choosing about one hundred pictures from thousands. Her goal was to show the [[pinnacle|L7-1549]] of the art, from the earliest blurred images to the most [[groundbreaking|L7-1533]] experiments.

Choosing the pictures is only part of the task. The museum's owners [[entrusted|L7-1543]] her with a fragile collection, so every photograph must be handled with great care. She also faces a heavy [[workload|L7-1552]]: writing labels, arranging loans from other museums, and working with designers, electricians, and guards. Even a small [[glitch|L7-1546]], such as a wrong light, can spoil a picture. For this reason, every plan includes a [[contingency|L7-1553]] for the unexpected, such as a late delivery or a broken frame.

Ms. Huang is [[candid|L7-1542]] about how hard it is to judge success. Counting visitors gives numbers, but a [[qualitative|L7-0801]] view matters as well. She reads the comments left by the public and listens when people explain how a picture changed their mood. One old photograph of a street market made an elderly visitor [[nostalgic|L7-1548]], and he spent an hour telling stories of his childhood. She says such moments are a real [[boon|L7-1541]] to someone who works behind the scenes. Not all feedback is kind, but she tries to [[heed|L7-0480]] criticism too, because a good curator keeps learning.

On opening night, the galleries fill with music and [[festivities|L7-1545]], and Ms. Huang stands quietly at the back. [[Arguably|L7-1255]], this is the best moment of her job: watching an idea she carried in her head for years become a place where strangers stop, look, and think. “A museum,” she says, “is a conversation between the past and the people who visit it. My work is just to help the conversation begin.” [[Nonetheless|L7-1236]], by the next morning she is already planning the next show.
zh: 參觀博物館的人看到的是安靜牆面上的美麗物件，但很少遇見挑選它們的人。這個人就是策展人，她的工作是策劃一場展覽：挑選、安排並解說作品，讓一個故事浮現出來。為了一場攝影史展，黃女士曾花兩年時間，從數千張照片中挑出約一百張。她的目標是呈現這門藝術的巔峰，從最早模糊的影像到最具開創性的實驗。
挑選照片只是工作的一部分。博物館的所有人把一批脆弱的收藏託付給她，所以每一張照片都必須小心處理。她還面對繁重的工作量：撰寫說明牌、安排向其他博物館借展，並與設計師、電工和警衛合作。即使是一個小故障，例如燈光不對，也可能毀掉一幅作品。因此，每項計畫都包含針對意外狀況的應變措施，例如延遲送達或相框破裂。
黃女士坦率地談到要判斷展覽是否成功有多困難。計算參觀人數能得到數字，但質性的觀點同樣重要。她閱讀民眾留下的意見，也傾聽人們說明一張照片如何改變了他們的心情。一張老舊的街頭市集照片讓一位年長的參觀者懷起舊來，他花了一個小時講述童年的故事。她說，這樣的時刻對幕後工作者而言是真正的福音。並非所有意見都很友善，但她也努力聽取批評，因為好的策展人會不斷學習。
開幕之夜，展廳裡充滿音樂與慶祝活動，黃女士安靜地站在後方。可以說，這是她工作中最棒的時刻：看著一個她在腦中醞釀多年的想法，變成陌生人會駐足、凝視、思考的地方。「博物館，」她說，「是過去與來訪者之間的一場對話。我的工作只是幫助這場對話開始。」儘管如此，到了隔天早上，她已經在規劃下一場展覽了。

title: Building for the Next Earthquake
paragraphs: Taiwan sits where two great plates of the Earth's crust push against each other, so earthquakes are part of life on the island. In September 1999, a powerful earthquake of high [[magnitude|L7-0613]] struck central Taiwan. In its [[aftermath|L7-0024]], scenes of [[rubble|L7-1561]] and broken roads shocked the whole country. Many of the buildings that fell had not been strong enough to resist the shaking, and the [[bleak|L7-0110]] days that followed taught engineers a hard lesson.

Since then, the rules for new buildings have become far more [[stringent|L7-1569]]. A tall building must now be [[compliant|L7-1571]] with standards that require strong frames, flexible joints, and careful use of materials. Before construction begins, engineers often [[simulate|L7-0941]] earthquakes on computers, testing how a design behaves as the ground moves. Some also use large shaking tables, where a model of a building is shaken to judge the [[viability|L7-1562]] of the plan. Builders who ignore the rules may face [[sanctions|L7-1243]], and the new standards apply [[nationwide|L7-0660]].

Not everyone agrees on how much safety is enough. [[Proponents|L7-1560]] of the strictest rules argue that every extra cost may save lives, while others note that money is limited. Many cities also contain old buildings whose strength shows signs of [[deterioration|L7-0294]] after decades of rain and wind. An expert's [[appraisal|L7-0056]] of such a building can decide whether it should be strengthened or replaced. Scientists also study every possible [[precursor|L7-1559]] of a quake, but so far no one can say exactly when the next one will come.

Because the future cannot be predicted, preparation matters. Today the island is [[poised|L7-0757]] to continue improving its buildings, but ordinary families have a part to play as well. Even [[mundane|L7-1567]] habits, such as fixing heavy furniture to the wall and keeping a bag of water and food near the door, can protect a household. In earthquake country, safety is not one great act but a thousand small, sensible ones.
zh: 台灣位於地殼兩大板塊相互擠壓的地方，所以地震是島上生活的一部分。1999 年 9 月，一場規模很大的強震襲擊了台灣中部。災後，滿是瓦礫與毀損道路的景象震驚了全國。許多倒塌的建築物強度不足以抵抗搖晃，而隨後那些黯淡的日子，給工程師上了一堂艱難的課。
自那以後，新建築的規範變得嚴格許多。高樓現在必須符合要求堅固結構、有彈性的接合處，以及謹慎使用建材的標準。開工之前，工程師經常在電腦上模擬地震，測試設計在地面移動時的表現。有些還使用大型震動台，把建築模型搖晃一番，以評估計畫的可行性。無視規定的建商可能受到制裁，而新標準適用於全國。
並非每個人都同意怎樣才算夠安全。最嚴格規範的支持者主張，每多花一分錢都可能救人一命，也有人指出經費有限。許多城市裡還有舊建築，經過數十年的風吹雨打，結構強度已出現惡化的跡象。專家對這類建築的評估，能決定它該被補強還是拆除重建。科學家也研究每一個可能的地震前兆，但到目前為止，還沒有人能說出下一次地震確切何時到來。
由於未來無法預測，準備工作就顯得重要。如今這座島已準備好持續改善它的建築，但一般家庭也有自己的一份責任。即使是平凡的習慣，例如把沉重的家具固定在牆上、在門邊放一袋水和食物，也能保護一個家庭。在地震頻繁的地方，安全不是一個偉大的行動，而是上千個細小而明智的舉動。

title: The Doctor of the Mountain Township
paragraphs: Dr. Chang Yu-Ting was born in a small mountain township where the nearest hospital was a three-hour bus ride away. Her [[upbringing|L7-1156]] was modest: her father repaired bicycles and her mother grew vegetables. When Yu-Ting was ten, her grandfather became ill during a typhoon, and the road to town was blocked for two days. The family's [[bleak|L7-0110]] wait left a lasting mark on her. She decided that someday she would become a doctor and return home.

She kept her promise. After medical school, she stood at a [[crossroads|L7-1511]]: city hospitals offered her a high salary, but the township had no doctor at all. Dr. Chang chose the township. Her first clinic was a single room with an old desk, and the days were often [[mundane|L7-1567]], filled with colds, sore backs, and children's cuts. Yet she soon noticed a pattern. Many older villagers suffered from long-term illnesses and could not travel to town, so she began visiting them on foot. Her [[pragmatic|L7-1505]] mind told her that medicine was useless if people could not reach it.

Her work grew into a [[grassroots|L7-1499]] movement. She trained local volunteers to check blood pressure and to recognize warning signs. In a community where [[hereditary|L7-1500]] heart disease was common, early checks made a real difference. Visitors called her a [[charismatic|L7-1509]] leader because she could persuade shy farmers to attend health talks, but she replied that she simply listened. Over time, the clinic's [[accessibility|L7-1476]] improved: a small bus brought patients from distant villages, and a telephone line let families ask questions at any hour.

One winter, an outbreak of flu produced a [[frenzy|L7-1556]] of fear in the township. The volunteers she had trained stayed calm and spread clear advice, and the crisis passed without serious harm. Local records show that life [[expectancy|L7-1498]] has gone up noticeably since her arrival.

Today, Dr. Chang is seventy and still works two days a week. Each autumn, the township holds a small festival to [[commemorate|L7-0205]] the day her clinic opened. [[Notwithstanding|L7-0680]] her fame, she remains humble. “I am only one link in a long chain,” she says. Her story is [[noteworthy|L7-1504]] not because of a single heroic act, but because of years of patient work that [[empowered|L7-1478]] an entire community to care for its own health.
zh: 張育婷醫師出生在一個小山區鄉鎮，離最近的醫院要搭三個小時的公車。她的成長環境很簡樸：父親修理腳踏車，母親種菜。育婷十歲那年，祖父在颱風期間生了病，通往鎮上的路被封了兩天。一家人那段黯淡的等待，在她心中留下了深刻的印記。她決定有一天要成為醫生，然後回到家鄉。
她信守了承諾。醫學院畢業後，她站在人生的十字路口：城市的醫院提供她高薪，但這個鄉鎮完全沒有醫生。張醫師選擇了鄉鎮。她的第一間診所只是一個房間，裡面有一張舊書桌，日子往往平凡乏味，充滿了感冒、背痛和孩子的傷口。然而她很快注意到一個規律。許多年長的村民患有長期疾病，卻無法前往鎮上，於是她開始徒步去探訪他們。她務實的頭腦告訴她，如果人們到不了醫療，醫學就毫無用處。
她的工作逐漸發展成一場草根運動。她訓練當地志工量血壓、辨認警訊。在遺傳性心臟病很常見的社區裡，早期檢查產生了真正的差別。訪客稱她為有魅力的領袖，因為她能說服害羞的農民來參加健康講座，但她回答說，自己只是在傾聽。隨著時間過去，診所的可及性提高了：一輛小巴士把遠處村落的病人載來，一條電話專線讓家屬可以在任何時刻發問。
有一年冬天，一場流感疫情在鄉鎮裡引發了一陣恐慌。她訓練的志工保持冷靜，傳遞清楚的建議，危機在沒有造成嚴重傷害下度過了。當地紀錄顯示，自她來到之後，平均壽命明顯上升。
如今，張醫師已七十歲，每週仍工作兩天。每年秋天，鄉鎮都會舉辦一場小型慶典，紀念她診所開張的那一天。儘管名聲在外，她仍然謙虛。「我只是一條長鏈上的一個環節，」她說。她的故事值得注意，不是因為某一次英勇的行為，而是因為多年耐心的努力，讓整個社區有能力照顧自己的健康。

title: The Actress Who Invented
paragraphs: In the 1930s and 1940s, Hedy Lamarr was one of the most [[iconic|L7-1227]] film stars in Hollywood. Audiences saw a beautiful face on the screen, but behind that [[facade|L7-1576]] was a curious and [[agile|L7-1585]] mind. Born in Vienna in 1914, she was [[endowed|L7-1591]] with great charm, yet she was never content to be only a pretty face. Friends said she was often [[immersed|L7-1593]] in her drawings, designing small inventions with pencil and paper, and her interests [[encompassed|L7-1590]] art, music, and science.

When the Second World War began, Lamarr wanted to be [[proactive|L7-1594]] rather than wait. She learned that radio-controlled torpedoes could be blocked, or jammed, by an enemy who found their signal. Together with a composer named George Antheil, she designed a system in which the signal jumped quickly from one radio channel to another, so an enemy could not follow it. The idea was inspired by the way a piano roll controls many notes in a fixed pattern. Their invention was granted a patent in 1942.

The military did not adopt the invention at that time. Perhaps the navy was [[constrained|L7-1587]] by its older equipment, or perhaps officials could not imagine that an actress had solved an engineering problem. The idea lay [[dormant|L7-1588]] for years. Only later did engineers find that similar ideas could make wireless communication more reliable. Today, wireless technology is [[ubiquitous|L7-1583]], found in phones, cars, and homes, and Lamarr's work is often described as an early step in that direction.

Late in life, Lamarr finally received awards for her work. Her story shows a [[disparity|L7-1575]] between how the world sees a person and who that person really is. Some people were [[misguided|L7-1579]] in thinking that a famous actress could not also be an inventor. [[Arguably|L7-1255]], her greatest [[testament|L7-1060]] is the example she leaves behind. Young people who hope to [[emulate|L7-1589]] her are reminded that great ideas can come from anyone, and that curiosity matters more than appearance.
zh: 在 1930 與 1940 年代，海蒂·拉瑪是好萊塢最具代表性的電影明星之一。觀眾在銀幕上看到的是一張美麗的臉，但在那層門面之後，是一顆好奇而靈活的頭腦。她 1914 年生於維也納，天生具有迷人的魅力，卻從不滿足於只當一個漂亮的臉孔。朋友說她常沉浸在畫稿之中，用鉛筆和紙設計小發明，她的興趣涵蓋了藝術、音樂和科學。
第二次世界大戰爆發時，拉瑪想要主動出力，而不是坐著等待。她得知無線電遙控的魚雷可能被發現訊號的敵人阻擾，也就是遭到干擾。她與一位名叫喬治·安塞爾的作曲家合作，設計出一種系統，讓訊號在不同的無線電頻道之間快速跳動，使敵人無法跟上。這個構想的靈感來自自動鋼琴的琴卷如何以固定模式控制許多音符。他們的發明在 1942 年獲得專利。
當時軍方並未採用這項發明。也許是海軍受限於較老舊的設備，也許是官員無法想像一位女演員解決了工程問題。這個構想沉睡了多年。直到後來，工程師才發現類似的想法能讓無線通訊更可靠。今天，無線科技無所不在，存在於手機、汽車和家庭中，而拉瑪的成果常被形容為朝那個方向邁出的早期一步。
晚年時，拉瑪終於因她的成就獲得獎項。她的故事顯示出，世人眼中的一個人與那個人真實的樣貌之間存在落差。有些人誤以為一位著名的女演員不可能同時是發明家，這種想法是錯誤的。可以說，她留下的典範就是她最好的見證。想要效法她的年輕人會被提醒：偉大的點子可以出自任何人，而好奇心比外表更重要。
