title: A Guide for Newcomers
paragraphs: Dear new students, welcome to Hill High School. We know that being a [[newcomer|L7-1609]] can feel [[daunting|L7-1601]]. The campus is large, the schedule is long, and every face seems unfamiliar. This guide, written by last year's student council, is meant to make your first month easier. The library is the [[hub|L7-1232]] of student life, and our office is [[adjacent|L7-0013]] to the gym, so you will always know where to find us.

On your first morning, you will [[traverse|L7-1115]] the long hall between the gate and your classroom, so please leave home a little early. Take time to learn the school's [[etiquette|L7-1605]]. Greet teachers politely, wait quietly in the lunch line, and keep the library silent. These habits are the [[cornerstone|L7-1614]] of a friendly campus, and they cost nothing. You will also learn our safety [[protocol|L7-1226]] during the first week, including what to do in an earthquake drill.

Making friends takes time. Your [[cohort|L7-1599]] of about three hundred students will share lessons, lunch, and trips, and many clubs welcome new members. Choose only [[reputable|L7-1596]] groups that are approved by the school, and ask a teacher if you are unsure. If you ever have [[grievances|L7-1617]], such as a problem with a classmate or a rule that seems unfair, tell someone you trust. You may also use the box outside the office, which protects your [[anonymity|L7-1612]]: no one will ask for your name, and every note receives a reply.

Finally, remember that mistakes are normal. A small [[deviation|L7-1602]] from your plan, such as arriving late or losing a book, is not a disaster. Try not to [[evade|L7-1615]] a problem by hiding it. It is [[futile|L7-1616]] to hope that trouble will go away by itself, and teachers are always happier to help early than late. We wish you a joyful year, and we offer our [[heartfelt|L7-1606]] welcome. With best wishes, the Student Council.
zh: 親愛的新同學，歡迎來到山丘高中。我們知道，身為新來的人可能會讓人感到畏懼。校園很大、課表很長，每張臉孔都很陌生。這本手冊由去年的學生會撰寫，目的是讓你的第一個月輕鬆一些。圖書館是學生生活的中心，我們的辦公室緊鄰體育館，所以你永遠知道去哪裡找我們。
在第一天早上，你需要走過校門與教室之間那條長長的走廊，所以請稍微早點出門。請花點時間認識學校的禮儀。要有禮貌地向老師問好、安靜地排隊領午餐，並保持圖書館的安靜。這些習慣是友善校園的基石，而且不花一毛錢。第一週你也會學到我們的安全規範，包括地震演習時該怎麼做。
交朋友需要時間。你們這一屆約三百名學生會一起上課、吃午餐、參加旅行，許多社團也歡迎新成員。請只選擇經學校核准、信譽良好的團體，如果不確定，就去問老師。如果你有任何不滿，例如和同學之間的問題，或是覺得不公平的規定，請告訴你信任的人。你也可以使用辦公室外的信箱，它能保護你的匿名性：沒有人會要你留名字，而每一張紙條都會得到回覆。
最後，請記住犯錯是正常的。與計畫稍有偏差，例如遲到或弄丟一本書，並不是什麼災難。請不要用藏起問題的方式來逃避它。希望麻煩會自己消失是徒勞的，而老師總是樂於早點幫忙，而不是晚點。祝你有個快樂的一年，也獻上我們由衷的歡迎。學生會 敬上。

questions.explain: 校園很大、課表很長、每張臉都陌生，所以新來的人會覺得「令人畏懼」，故選 (D)。

vocab.explain: 護士說的話「由衷的」，讓家屬感到安慰，故選 heartfelt。futile（徒勞的）、ominous（不祥的）、daunting（令人畏懼的）都不會讓人安慰。

title: Your First Ten Kilometers
paragraphs: Many people dream of running a long race but give up before they begin. One common reason is [[inhibition|L7-0524]]: they fear that other people will laugh at their slow pace. Another is the [[delusion|L7-1638]] that runners are simply born that way. In fact, [[stamina|L7-1622]] is built, not given, and almost anyone can develop it with a patient plan.

Coaches recommend an [[incremental|L7-1628]] approach. A beginner might alternate between walking for two minutes and running for one, then slowly raise the running time each week. This [[intermittent|L7-0542]] pattern protects the body while it adapts. The gain from a single session may seem [[negligible|L7-0663]], and no one becomes fit in a day. After two months, however, the changes add up. Progress is rarely [[linear|L7-0589]]. Because of the [[variability|L7-1632]] of sleep, weather, and mood, some days feel easy and others feel hard, and experts say you should expect both.

Advice about running is [[pervasive|L7-1618]], from videos to books, and the opinions are often [[divergent|L7-1625]]. Some coaches prefer long, slow runs, while others favor short, fast ones. A beginner should choose one plan from an [[exemplary|L7-1626]] source and stay with it long enough to see results. Doing too much too soon can have painful [[repercussions|L7-1621]], such as sore knees that last for weeks. Rest days are [[decidedly|L7-1637]] part of training, not a sign of weakness.

Regular running also seems to [[confer|L7-1624]] benefits beyond the body. Research [[findings|L7-1219]] suggest that exercise can improve mood and sleep, and many runners enjoy the quiet time to think. [[Nonetheless|L7-1236]], the most important step is the first one. Put on comfortable shoes, choose a park or riverside path, and begin. Ten kilometers may sound far, but, as the saying goes, every long road is made of short steps. Your [[optimal|L7-1247]] pace will change as you improve, so do not worry about speed at the start.
zh: 許多人夢想跑一場長距離的比賽，卻在開始之前就放棄了。一個常見的原因是顧忌：他們擔心別人會笑自己跑得慢。另一個原因是一種錯覺，以為跑者天生就是那樣。事實上，耐力是練出來的，不是天生給的，幾乎任何人都能用一份耐心的計畫培養出來。
教練建議採取漸進的方式。初學者可以交替走路兩分鐘、跑步一分鐘，然後每週慢慢增加跑步的時間。這種間歇式的模式能在身體適應的同時保護它。單次練習的收穫可能微不足道，沒有人能在一天內變得健壯。然而兩個月後，這些改變就累積起來了。進步很少是直線上升的。由於睡眠、天氣和心情的變動，有些日子感覺輕鬆，有些日子則感覺辛苦，專家說你應該預期這兩種情況都會發生。
關於跑步的建議無所不在，從影片到書籍都有，而且意見往往分歧。有些教練偏好長而慢的跑法，有些則主張短而快。初學者應該從一個值得效法的來源選擇一份計畫，並堅持夠久，才能看到成果。一次做得太多太快，可能產生痛苦的後果，例如持續數週的膝蓋痠痛。休息日明顯是訓練的一部分，不是軟弱的表現。
規律的跑步似乎也能帶來身體以外的益處。研究結果顯示，運動可以改善心情和睡眠，許多跑者也享受那段安靜思考的時光。儘管如此，最重要的一步是第一步。穿上舒適的鞋子，選一個公園或河濱步道，然後開始。十公里聽起來或許很遠，但俗話說，每一條長路都是由短短的步伐築成的。隨著進步，你最合適的步速會改變，所以一開始不要擔心速度。

questions.stem: What is the main message of the passage?
options: Only young people can run long distances.
Running is too dangerous for beginners.
A beginner can build stamina through patient, gradual steps.
The fastest runners are born, not made.
questions.explain: 全文說明耐力是練出來的，初學者可用漸進計畫慢慢累積，故選 (C)。(D) 與第一段「耐力是練出來的」相反。
questions.evidence: In fact, stamina is built, not given, and almost anyone can develop it with a patient plan.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, what can happen if a beginner does too much too soon?
options: The person may have problems such as sore knees for weeks.
The person will no longer need rest days.
The person will quickly lose interest in sleeping.
questions.explain: 第三段說做得太多太快可能有痛苦的後果，例如持續數週的膝蓋痠痛，故選 (B)。(C) 文中說休息日是訓練的一部分。
questions.evidence: Doing too much too soon can have painful repercussions, such as sore knees that last for weeks.

questions.stem: The word "negligible" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 後面說沒有人能在一天內變得健壯，所以單次練習的收穫「微不足道」，故選 (A)。
questions.evidence: The gain from a single session may seem negligible, and no one becomes fit in a day.

questions.stem: What does the writer suggest about speed at the beginning?
options: It is the most important thing.
It matters less than starting and keeping going.
It should be measured every day.
It is decided by sleep alone.
questions.explain: 最後說步速會隨進步而改變，一開始不要擔心速度，可見開始並持續比速度重要，故選 (B)。
questions.evidence: Your optimal pace will change as you improve, so do not worry about speed at the start.

vocab.stem: The weather in the mountains is full of ______, so a morning of sun can turn into an afternoon of storms.
vocab.explain: 山區天氣多「變化」，早晨晴天下午就可能暴風雨，故選 variability。inhibition（拘束）、retribution（報應）、utopia（烏托邦）都不合語意。

vocab.stem: A good coach knows that it is better to improve in small, ______ steps than to try to change everything at once.
vocab.explain: 小幅、一步一步「漸進」的改善優於一次改變一切，故選 incremental。obnoxious（討人厭的）、arid（乾旱的）、tainted（受污染的）都不能形容 steps。

title: The Lamp in the Window
paragraphs: Ken had spent his whole life in a big, [[cosmopolitan|L7-0247]] city, so the mountain village felt like another world. The houses were [[sparse|L7-1655]], the road was a narrow path of mud, and rain had been falling for hours. By the time he reached the last house, he was cold, wet, and almost [[wretched|L7-1209]]. A dim light burned in the window of a [[rustic|L7-1646]] inn, and he knocked on the door with a shaking hand.

The innkeeper, Mr. Wu, had a calm [[temperament|L7-1050]] and a [[subdued|L7-1647]] voice. The small room he showed Ken was [[immaculate|L7-1643]], and a warm fire burned in the stove. To Ken it felt like a [[haven|L7-0472]]. Dinner was served on an [[improvised|L7-1644]] table made from a wooden box and a board. Ken had been ready to pay a [[hefty|L7-1653]] price for anything warm, but Mr. Wu asked for only a few coins.

While they ate, Mr. Wu told an [[anecdote|L7-1648]] about the inn. Most guests, he said, were [[transient|L7-1113]]; they stayed for one night and left before dawn, yet he remembered every face. Ken was [[baffled|L7-1650]]. Why would a man choose such a lonely life? Before he could ask, someone knocked loudly at the door. An [[agitated|L7-1657]] young woman stood outside, holding a lamp. Her small dog had run into the dark, she said, and she could not find it.

Without a word, Mr. Wu took his coat, and Ken followed, [[seemingly|L7-1229]] forgetting how tired he was. They searched the paths for an hour, calling softly. At last, a thin bark came from under a bridge [[adjacent|L7-0013]] to the stream. When the woman held her dog again, she was [[ecstatic|L7-0335]] and thanked them again and again. Back at the inn, Ken finally understood. Mr. Wu's life looked lonely to a stranger. [[Nonetheless|L7-1236]], it was full of small kindnesses, and each of them began with a lamp left burning in a window.
zh: 肯這輩子都住在一座國際化的大城市裡，所以這座山間小村落讓他覺得像是另一個世界。房子稀稀落落，路是一條泥濘的窄徑，雨已經下了好幾個小時。當他走到最後一間屋子時，已經又冷又濕，幾乎狼狽不堪。一間質樸的小旅店窗口亮著一盞微弱的燈，他用發抖的手敲了門。
旅店老闆吳先生性情平和，聲音低柔。他領肯去的小房間一塵不染，爐子裡燃著溫暖的火。對肯來說，這裡簡直像一座避風港。晚餐擺在一張臨時湊成的桌子上，是用一個木箱和一塊木板做的。肯本來已準備為任何熱的東西付一大筆錢，但吳先生只收了幾枚銅板。
他們吃飯時，吳先生講了一則關於這家旅店的趣聞。他說大部分客人都只是過客；他們住一晚，天亮前就離開，但他記得每一張臉。肯感到困惑不解。為什麼有人會選擇這樣孤單的生活？在他開口問之前，有人大聲敲門。一位焦急不安的年輕女子站在外面，手裡提著一盞燈。她說她的小狗跑進了黑暗裡，她找不到牠。
吳先生二話不說拿起外套，肯跟了上去，似乎忘了自己有多累。他們沿著小路找了一個小時，輕聲呼喚。終於，從緊鄰溪流的一座橋下傳來一聲微弱的狗叫。當女子再度抱起她的小狗時，她欣喜若狂，一再向他們道謝。回到旅店後，肯終於明白了。吳先生的生活在陌生人眼裡看來孤單。儘管如此，它卻充滿了小小的善意，而每一份善意，都始於窗口那盞一直點亮的燈。

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
options: A boy who loses his way in the city
A traveler who learns that a quiet innkeeper's life is full of kindness
A dog that is trained by a farmer
How an inn was built from wooden boxes
questions.explain: 故事寫旅人在山中旅店，看到老闆為尋找走失的小狗而幫忙，最終明白老闆的生活充滿善意，故選 (B)。
questions.evidence: Mr. Wu's life looked lonely to a stranger.

questions.stem: Why was the young woman agitated?
options: She had lost her way in the village.
She wanted to rent a room.
Her small dog had run into the dark and she could not find it.
Mr. Wu had refused to open the door.

title: The Tulip Craze
paragraphs: In the 1630s, a strange [[craze|L7-1659]] swept through the Dutch Republic. Merchants, farmers, and even servants began to [[vie|L7-1669]] for a single flower: the tulip. The flower had reached Europe from the Ottoman lands in the late 1500s, and the rarest bulbs, marked with bright stripes, soon became the most [[coveted|L7-1676]] objects in the country. Today we know a virus caused the stripes, but then nobody knew why.

At first, the trade was quite ordinary. Growers sold bulbs in autumn, and customers planted them for spring. But as demand grew, traders found an [[ingenious|L7-0520]] way to [[capitalize|L7-1673]] on it. Instead of waiting for the flowers, they signed papers promising to buy bulbs that were still under the ground. One paper could change hands many times in a single winter, and each customer hoped to sell it again at a higher price without ever seeing a flower. A more [[prudent|L7-1595]] market might have kept such trade small, but this one was anything but careful.

Prices began to [[escalate|L7-0372]] quickly. Each new record price [[ignited|L7-0504]] fresh excitement, and more people rushed in. Dealers who were [[ostensibly|L7-1663]] honest sometimes sold common bulbs as rare ones, and a customer who found a [[phony|L7-1665]] bulb could do little about it. A few writers were [[outspoken|L7-1664]] critics who called the whole business foolish, yet their warnings seemed only to attract more curious people.

In February 1637, the market collapsed. Customers stopped coming to the sales, and the paper promises lost most of their value. Historians still debate how harmful the crash really was. Few records survive, so it is hard to [[pinpoint|L7-1666]] how many people took part or how much money was lost. Even so, the story is still told as a warning. It shows how easily a confident seller with [[charisma|L7-1674]] and a reputation for business [[prowess|L7-1667]] can persuade others that prices will rise forever. The flower has become [[ubiquitous|L7-1583]] in Dutch fields, and the [[disparity|L7-1575]] between its price then and now reminds us that value depends on what people believe.
zh: 1630 年代，一股奇特的狂熱席捲了荷蘭共和國。商人、農夫，甚至僕人，都開始爭奪一種花：鬱金香。這種花在十六世紀末從鄂圖曼的土地傳到歐洲，而帶有鮮豔條紋的稀有球莖，很快成為全國最令人夢寐以求的東西。如今我們知道條紋是病毒造成的，但當時沒有人明白原因。
起初，這門買賣相當平常。種植者在秋天賣球莖，顧客把它們種下，等待春天開花。但隨著需求增加，交易商想出了一個巧妙的方法來利用這股需求。他們不等花開，而是簽下文件，承諾購買仍在地底下的球莖。一張文件可以在一個冬天裡轉手許多次，每個顧客都希望以更高的價格再賣出去，卻從未見過一朵花。比較謹慎的市場也許會讓這類交易維持小規模，但這個市場一點也不小心。
價格迅速攀升。每一次新的天價都點燃了新的興奮，更多人湧入市場。表面上誠實的商人有時會把普通球莖當成稀有品種賣出，而買到假球莖的顧客往往無計可施。少數作家直言批評，說這整門生意很愚蠢，但他們的警告似乎只吸引了更多好奇的人。

1637 年 2 月，市場崩盤。顧客不再出現在拍賣會上，那些文件承諾也失去了大部分價值。歷史學家至今仍在爭論這次崩盤究竟有多嚴重。留存的紀錄很少，因此很難確切指出有多少人參與，或損失了多少錢。即便如此，這個故事仍被當作警惕的例子流傳。它顯示，一位有魅力、又以商業本領聞名的賣家，多麼容易說服別人相信價格會永遠上漲。如今鬱金香在荷蘭的田野上隨處可見，而它當年與現在的價差，提醒我們價值取決於人們的信念。

title: Should Websites Ask for Real Names?
paragraphs: Few features of the internet are as [[ubiquitous|L7-1583]] as the nickname. On most websites, people can post without showing their real names. Yet the same freedom can also be used to hurt others. Should websites require real names? There are strong arguments on both sides.

Defenders of [[anonymity|L7-1612]] point out that it protects people who have real [[grievances|L7-1617]] but fear punishment. A worker who wants to report unsafe conditions may stay silent if his boss could find him. A [[newcomer|L7-1609]] to a serious illness, or a teenager who feels alone, may speak more honestly to strangers than to friends. In such cases, a nickname can be the [[cornerstone|L7-1614]] of honest talk, because it lets people be heard without being judged for who they are. Some of the most [[substantive|L7-1597]] conversations online begin when people feel safe.

Critics answer that the same shield also protects bullies. Behind a fake name, a person may say cruel things that he would never say face to face, and the [[culprit|L7-1600]] is almost impossible to [[pinpoint|L7-1666]]. A small quarrel can [[escalate|L7-0372]] into a wave of insults within hours. Good [[etiquette|L7-1605]], they say, depends on knowing that others can see who we are. Some users even create a [[phony|L7-1665]] identity to trick others, and honest users end up paying the price. Many critics of anonymity are [[outspoken|L7-1664]] about this.

Perhaps the answer lies between the two extremes. Websites can be [[proactive|L7-1594]]: they can remove cruel messages quickly, give users simple ways to report abuse, and allow nicknames while keeping private records that could be shown to the police if a real crime occurs. It would also be [[prudent|L7-1595]] to avoid easy solutions. Forcing everyone to use a real name might silence the very people who most need to speak, and a determined bully can still [[evade|L7-1615]] the rule by borrowing someone else's name. A blanket ban would be [[futile|L7-1616]] as well as unfair.

In the end, the rules should depend on the purpose of the site. A [[heartfelt|L7-1606]] support group for patients needs different rules from a news site. What matters is that both the freedom to speak and the duty to treat others fairly are protected, and that we keep asking which of the two needs more care in each place.
zh: 很少有網路功能像暱稱一樣無所不在。在大多數網站上，人們可以不顯示真實姓名就發文。然而，同樣的自由也可能被用來傷害他人。網站應該要求使用真名嗎？兩邊都有強而有力的論點。
匿名的捍衛者指出，它保護了那些有真正不滿、卻害怕受罰的人。想舉報不安全工作環境的員工，如果老闆能找出他，可能就會保持沉默。剛得知自己罹患重病的新手，或是覺得孤單的青少年，對陌生人說的話可能比對朋友更誠實。在這種情況下，暱稱可以是誠實對話的基石，因為它讓人不必因為自己是誰而被評斷，就能被聽見。網路上一些最有實質內容的對話，就是在人們覺得安全時展開的。
批評者則回應說，同一面盾牌也保護了霸凌者。躲在假名後面，一個人可能說出當面絕對不會說的惡毒話，而肇事者幾乎無法被找出來。一場小爭吵可能在幾小時內演變成一波侮辱。他們說，良好的禮儀有賴於知道別人看得到我們是誰。有些使用者甚至製造假身分來欺騙別人，結果誠實的使用者要付出代價。許多反對匿名的人對此直言不諱。
也許答案在兩個極端之間。網站可以主動出擊：快速刪除惡意訊息，提供使用者簡單的檢舉管道，並允許使用暱稱，同時保留私人紀錄，萬一發生真正的犯罪，這些紀錄可以交給警方。同樣謹慎的做法是避免簡單的解決方案。強迫每個人使用真名，可能讓最需要發聲的人噤聲，而且意志堅定的霸凌者仍然可以借用別人的名字來規避規定。全面禁止既不公平，也是徒勞的。
最後，規則應該取決於網站的目的。給病患的真誠互助團體，需要的規則和新聞網站不同。重要的是，說話的自由和公平對待他人的責任都能受到保護，並且我們要不斷追問：在每個地方，這兩者中哪一個需要更多關照。

title: I Knew It All Along
paragraphs: After a football match ends, many fans say the same thing: "I knew they would lose." After an exam, a student may say that the hard question was [[foreseeable|L7-1684]] all along. Psychologists call this feeling [[hindsight|L7-1685]] bias. Once we know how something turned out, the result seems obvious, and we forget how little we were sure of before it happened.

In the 1970s, Baruch Fischhoff asked people to guess what would happen in some coming events. After the events took place, he asked the same people to remember what they had guessed. Many of them recalled being closer to the truth than they really were. Their first answers were mere [[conjecture|L7-1658]], but later they spoke as if they had known.

This habit can cause real trouble. Looking back at a disaster, people may call the warning signs [[undeniable|L7-1694]] and the leaders who missed them fools. They may call a failed plan pure [[folly|L7-1683]], or even say that its goals were [[ludicrous|L7-1686]] from the start. A fierce quarrel may [[ensue|L7-1681]] when a manager blames a team for something nobody could have seen, and small mistakes may receive a [[disproportionate|L7-1678]] share of the blame. But the people who made the plan did not know the ending. If we judge them by what we know now, we are unfair. Worse, when a similar crisis begins to [[loom|L7-0601]] again, we may feel far too sure of ourselves.

How can we guard against it? Writing down predictions before an event is one of the best habits, because a written note cannot be changed by a changing memory. Another useful step is to ask, "What else could have happened?" Some people become [[adept|L7-1696]] at this and even keep a decision diary. Staying [[vigilant|L7-1695]] is hard, because the mind is an [[erratic|L7-1682]] judge of the past. Still, a clear record can act as a [[deterrent|L7-1697]] against fooling our own minds. Being [[prudent|L7-1595]] does not mean always being right. It means remembering how uncertain the past once was, and it may help us to [[evade|L7-1615]] the trap of thinking that everything was easy to see.
zh: 足球賽結束後，許多球迷會說同一句話：「我早就知道他們會輸。」考試之後，學生可能會說那道難題其實早就可以預料。心理學家把這種感覺稱為「後見之明偏誤」。一旦知道事情的結果，結果就顯得理所當然，我們也忘了事情發生前自己其實沒有多少把握。
1970 年代，費施霍夫（Baruch Fischhoff）請人們猜測一些即將發生的事件會如何發展，事件發生後，再請同一批人回想自己當時猜了什麼。許多人記得自己猜得比實際上更接近真相。他們最初的答案只是臆測，但事後卻說得好像自己早就知道。
這個習慣可能造成真正的麻煩。回顧一場災難時，人們可能會說警訊明明無可否認，而沒注意到的領導者都是傻瓜。他們可能把失敗的計畫說成純粹的愚行，甚至說它的目標從一開始就很荒謬。當主管為了誰也無法預見的事責怪團隊時，可能會引發激烈爭吵，小錯也可能承擔過大比例的責任。但制定計畫的人並不知道結局。如果我們用現在所知的一切去評判他們，並不公平。更糟的是，當類似的危機再度逼近時，我們可能會過度自信。
我們該如何防範呢？在事件發生前寫下預測，是最好的習慣之一，因為白紙黑字不會隨著記憶的改變而改變。另一個有用的做法是問自己：「還有什麼可能發生？」有些人對此相當擅長，甚至會寫決策日記。保持警覺並不容易，因為心智對過去的判斷是變化不定的。不過，清楚的紀錄可以成為阻止我們自欺的嚇阻力。謹慎並不是指永遠正確，而是記得過去曾經多麼不確定，這也可能幫助我們避開「覺得一切都很容易看穿」的陷阱。

title: The Doctor Who Washed His Hands
paragraphs: In 1847, a young doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis worked in a [[hectic|L7-1703]] hospital in Vienna. The hospital had two clinics for mothers. In the first, doctors and students helped women give birth; in the second, trained nurses did. Strangely, far more mothers died in the first clinic. Women begged to be sent to the second one, and the difference seemed almost [[uncanny|L7-1712]].

Semmelweis tested one explanation after another, but none fit. Then a close colleague died after being cut by a knife during an examination of a dead body, and his illness looked like that of the sick mothers. Semmelweis realized that doctors who came straight from such work might carry something invisible on their hands. Today we call such things [[pathogens|L7-1709]], but nobody knew of them yet. His solution was [[ingenious|L7-0520]] in its simplicity: everyone had to wash with a strong cleaning liquid before touching a patient. Deaths in the first clinic fell sharply.

One might expect the doctors to be [[receptive|L7-1715]] to such good news. Instead, many were insulted by the idea that their hands could be unclean. Critics called his explanation [[simplistic|L7-1717]] because it did not fit the science of the day. Semmelweis grew [[outspoken|L7-1664]] and angry, which only made matters worse. He left Vienna, and when he died in 1865, his work seemed headed for [[oblivion|L7-1714]].

Only later did scientists such as Louis Pasteur [[bolster|L7-0119]] the germ theory that explained his results. Today, clean hands and [[pristine|L7-1711]] tools are the rule in every hospital, and doctors sometimes [[invoke|L7-1706]] his name when they speak of patient safety. His simple habit has saved [[untold|L7-1718]] lives. His story is sad, but it is also an [[uplifting|L7-1719]] reminder of an important rule of science: evidence should take [[precedence|L7-1710]] over pride. Hand-washing is now [[ubiquitous|L7-1583]], and we owe it to a man who was not listened to.
zh: 1847 年，一位名叫塞麥爾維斯（Ignaz Semmelweis）的年輕醫生在維也納一家忙亂的醫院工作。這家醫院有兩個產婦診所。在第一個診所，由醫生和學生協助婦女生產；在第二個診所，則由受過訓練的護理人員接生。奇怪的是，第一個診所死亡的母親要多得多。婦女們苦苦哀求要被送去第二個診所，這種差別幾乎令人覺得詭異。
塞麥爾維斯一個接一個地檢驗各種解釋，卻都不符合。後來，他的一位好友在一次檢驗遺體時被刀割傷，之後死去，病情和生病的母親們很像。塞麥爾維斯意識到，剛做完那種工作就直接過來的醫生，手上可能帶著看不見的東西。今天我們把這類東西稱為病原體，但當時沒有人知道它們。他的解決辦法簡單而巧妙：每個人在接觸病人之前，都必須用強力的清潔液洗手。第一個診所的死亡人數大幅下降。
人們或許以為醫生們會樂於接受這個好消息。相反地，許多人覺得自己的手可能不乾淨這種想法是種冒犯。批評者說他的解釋過於簡化，因為它不符合當時的科學。塞麥爾維斯變得直言不諱又憤怒，結果只讓情況更糟。他離開了維也納，1865 年去世時，他的研究似乎註定要被遺忘。
直到後來，巴斯德（Louis Pasteur）等科學家才以細菌致病說來支持並解釋他的成果。如今，乾淨的雙手與潔淨的器械是每家醫院的規矩，醫生談到病人安全時，有時也會提起他的名字。他這個簡單的習慣拯救了無數的生命。他的故事令人感傷，卻也是一個振奮人心的提醒，點出科學的重要原則：證據應該優先於自尊。如今洗手隨處可見，而我們要把這一切歸功於一位沒有人聽他說話的人。

title: Restoring Willow Pond
paragraphs: Report summary. Ten years ago, Willow Pond on the [[periphery|L7-1737]] of our town was a sad sight. The water was green and [[stagnant|L7-1732]], trash lay along the banks, and the smell kept visitors away. Experts said the pond was badly [[degraded|L7-1723]]. A small [[remnant|L7-0841]] of the old plants was all that was left of the green land that once surrounded it.

The project began when a group of [[valiant|L7-1161]] volunteers refused to give up on the pond. Their first plan met resistance. Some neighbors felt that spending money on a pond was a waste, and a few were [[entrenched|L7-1726]] in the habit of dumping garbage there. Others made the matter [[contentious|L7-1722]] by arguing that the land should be sold for a parking lot. In the end, the city agreed to a trial and asked the volunteers to [[dismantle|L7-1724]] the old concrete wall that stopped the water from moving.

Results arrived slowly. The team opened a small stream so that water could flow, planted local grasses, and removed the trash. After one year, university students found no [[conclusive|L7-1734]] proof that the pond was healthier, though the water looked clearer. By the third year, however, the signs were clear: fish returned, dragonflies flew over the surface, and the pond saw a [[resurgence|L7-1730]] of frogs. A later water test showed a few [[irregularities|L7-1727]], but the team was able to pinpoint the cause, a broken pipe, and it has since been fixed.

We [[commend|L7-1733]] the volunteers for their patience. The work was [[constrained|L7-1587]] by a small budget, yet it succeeded because the team was [[proactive|L7-1594]] and stayed [[vigilant|L7-1695]] about problems. The project also shows that a pond is not an island. Once the water recovered, birds and insects began to [[disperse|L7-0308]] widely and carry life to nearby gardens. We see this success as a [[prelude|L7-1739]] to a larger plan, and we recommend that the city support the restoration of two more ponds.
zh: 報告摘要。十年前，位於本鎮邊緣的柳樹池塘是個令人難過的景象。水面發綠而且不流動，岸邊堆滿垃圾，臭味讓遊客不敢靠近。專家說這座池塘嚴重退化。曾經環繞池塘的綠地，只剩下一小片舊有植物的殘跡。
這項計畫始於一群勇敢的志工，他們不肯放棄這座池塘。他們的第一個方案遇到了阻力。有些鄰居覺得把錢花在池塘上是浪費，少數人則已習慣根深蒂固地往那裡亂丟垃圾。還有人讓這件事更具爭議，主張這塊地應該賣掉蓋停車場。最後，市府同意試辦，並請志工拆掉那道阻止水流動的舊水泥牆。
成果來得很慢。團隊打開一條小溪讓水能流動，種下當地的草類，並清除垃圾。一年後，大學生的研究並未找到確切證據證明池塘變得更健康，不過水看起來清澈許多。然而到了第三年，跡象就很明顯了：魚回來了，蜻蜓在水面上飛舞，青蛙也再度大量出現。後來的水質檢測發現了幾處異常，但團隊能夠找出原因，是一條破裂的水管，目前已修復。
我們讚揚志工們的耐心。這項工作受限於微薄的預算，卻能成功，是因為團隊主動積極，並對問題保持警覺。這項計畫也顯示，池塘並不是一座孤島。水質恢復之後，鳥類和昆蟲開始四處散布，把生命帶到附近的庭園。我們認為這次成功是更大計畫的序曲，並建議市府支持再修復兩座池塘。

title: The Night the Lights Went Out
paragraphs: Mia and Ben were an unlikely [[duo|L7-1755]]. She wrote the [[lyrics|L7-1743]] for their songs, and he played the guitar. When the school [[dean|L7-1742]] announced a music night, they signed up at once. Their only problem was the equipment. The school's speakers were poor, so Ben came up with an [[ingenious|L7-0520]] idea: he borrowed his grandfather's [[vintage|L7-1174]] amplifier, a heavy machine that used glass tubes called [[valves|L7-1162]].

On the afternoon of the show, Mia stood on the stage and checked the [[setup|L7-1754]] one more time. She had painted the [[artwork|L7-1751]] on the poster herself, and the hall was already filling with students and parents. Her [[charisma|L7-1674]] was clear as soon as she stepped up to the microphone, and Ben's [[prowess|L7-1667]] on the guitar made the first song sound easy. The audience clapped, and the [[arc|L7-0061]] of the evening seemed to be rising.

Then, halfway through the second song, every light in the building went out. A storm had damaged the power [[grid|L7-1749]] across the district. The hall fell silent, and Mia's heart sank. In the dark, Ben whispered, "Don't worry. We still have the [[backup|L7-1746]]." He pulled a small battery speaker out of his bag, and a friend held up a phone light. The old amplifier could not work without power, so Ben played softly and Mia sang without a microphone.

It was not the show they had planned, but the room was so quiet that every word of the song could be heard. When they finished, nobody clapped at first. Then the whole hall broke into cheers. Later, the dean said the pair had played like [[aces|L7-0007]], and Ben joked that they had only been testing the [[beta|L7-1747]] version of their act. Mia laughed. She knew the real lesson: a good plan is useful, but a calm mind is what keeps the music going.
zh: 米婭和班是一對不太可能搭檔的二人組。她負責為他們的歌寫歌詞，他則彈吉他。學校的教務長宣布要辦音樂之夜時，他們立刻報了名。唯一的問題是設備。學校的喇叭很差，所以班想出一個巧妙的主意：借祖父那台老式擴大機，一台笨重的機器，用的是叫做真空管（valve）的玻璃管。
演出當天下午，米婭站在舞台上，又檢查了一次設備配置。海報上的圖畫是她自己畫的，禮堂裡已經漸漸坐滿了學生和家長。她一走上麥克風前，魅力便展露無遺，而班高超的吉他功夫讓第一首歌聽起來毫不費力。觀眾鼓掌，整個夜晚的情勢似乎正在攀升。
接著，在第二首歌進行到一半時，整棟大樓的燈全都熄了。一場風暴損壞了整個地區的電網。禮堂陷入寂靜，米婭的心沉了下去。在黑暗中，班低聲說：「別擔心，我們還有備案。」他從包包裡拿出一個小型電池喇叭，一位朋友舉起手機燈光。老擴大機沒有電就無法運作，於是班輕輕地彈，米婭不用麥克風地唱。
這不是他們原先計畫的演出，但禮堂安靜得連歌裡的每個字都聽得見。唱完時，一開始沒有人鼓掌。接著整個禮堂爆出歡呼。後來，教務長說這對搭檔表現得像頂尖高手，班則開玩笑說，他們只是在測試節目的測試版。米婭笑了。她明白真正的教訓：好的計畫很有用，但冷靜的心才能讓音樂繼續下去。

title: From Wax to Vinyl
paragraphs: In 1877, Thomas Edison built a machine that could record a human voice. It used a sheet of metal wrapped around a [[cylinder|L7-0271]], and later models used wax. Soon, such cylinders became a popular way to keep music. The early recordings were purely [[acoustic|L7-0008]]: singers had to shout into a large horn, because there was no electricity to make sounds louder.

By the early 1900s, flat discs began to replace cylinders, and by the middle of the century the [[vinyl|L7-1175]] record had arrived. A needle followed a thin line cut into the surface and turned tiny bumps into sound. Records stayed popular for decades, and a singer whose album sold a huge number of copies could win a [[platinum|L7-1760]] award. Each new format seemed like a [[sequel|L7-1765]] to the one before.

Then technology moved on. Tapes, then compact discs, and finally files stored on [[silicon|L7-0938]] chips made music easier to carry. Today a phone needs only a small [[voltage|L7-1180]] to play thousands of songs, and music has become [[ubiquitous|L7-1583]]. Sales of records fell sharply, and many shops closed. For libraries, the change was not simple. Their [[holdings|L7-1763]] of old records needed new homes, and music that was never copied could be lost.

Yet the story did not end there. In the 2000s, vinyl made a surprising [[comeback|L7-0203]]. Sales have risen for a [[streak|L7-0995]] of years, led by young listeners who want something they can hold. Collectors say the warm sound and the large cover art make a record feel like an event, and old copies of famous albums have become [[coveted|L7-1676]] items. Whether the trend will last is hard to say, and some people fear it is only another short [[craze|L7-1659]]. But the pleasure these listeners find is [[undeniable|L7-1694]], and it shows that new tools do not always push out old ones. The [[finale|L7-1758]] of this story has not been written yet.
zh: 1877 年，愛迪生造出一台能錄下人聲的機器。它使用一張包在圓筒上的金屬片，後來的型號則改用蠟。不久，這種圓筒就成了保存音樂的流行方式。早期的錄音純粹是聲學錄音：歌手必須對著一個大喇叭喊，因為當時沒有電可以讓聲音變大。
到了 1900 年代初，平面唱片開始取代圓筒，到了本世紀中葉，黑膠唱片問世了。唱針沿著刻在表面上的細紋前進，把微小的起伏變成聲音。唱片流行了幾十年，專輯賣出大量張數的歌手可以獲得白金獎。每一種新格式似乎都是前一種的續集。
後來科技繼續前進。錄音帶、光碟，最後是儲存在矽晶片上的檔案，讓音樂更容易攜帶。如今一支手機只需要很小的電壓，就能播放數千首歌，音樂也變得無所不在。唱片的銷量大幅下滑，許多店鋪關門。對圖書館來說，這個變化並不簡單。他們收藏的舊唱片需要新的安置處，而從未被複製的音樂可能就此消失。
然而故事並未就此結束。2000 年代，黑膠出人意料地捲土重來。銷量連續多年成長，帶動的是想要擁有可以握在手中之物的年輕聽眾。收藏者說，溫暖的音色和大幅的封面藝術讓一張唱片像是一場盛事，而知名專輯的老版本也成了令人夢寐以求的收藏品。這股趨勢能否持續很難說，有些人擔心它只是另一陣短暫的風潮。但這些聽眾所感受到的樂趣是無可否認的，它也顯示新工具並不一定會把舊工具擠掉。這個故事的終章，還沒有寫成。

options: Certain that it will end soon

questions.explain: 作者說這股趨勢能否持續很難說，卻也肯定聽眾的樂趣，顯得不確定但感興趣，故選 (D)。

title: The Quiet Physicist
paragraphs: Lena Park grew up in a mountain village where the power often failed. When the lights went out, her father repaired old radios by candlelight, and she learned to watch every move of his hands. Her teachers soon saw that she was [[adept|L7-1696]] with numbers, and some neighbors found her questions about electricity almost [[eerie|L7-1699]] for a child of eight.

At university, she chose to study [[quantum|L7-0804]] physics, the science of the smallest pieces of matter. Some professors felt a quiet [[disdain|L7-1698]] for such work, since it seemed so far from daily life. Park saw it differently. Her first paper, on how tiny particles can stay linked across a distance, was a [[prelude|L7-1739]] to ten years of work, much of it done in a small room with a few mirrors, a laser, and a borrowed computer.

The field was [[contentious|L7-1722]], and rivals argued that her results were a mistake. Park did not answer with angry words. She simply repeated her tests, week after week, until the results were [[undeniable|L7-1694]]. Some days, nothing worked, and she went home with a sore back and no answers. Years later she told a student that patience, not brilliance, had won the argument, and that every honest mistake along the way had taught her something.

In 2004, she became [[dean|L7-1742]] of the science faculty, a job so [[hectic|L7-1703]] that she had little time for the laboratory. Yet she took a [[holistic|L7-1704]] view of education. She believed that students learn best when science, art, and writing are taught together, and she gave [[precedence|L7-1710]] to young researchers whose ideas had not yet been heard. Colleagues said that she was [[receptive|L7-1715]] even to harsh criticism.

After her retirement, Park made a [[comeback|L7-0203]] of her own. She also gave talks at local schools, hoping that children would see science as a friend. Her last paper, on tiny chips made of [[silicon|L7-0938]] that work at very low [[voltage|L7-1180]], is still read today. In [[hindsight|L7-1685]], her slow and careful methods were the best way to build trust in a divided field. Students who knew her describe a woman who was [[revered|L7-1690]] but humble, and who never stopped asking questions.
zh: 李娜．朴成長於一個常常停電的山村。燈一熄，父親就在燭光下修理舊收音機，她學著注意他雙手的每個動作。老師很快就發現她擅長數字，有些鄰居則覺得，一個八歲孩子問的那些關於電的問題，幾乎有點詭異。
大學時，她選擇研究量子物理，這門科學研究的是最微小的物質單位。有些教授對這類研究暗暗不屑，因為它似乎離日常生活太遠。朴有不同的看法。她的第一篇論文探討微小粒子如何在相隔一段距離時仍保持連結，這是十年研究的序曲，其中大部分在一個小房間裡完成，只有幾面鏡子、一支雷射和一台借來的電腦。
這個領域充滿爭議，對手主張她的結果是個錯誤。朴並沒有用憤怒的言語回應。她只是週復一週重複她的實驗，直到結果無可否認。有些日子什麼都不順，她帶著痠痛的背和沒有答案的疑問回家。多年後，她告訴一位學生，贏得這場爭論的是耐心，而不是才華，而一路上每一個誠實的錯誤，都讓她學到了東西。
2004 年，她成為理學院院長，這份工作忙亂到她幾乎沒有時間進實驗室。然而，她對教育抱持整體性的看法。她相信，當科學、藝術與寫作一起教時，學生學得最好，她也把優先機會給那些想法尚未被聽見的年輕研究者。同事說，她甚至樂於接受嚴厲的批評。
退休之後，朴也有了屬於自己的東山再起。她也到當地學校演講，希望孩子把科學當成朋友。她最後一篇論文探討以極低電壓運作的矽晶片，至今仍被人閱讀。事後回頭看，她緩慢而謹慎的方法，是在一個意見分歧的領域建立信任的最佳途徑。認識她的學生形容，她是一位受人尊敬卻謙虛的人，從未停止發問。

title: From Bus Depot to Public Plaza
paragraphs: To the City Planning Committee: We are writing to propose that the old bus [[depot|L7-1770]] on Mill Street become a public [[plaza|L7-1778]]. The building has been empty for eight years. Its wide floor and high [[vaulted|L7-1779]] roof are too good to waste, and we believe that a [[proactive|L7-1594]] plan can turn them into a place the whole neighborhood will enjoy.

Our plan has three parts. First, the central floor would hold a market built from [[modules|L7-1781]] that can be moved, small stalls arranged in a different [[configuration|L7-0220]] each week for food, books, or art. Second, we would plant a small [[grove|L7-0453]] of trees along the north side, so that visitors and older residents can rest in the shade. Third, a stage in the corner would give local musicians, such as a student [[trio|L7-1123]], a place to play.

We expect the plaza to bring a lively [[vibe|L7-1773]] to a part of the city that now feels quiet and empty. Several local cooks are interested, including one who runs a [[vegan|L7-1772]] kitchen. A group of [[alumni|L7-1780]] from the nearby high school has offered to help raise money, and we would publish a [[catalog|L7-1777]] of local artists so that visitors can easily find them. Cities with lively public spaces often do well in [[rankings|L7-1768]] of the best places to live, which can bring in more visitors and help small shops to [[capitalize|L7-1673]] on the new crowds.

We know that the project will cost money, and we do not ask the city to pay for everything. A [[prudent|L7-1595]] first step would be a six-month trial using only the central floor. If it succeeds, the larger plan can follow. We would be glad to meet the committee at any time to explain our ideas in more detail, and we thank you for your time and attention. Sincerely, The Mill Street Neighbors
zh: 致市政規劃委員會：我們寫信是要提議，將米爾街上那座老舊的公車場改建為公共廣場。這棟建築已經閒置八年。它寬闊的地面和高聳的拱形屋頂浪費了太可惜，我們相信一項積極主動的計畫，可以把它們變成整個社區都能享受的地方。
我們的計畫分為三部分。第一，中央空地將設置一個由可移動模組搭成的市集，也就是小攤位，每週可以用不同的配置排列，販售食物、書籍或藝術品。第二，我們想在北側種一小片樹林，讓購物的人和年長的居民能在樹蔭下休息。第三，角落裡的舞台將讓當地音樂人，例如一組學生三重奏，有表演的地方。
我們期待這座廣場能為這個目前顯得冷清空蕩的城區帶來熱鬧的氛圍。有幾位當地廚師已表示有興趣，其中一位經營的是純素廚房。附近高中的一群校友提出願意協助募款，我們也會出版一本在地手作者名錄，讓訪客能輕易找到他們。擁有活躍公共空間的城市，常能在宜居城市的排名中表現良好，這可以吸引更多遊客，也幫助小店鋪利用新增的人潮。
我們知道這項計畫需要經費，也不要求市府負擔全部。謹慎的第一步，可以是只使用中央空地的六個月試辦。如果成功，再推行更大的計畫。我們很樂意隨時與委員會見面，進一步說明我們的想法，並感謝您撥冗關注。敬上，米爾街鄰居們

title: The Field Trip
paragraphs: On Friday morning, Class 3-B boarded a bus for a science field trip. Mia was worried about her team. Her three [[teammates|L7-1046]], Ken, Leo, and Nina, had barely spoken to each other all term. Mr. Lin gave each team a thick [[handbook|L7-0466]] and said, "Your task is to find five kinds of rock and plants. Bring back pictures, not stones."

The trail began at a wooden [[ramp|L7-1789]] and climbed toward a wall of gray [[granite|L7-1787]]. Ken, who was always [[outspoken|L7-1664]] and loved to show off, tried a silly [[stunt|L7-0999]], jumping from rock to rock. Halfway across, he slipped on wet [[moss|L7-0646]] and landed hard. A small cut on his [[forehead|L7-1785]] began to bleed. Mia wanted to [[clutch|L7-0195]] her notebook and run for help, but Nina stayed calm. She cleaned the cut with water, and Leo found the right page of the handbook for treating small injuries.

After a short rest, the group went on, and this time everyone moved with care. The path led into a wide [[marsh|L7-0621]], where the ground was soft and cold. Only [[hardy|L7-0471]] plants could grow there, and the team found three kinds. "Look at this!" Nina cried, pointing at a tiny purple flower hiding in the grass. It was a real [[gem|L7-1786]] of a find, and Leo took a picture while Mia wrote down its name. The weather was [[erratic|L7-1682]], with sun one minute and rain the next, so they stayed [[vigilant|L7-1695]] and kept the notebook dry.

By the time they returned to the bus, the four of them had begun to [[gel|L7-0431]] as a team. Ken sat quietly with a bandage on his head. "No more stunts," he said softly. "Sorry I slowed us down." Mr. Lin, who seemed to Mia like a wise [[sage|L7-1790]], looked at their pictures and smiled. "This is the best work I have seen today," he said. Mia smiled too. She had come to the trip worried about a group of strangers, and she was going home with three friends.
zh: 星期五早上，三年乙班搭上巴士，前往一趟自然科的校外教學。米婭很擔心她的小組。她的三位組員肯、里奧和妮娜，整個學期幾乎沒有彼此說過話。林老師給每組一本厚厚的手冊，並說：「你們的任務是找出五種岩石和植物。帶回來的是照片，不是石頭。」
步道從一道木頭斜坡開始，向上通往一面灰色的花崗岩壁。總是直言不諱又愛現的肯，嘗試了一個愚蠢的特技動作，在岩石間跳來跳去。跳到一半，他在濕滑的苔蘚上滑倒，重重摔在地上。他額頭上一道小傷口開始流血。米婭想緊抓著筆記本跑去求救，但妮娜保持冷靜。她用水把傷口洗乾淨，里奧則在手冊裡找到處理小傷的那一頁。
稍作休息後，一行人繼續前進，這次每個人都走得很小心。小路通向一大片沼澤，地面又軟又冷。只有耐寒耐勞的植物才能在那裡生長，小組找到了三種。「你們看！」妮娜大叫，指著藏在草叢裡的一朵小小紫花。這真是個難得的珍貴發現，里奧拍了照，米婭則寫下它的名字。天氣變化無常，一會兒出太陽，一會兒下雨，所以他們保持警覺，把筆記本護得乾乾的。
回到巴士時，這四個人已經開始成為一個有默契的團隊。肯安靜地坐著，頭上包著繃帶。「不會再有特技了，」他輕聲說。「抱歉拖慢了大家。」林老師在米婭眼中像一位智者，他看了他們的照片，微笑著說：「這是我今天看到最好的成果。」米婭也笑了。她來時擔心的是一群陌生人，回家時卻多了三位朋友。

title: Life Without Sunlight
paragraphs: In 1977, scientists in a small submarine dived to the sea floor near the Galapagos Islands. They expected a cold, dark desert. Instead, they found a [[vent|L7-1166]] pouring out hot water, and around it lived crowds of strange animals, including giant worms. This discovery changed how we think about life. Until then, scientists believed that almost all living things depended on sunlight.

How can life exist without the sun? The answer lies in tiny living things that use chemicals from the vent instead of light. Their cells contain an [[enzyme|L7-0362]] that helps them turn gases from inside the Earth into food. Hot water rising from deep below carries these gases through cracks in the sea floor, and the tiny cells take energy from them. Larger animals then feed on these cells, or even keep them inside their bodies.

Each cell is wrapped in a thin skin called a [[membrane|L7-1793]], which controls what goes in and out. At the heart of the chemical process is the movement of an [[electron|L7-0343]], the tiny particle that carries electric charge from one molecule to another, a little like a ball passed along a line. Some of these cells use carbon [[dioxide|L7-1794]] from the water to build the sugars they need. Around the vents, hard, [[metallic|L7-0631]] minerals form tall chimneys that can rise like towers from the sea floor.

Why does this matter? Many scientists now think that the first living things may have formed in a similar place, long before there were any plants. The idea is still partly [[conjecture|L7-1658]], but it is a [[geological|L7-1792]] puzzle as much as a biological one, because the early Earth had hot rocks and plenty of water. Others ask a [[cosmic|L7-0246]] question: if life can live in the dark, then oceans on other worlds may hold it too. The sea floor is a nearly [[pristine|L7-1711]] place, and the first picture of it in any [[atlas|L7-1797]] was drawn only in recent decades. Even so, the value of this research is [[undeniable|L7-1694]], and hot water has become a [[fixture|L7-0403]] of every serious talk about where life began.
zh: 1977 年，一艘小型潛水艇上的科學家潛入加拉巴哥群島附近的海底。他們原本預期會看到一片冰冷黑暗的沙漠。結果，他們發現了一個噴出熱水的出水口，周圍住著成群奇特的動物，包括巨大的蟲。這項發現改變了我們對生命的想法。在那之前，科學家相信幾乎所有生物都依賴陽光。
沒有太陽，生命怎麼可能存在？答案在於一些微小的生物，它們利用出水口的化學物質來代替光。它們的細胞中含有一種酵素，能幫助它們把來自地球內部的氣體轉變成食物。從深處上升的熱水，沿著海底的裂縫帶來這些氣體，微小的細胞便從中獲取能量。較大的動物再以這些細胞為食，甚至把它們養在自己的身體裡。
每個細胞都包著一層叫做細胞膜的薄皮，控制著什麼可以進出。這個化學過程的核心，是電子的移動；電子是攜帶電荷的微小粒子，會從一個分子傳到另一個分子，有點像沿著一列人傳遞的球。其中一些細胞利用水中的二氧化碳來製造所需的糖。在出水口周圍，堅硬的金屬礦物形成高高的煙囪，可以像塔一樣從海底升起。

這為什麼重要呢？許多科學家現在認為，最初的生命可能就形成在類似的地方，遠在任何植物出現之前。這個想法在某種程度上仍是臆測，但它既是生物學的謎，也是地質學的謎，因為早期的地球有熾熱的岩石和大量的水。另一些人則提出宇宙層面的問題：如果生命能在黑暗中生存，那麼其他星球上的海洋也可能孕育生命。海底幾乎是一片未受破壞的地方，任何一本地圖集中的第一幅海底圖，也是近幾十年才繪成的。即便如此，這項研究的價值無可否認，而熱水也已成為每一場認真討論生命從哪裡開始的固定話題。

title: A Farm That Thinks
paragraphs: At dawn, farmer Wu Ming's [[tractor|L7-1098]] drives down the field with nobody holding the wheel. A small [[antenna|L7-0049]] on its roof receives signals from satellites, and the machine follows each row within a few centimeters. This is not science fiction. On many farms today, computers have become [[ubiquitous|L7-1583]], and they are changing how food is grown.

Behind the work is a flood of data. Sensors in the soil measure water and [[nitrogen|L7-0675]], the chemical that plants need to grow green leaves. Software for [[analytics|L7-1809]] studies the numbers and tells the farmer which corner of the field is thirsty. A [[neural|L7-1813]] network, a computer program that learns from examples, can even look at photos of leaves and spot signs of disease. Too much water is also a problem, because it can lead to [[mold|L7-0642]], so good [[drainage|L7-0323]] keeps the roots healthy.

Smart tools also help protect the land. A farmer can add [[limestone|L7-1822]] only where the soil is too sour, instead of covering the whole field. A fine [[mesh|L7-1823]] placed over young plants keeps insects away without chemicals, and wooden poles [[prop|L7-0783]] up the young vines when the wind is strong. To make all this work, farmers must often [[enlist|L7-1819]] the help of young engineers, and the engineers must learn to hear what the farmers know. Software cannot [[pinpoint|L7-1666]] a problem that nobody has told it about.

Not everyone is happy. Machines are expensive, and a small family farm may be [[constrained|L7-1587]] by a limited budget. Some older farmers worry that they cannot learn new skills, and others say the data should belong to the farmer, not to the companies. Yet many people see a hopeful future. A [[proactive|L7-1594]] farmer who makes wise decisions instead of guesses can grow more food with less water and fertilizer. As Wu Ming says, "The soil still teaches us. The machine only helps us listen."
zh: 黎明時分，農夫吳明的曳引機在田裡自己行駛，沒有人握著方向盤。車頂上的一根小天線接收來自衛星的訊號，機器沿著每一行作物前進，誤差只有幾公分。這不是科幻小說。如今在許多農場，電腦已經無所不在，並且正在改變食物生產的方式。
這些工作的背後是大量的數據。土壤中的感測器測量水分和氮，氮是植物長出綠葉所需要的化學物質。數據分析軟體研究這些數字，告訴農夫田裡哪個角落缺水。神經網路是一種能從範例中學習的電腦程式，甚至能看著葉片的照片，發現病害的跡象。水太多也是個問題，因為可能導致發霉，所以良好的排水能讓根保持健康。
智慧工具也有助於保護土地。農夫可以只在土壤太酸的地方加石灰岩粉，而不必覆蓋整片田地。蓋在幼苗上的細網能不靠化學藥劑擋住昆蟲，風大的時候，木桿則能撐住年輕的藤蔓。要讓這一切運作，農夫往往得請年輕的工程師幫忙，而工程師也必須學習聆聽農夫所知道的事。軟體無法找出沒有人告訴過它的問題。
並非每個人都滿意。機器很昂貴，小型家庭農場可能受限於有限的預算。一些年長的農夫擔心自己學不會新技能，也有人說數據應該屬於農夫，而不是公司。然而許多人看見了充滿希望的未來。一位主動積極、以明智決定取代猜測的農夫，可以用更少的水和肥料種出更多的糧食。正如吳明所說：「土壤仍然在教導我們。機器只是幫助我們聆聽。」

title: Big Art from Tiny Squares
paragraphs: Look closely at an old video game, and you will see that every picture is made of small squares of color. Each square is a [[pixel|L7-1844]]. In the early days of computers, screens could show only a few hundred squares across, and the memory of a machine was tiny, so artists had to draw faces, trees, and heroes with just a few dozen of them. The limits seemed like a problem, but they also forced artists to be [[ingenious|L7-0520]].

The first thing an artist had to choose was a [[palette|L7-1832]]. Many early machines could use only a handful of colors at once, so every shade had to count. A good artist could paint a night sky with just three blues, or suggest the glow of an [[aurora|L7-1836]] with a few green and purple squares. In a noisy [[arcade|L7-1835]], these small pictures had to be noticed in a second, and an artist's [[prowess|L7-1667]] showed in how much a picture could say with so little.

As computers grew stronger, many people expected pixel art to disappear. It did not. Today it is [[retro|L7-1840]] in the best sense: designers choose it on purpose because it feels warm and friendly. Some artists work [[offline|L7-1831]] at first, drawing on paper with a ruler before they open any software. Others mix [[analog|L7-1834]] and digital tools, drawing by hand and then scanning their pictures into a computer. The style is now [[ubiquitous|L7-1583]], appearing on posters, in games, and even on [[apparel|L7-1841]] such as shirts and bags.

Pixel art also teaches an important lesson in design: limits can make us creative. When an artist has every tool, it is easy to add too much; when the choice is small, each decision matters. In computer code, a [[null|L7-1839]] value means that nothing is there, but in pixel art, an empty space is also a choice. For students who are just learning, this makes pixel art a [[beacon|L7-1826]] of hope. It shows that a [[bounty|L7-1827]] of ideas can grow from the smallest squares.
zh: 仔細看一款老電玩，你會發現每一幅畫面都是由小小的彩色方塊組成。每個方塊就是一個像素。在電腦的早期，螢幕橫向只能顯示幾百個方塊，機器的記憶體也很小，所以藝術家只能用幾十個方塊來畫臉孔、樹木和英雄。這些限制看似是個問題，卻也逼著藝術家想出巧妙的辦法。
藝術家首先要選的是調色盤。許多早期的機器一次只能使用少數幾種顏色，所以每一種色調都很重要。優秀的藝術家能用三種藍色畫出夜空，或用幾個綠色和紫色的方塊暗示極光的光輝。在嘈雜的遊樂場裡，這些小畫面必須在一秒內被人注意到，而藝術家的本領，就表現在如何用這麼少的東西說出這麼多。
隨著電腦變得更強，許多人以為像素藝術會消失。它沒有。如今它在最好的意義上是復古風：設計師刻意選擇它，因為它感覺溫暖友善。有些藝術家一開始會在離線狀態下工作，先用尺在紙上作畫，才打開任何軟體。也有人混用類比與數位工具，先手繪，再把圖掃描進電腦。這種風格如今隨處可見，出現在海報、遊戲，甚至襯衫和包包等服飾上。
像素藝術也教了我們一個重要的設計課題：限制可以讓人更有創意。當藝術家擁有所有工具時，很容易加得太多；當選擇很少時，每個決定都很重要。在電腦程式碼中，null 值表示什麼都沒有，但在像素藝術裡，空白也是一種選擇。對剛開始學習的學生來說，這讓像素藝術成為希望的燈塔。它顯示，豐富的點子可以從最小的方塊長出來。

title: The Falcon and the Aurora
paragraphs: In the far north, where winter nights last for weeks, twelve-year-old Ana lived with her grandfather in a wooden house at the edge of a [[marsh|L7-0621]]. The nearest bus [[depot|L7-1770]] was two hours away, and the internet was usually [[offline|L7-1831]]. Her grandfather had worked for forty years as a [[veterinary|L7-1824]] assistant, and people in the village still brought him their sick animals.

One evening, Ana heard a weak cry outside. In the snow lay a young [[falcon|L7-1830]], one wing bent at a strange angle. She lifted it with both hands, and the bird's feet gripped her glove. Her grandfather, whose [[hardy|L7-0471]] hands were as rough as [[granite|L7-1787]] yet very gentle, felt the wing carefully. "It is not broken," he said. "Only hurt. We will keep it by the stove."

For a week the falcon rested in a box, and Ana fed it small pieces of meat. On the eighth night, a storm arrived. The snow was thick, and the wind shook the windows. The old [[analog|L7-1834]] radio on the shelf, joined to a tall [[antenna|L7-0049]] on the roof, began to make strange noises. Through the noise, Ana heard a man's voice. It was Mr. Hale, a neighbor, whose [[tractor|L7-1098]] had broken down on the road. He could no longer see the way home. "He needs a light," said her grandfather. "A big one."

They tied a bright lamp to a long pole, and Ana held the ladder while her grandfather climbed. The wind hurt her [[forehead|L7-1785]], and her hands were cold, but she did not let go. She [[clutched|L7-0195]] the ladder until it stopped shaking. The lamp became a [[beacon|L7-1826]] in the white night. "Keep it steady!" came Mr. Hale's voice from the radio. "I can see it!" An hour later, a dark shape stumbled out of the snow, a [[halo|L7-1821]] of ice around his hat.

By morning, the storm had passed, and in the clear night that followed, a green [[aurora|L7-1836]] rippled over the marsh like a slow river of light. The falcon had healed. Ana carried it outside, and it spread its wings and tried the cold air. Then it rose and was gone. "Will it come back?" she asked. Her grandfather smiled. "Maybe. Some friends only visit."
zh: 在遙遠的北方，冬天的夜晚能持續好幾週，十二歲的安娜和祖父住在沼澤邊的一棟木屋裡。最近的公車站要兩小時才到得了，而且網路通常是斷線的。她的祖父當了四十年的獸醫助手，村民們還是會把生病的動物帶來給他。
某個傍晚，安娜聽見外面傳來微弱的叫聲。雪地上躺著一隻年輕的獵鷹，一邊翅膀彎成奇怪的角度。她用雙手把牠捧起來，鳥的腳緊緊抓住她的手套。祖父那雙粗糙如花崗岩、卻非常溫柔的耐勞的手，小心地摸了摸翅膀。「沒有斷，」他說，「只是受傷了。我們把牠放在火爐旁。」
整整一週，獵鷹都待在一個箱子裡休息，安娜餵牠吃小塊的肉。第八天夜裡，暴風雪來了。雪佈滿空中，風搖著窗戶。架上那台老舊的類比式收音機連著屋頂上一根高高的天線，開始發出奇怪的雜音。在雜音中，安娜聽見一個男人的聲音。是鄰居黑爾先生，他的曳引機在路上拋錨了，再也看不見回家的路。「他需要光，」祖父說，「很大的光。」
他們把一盞明亮的燈綁在一根長桿上，安娜扶著梯子，祖父往上爬。風刺痛她的額頭，雙手冰冷，但她沒有放手。她緊緊抓著梯子，直到它不再搖晃。那盞燈成了白茫茫的夜裡的信號燈。「穩住！」黑爾先生的聲音從收音機傳來，「我看到了！」一小時後，一個黑影從雪中跌跌撞撞地走出來，帽子周圍罩著一圈冰暈。
到了早晨，暴風雪過去了，隨後的晴朗夜晚，一道綠色的極光像一條緩緩流動的光之河，在沼澤上方蕩漾。獵鷹已經痊癒。安娜把牠抱到外面，牠展開翅膀，試探冰冷的空氣。然後牠飛起來，不見了。「牠會回來嗎？」她問。祖父微笑著說：「也許吧。有些朋友只是來拜訪。」

questions.stem: The word "beacon" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 那盞燈在白茫茫的黑暗中為黑爾先生指引方向，beacon 即「信號燈、指引」，故選 (D)。(B) 文中沒有提到警告鈴聲。

vocab.stem: A thin ring of ice formed a ______ around the old street lamp in the freezing air.
vocab.explain: 燈周圍形成的一圈薄冰光暈，是 halo（光環、光暈）。tractor（曳引機）、depot（車站）、granite（花崗岩）都不能用來描述環繞燈的光圈。

vocab.stem: In the winter sky over the lake, we waited quietly to see the green lights of the ______.
vocab.explain: 在冬季夜空中等待看見綠色的光，是「極光」，用 aurora。antenna（天線）、veterinary（獸醫的）、falcon（獵鷹）都不是天空中的光。

title: The Night Watchers of the Mountain
paragraphs: A narrow road wound up through the forest toward the [[apex|L7-1847]] of the mountain. Mia sat in the last truck of a long [[convoy|L7-0239]] carrying food, tools, and equipment. She had just finished studying [[quantum|L7-0804]] physics, and this was her first real job at a mountain [[observatory|L7-1851]], far from the noise of the city. Through the window she could see a wide [[vista|L7-1855]] of green hills, and she felt both excited and afraid.

The director, Mr. Chen, met her at the gate. "The work here is not easy," he said, "but it is honest." He showed her the great telescope, which looked like a white [[pod|L7-1852]] sitting on a tall stone tower. Its camera used [[infrared|L7-1849]] light to see through the dust where new stars are born. On the wall hung an old [[analog|L7-1834]] clock, and under it the team had written a long line of numbers, an attempt to prove a [[theorem|L7-1854]] about the way stars move.

Life on the mountain was simple. Breakfast was [[crisp|L7-1857]] toast and hot tea with a little [[cinnamon|L7-1856]]. The air was cold, and after dark the wind pushed hard against the walls. One night a storm sent a huge [[boulder|L7-1848]] rolling onto the road, and the whole staff worked until morning to move it. Nobody complained, because everyone knew the telescope needed supplies, and the supplies needed a road.

Weeks passed, and Mia never let herself become [[slack|L7-0947]]. She checked every instrument twice. Then, on a clear night, her screen showed a tiny change in the light from a distant [[stellar|L7-1815]] system, a signal no one had expected. Mr. Chen read the numbers and smiled. "People once believed the sky held a [[prophecy|L7-1853]] for kings," he said. "Now it holds data for anyone patient enough to read it." When Mia stepped outside, the lights of the dome shone like a [[beacon|L7-1826]] on the dark mountain, and she knew she was exactly where she belonged.
zh: 一條狹窄的道路穿過森林，蜿蜒通往山頂。米亞坐在一長列車隊的最後一輛卡車上，車隊載著食物、工具和設備。她剛念完量子物理，而這是她在一座山上天文台的第一份正式工作，遠離城市的喧囂。從車窗望出去，她能看見一片遼闊的綠色山景，心中既興奮又害怕。
主任陳先生在大門口迎接她。「這裡的工作並不輕鬆，」他說，「但很踏實。」他帶她看那座大型望遠鏡，它看起來像一個白色的豆莢，坐落在高高的石塔上。它的相機利用紅外線穿透塵埃，看見新恆星誕生的地方。牆上掛著一只老舊的指針式時鐘，時鐘下方，團隊寫了一長串數字，試圖證明一個關於恆星運動方式的定理。
山上的生活很簡單。早餐是酥脆的吐司，配一杯加了一點肉桂的熱茶。空氣很冷，天黑之後，風猛烈地推撞著牆壁。有一晚，暴風雨讓一顆巨大的圓石滾到路上，全體員工忙到天亮才把它移開。沒有人抱怨，因為大家都知道，望遠鏡需要補給，而補給需要一條路。
幾個星期過去了，米亞從不讓自己鬆懈。她把每一項儀器都檢查兩遍。然後，在一個晴朗的夜晚，她的螢幕顯示，一個遙遠恆星系統的光出現了微小的變化，那是沒有人預料到的訊號。陳先生看了數字，露出微笑。「人們曾經相信天空為君王留下了預言，」他說，「現在它為任何有耐心閱讀的人留下了數據。」當米亞走到屋外，圓頂的燈光像一座燈塔，照亮漆黑的山，而她知道，自己正身在最適合的地方。

questions.explain: 第三段說大家都知道望遠鏡需要補給，而補給需要一條路，所以通宵移開圓石，故選 (B)。
questions.evidence: Nobody complained, because everyone knew the telescope needed supplies, and the supplies needed a road.

questions.stem: The word "slack" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.explain: 米亞每項儀器都檢查兩遍，所以「從不讓自己 slack」是指不讓自己鬆懈、馬虎，故選 (C) careless。

questions.stem: What does Mr. Chen's last remark suggest?

Kings were once the best astronomers.

vocab.stem: The hikers rested beside a huge ______ before the final climb.
vocab.explain: 登山客在最後一段攀登前休息的地方，會是一顆巨大的「圓石」，故選 boulder。cinnamon（肉桂）、theorem（定理）、prophecy（預言）都不合句意。

vocab.stem: A long ______ of trucks carried food and water to the flooded town.
vocab.explain: 一長列載運食物與水的卡車，稱為「車隊」convoy。vista（遠景）、crisp（酥脆的）、apex（頂點）都不能用來指一列卡車。

title: Seven Days in the Trench
paragraphs: On the first morning of the summer dig, Ken pulled on his oldest [[trousers|L7-1867]] and followed the team up into the [[highland|L7-1862]]. His uncle, an [[archaeological|L7-1877]] scientist, had invited him to help for two weeks. Ken, the [[eldest|L7-1870]] of three brothers, had never done anything like this, and he was not sure he would be any use.

The team had cut a deep [[trench|L7-1120]] through the soft ground. After the rain, the bottom was covered with [[gravel|L7-1861]] and mud, and Ken sank in up to his [[shin|L7-1874]] with every step. He worked slowly with a small brush, moving the dirt away from a pale piece of [[quartz|L7-0810]] that shone in the sunlight. "Careful," said his uncle. "This land has kept its secrets for a [[millennium|L7-1863]]. We should not hurry it."

By noon, the team had found the low walls of a small temple. A woman from the village said that long ago, people had come to an [[oracle|L7-1864]] on this hill to ask about the weather and the harvest. Beside the ruins stood an old [[willow|L7-1876]] whose roots had held the stones together for centuries. Ken wrote everything in his notebook. [[Midway|L7-1872]] through the second week, a cousin played a [[prank|L7-1865]] by hiding a plastic coin in the mud, and the whole team laughed so hard that work stopped for ten minutes.

On the last day, the team placed a bronze [[plaque|L7-1873]] near the wall, so that future visitors would know what lay beneath their feet. Ken was surprised by how sad he felt to leave. His uncle had once written a long [[dissertation|L7-1858]] about ancient temples, but Ken learned more from a few days in the trench than from any book. On the bus home, he remembered the wide [[vista|L7-1855]] from the hill, the strange [[flora|L7-1859]] along the path, and the dry [[crust|L7-0266]] of bread they ate at lunch, and he decided to come back next summer.
zh: 暑期挖掘的第一天早上，阿肯穿上他最舊的長褲，跟著團隊爬上高地。他的叔叔是一位考古學家，邀請他來幫忙兩個星期。阿肯是三兄弟中的老大，從來沒做過這樣的事，他不確定自己能不能派上用場。
團隊在鬆軟的土地上挖出一條很深的壕溝。下過雨後，溝底鋪滿了碎石和泥巴，阿肯每走一步，小腿都陷進泥裡。他拿著一把小刷子慢慢工作，把泥土從一塊在陽光下閃閃發亮的淡色石英旁撥開。「小心，」他叔叔說，「這片土地已經把祕密藏了一千年。我們不該催它。」
到了中午，團隊發現了一座小神殿低矮的牆。村裡一位婦人說，很久以前，人們會來到這座山丘上的神諭所，詢問天氣和收成。遺跡旁站著一棵老柳樹，它的根已經把石頭固定在一起好幾個世紀。阿肯把所有東西都寫進筆記本。第二週過到一半時，一位表哥惡作劇，把一枚塑膠硬幣藏進泥巴裡，全隊笑得太厲害，工作因此停了十分鐘。
最後一天，團隊在牆邊放了一塊銅製紀念牌，讓日後的訪客知道腳下埋著什麼。阿肯很驚訝自己離開時竟如此難過。他的叔叔曾寫過一篇關於古代神殿的長篇博士論文，但阿肯從這幾天待在壕溝裡學到的，比任何一本書都多。在回家的巴士上，他想起山丘上遼闊的景色、小徑旁奇特的植物群，還有他們午餐吃的乾硬麵包皮，並決定明年夏天再回來。

title: Newspaper, Foam, and Friends
paragraphs: Every spring, the drama club at Lena's school puts on a [[theatrical|L7-1062]] show for the yearly school [[gala|L7-1886]]. This year's play was about a king who lives for a [[millennium|L7-1863]] and learns that a long life is not the same as a good life. The club had only three weeks and almost no money, so everyone had to be creative.

Lena, the club's chief builder, made the king's golden crown as a [[replica|L7-1890]] of one she had seen in a museum. She shaped it from [[pulp|L7-1883]] made of old newspapers and covered it with gold paint. The set was harder. A giant [[boulder|L7-1848]] that blocked the hero's path was built from foam [[insulation|L7-1887]] that her uncle had left in his garage. Nobody in the audience would guess that it weighed almost nothing.

Then things went wrong. A [[courier|L7-0252]] delivered the costumes a day late, and the knight's metal helmet had a large [[dent|L7-1885]] in it. The director, Mr. Lin, began a long [[rant|L7-1889]] about careless delivery companies. Ken, the club's tech [[nerd|L7-1896]], waited until he had finished and said quietly, "We can fix it." He wrapped silver tape from a [[reel|L7-0829]] around the helmet until the dent looked like part of the design. Then he marked the [[perimeter|L7-1882]] of the stage with tape, so that no actor would step off in the dark. The queen's dress, made from old curtains, looked surprisingly [[chic|L7-1879]].

On the night of the show, the hall was full. In the final scene, a hidden fan blew hundreds of paper stars into the air, and the whole stage filled with [[airborne|L7-1884]] silver light. For a moment, nobody moved. Then came the [[crisp|L7-1857]] sound of clapping, growing louder and louder. Lena stood in the dark behind the curtain and smiled. It was the [[apex|L7-1847]] of her school life, and she had built it from newspaper, foam, and friends.
zh: 每年春天，蕾娜學校的戲劇社都會為一年一度的校慶晚會演出一齣戲。今年的戲是關於一位活了一千年的國王，他學到長壽並不等於過得好。社團只有三個星期的時間，而且幾乎沒有經費，所以每個人都得發揮創意。
社團的總建造師蕾娜，把國王的金色王冠做成她在博物館見過的一頂王冠的複製品。她用舊報紙做成的紙漿塑形，再塗上金漆。布景更難。一顆擋住英雄去路的巨大圓石，是用她叔叔留在車庫裡的泡棉隔熱材料做成的。觀眾沒有人會猜到，它幾乎沒有重量。
接著事情出了差錯。快遞員把戲服晚了一天才送到，而騎士的金屬頭盔上有一個很大的凹痕。導演林老師開始對粗心的快遞公司長篇大論地抱怨。社團裡的科技宅男阿肯等他說完，輕聲說：「我們可以修好它。」他把一捲銀色膠帶纏在頭盔上，直到那個凹痕看起來像是設計的一部分。接著，他用膠帶標出舞台的邊界，讓演員在黑暗中不會走出舞台。皇后的禮服是用舊窗簾做成的，看起來出奇地時髦。
演出那天晚上，禮堂座無虛席。在最後一幕，一台藏起來的風扇把數百顆紙星星吹向空中，整個舞台充滿了在空中飄浮的銀色光芒。有那麼一刻，沒有人動。接著傳來清脆的掌聲，越來越響亮。蕾娜站在布幕後的黑暗中微笑。這是她學生生活的最高點，而她是用報紙、泡棉和朋友建造出來的。

title: A Weekend in the Hamlet
paragraphs: The train from London was nearly empty. Anna sat alone in a small [[compartment|L7-0210]] and watched the countryside roll past. Her destination was a tiny [[hamlet|L7-1907]] with only twelve houses, where her aunt had lived for many years. When the train stopped, she climbed down onto a platform that had a single bench and a [[willow|L7-1876]] leaning over the tracks.

The walk to the house led through a quiet [[woodland|L7-1203]]. Along the path grew wild [[blackberry|L7-1899]] bushes, and Anna ate so many that her fingers turned purple. Her aunt told her that, in the village stories, an [[elf|L7-1903]] guarded the trees and punished anyone who took too much. "Then I am in trouble," Anna laughed. At the [[crest|L7-1901]] of the hill, she saw a wide [[vista|L7-1855]] of fields and, far away, a silver sea around a small [[cove|L7-1915]].

The next day, they visited an old [[monastery|L7-1910]] built in the [[gothic|L7-1905]] style, with tall windows and pointed arches. Inside, a guide showed them [[graffiti|L7-1906]] scratched into the stone by visitors six hundred years ago: names, dates, and even small drawings of ships. "People have always wanted to leave a mark," he said. Behind the building was a hedge [[maze|L7-1909]], and Anna was lost in it for twenty minutes, laughing the whole time. When she finally found the way out, she followed the [[gravel|L7-1861]] path back to the gate.

That evening, her aunt made a pot of strong tea, and they sat by the window to let it [[brew|L7-0136]]. Rain began to fall on the [[zinc|L7-1217]] roof, a soft and steady sound. [[Midway|L7-1872]] through the evening, Anna realized that she had not looked at her phone once. In the city, she thought, time always seemed to run. Here, it walked. Her aunt asked whether she wanted to stay another week. Anna said yes before the question was even finished.
zh: 從倫敦出發的火車幾乎是空的。安娜獨自坐在一個小隔間裡，看著鄉間景色一一掠過。她的目的地是一個只有十二戶人家的小村落，她的阿姨已經在那裡住了很多年。火車停下時，她走下月台，那裡只有一張長椅，和一棵斜靠在鐵軌上方的柳樹。
通往阿姨家的路穿過一片安靜的林地。小路旁長著野生黑莓叢，安娜吃了好多，手指都變紫了。阿姨告訴她，在村裡的傳說中，有一位精靈守護著這些樹，會懲罰拿太多的人。「那我麻煩大了，」安娜笑著說。在山丘的頂端，她看見一大片田野的遼闊景色，遠處還有一片銀色的海水環繞著一個小海灣。
隔天，她們參觀了一座以哥德式風格興建的古老修道院，有高高的窗戶和尖尖的拱門。在裡面，導覽員給她們看六百年前的訪客刻在石頭上的塗鴉：名字、日期，甚至還有小小的船的圖畫。「人們一向都想留下痕跡，」他說。建築物後面有一座樹籬迷宮，安娜在裡面迷路了二十分鐘，一路笑個不停。她終於找到出口時，沿著碎石小徑走回大門。
那天晚上，阿姨泡了一壺濃茶，她們坐在窗邊讓茶慢慢泡開。雨開始落在鋅板屋頂上，聲音輕柔而規律。夜晚過到一半時，安娜發現自己一次都沒有看手機。她心想，在城市裡，時間總像在奔跑；在這裡，它是用走的。阿姨問她想不想再多待一個星期。問題都還沒問完，安娜就說好了。

title: Summary Report: The Green Valley Project
topic: 實用文本・環保報告摘要
paragraphs: Over the past three years, nine [[municipalities|L7-1919]] in the [[alpine|L7-1931]] region have worked together on the Green Valley Project. Their goal was simple: to reduce pollution without making life harder for ordinary families. Some of the places involved are large towns, but others are small villages like the old [[hamlet|L7-1907]] of Stone Bridge. This summary describes the main actions and what the project has learned so far.

Energy. A single wind [[turbine|L7-1131]] was built [[atop|L7-1924]] a hill on the northern [[flank|L7-0404]] of the valley, where the wind blows steadily. Its long blades are made of a light [[polymer|L7-1921]] that is strong but easy to carry up the narrow road. Planners were worried about the nearby [[woodland|L7-1203]], so the machine was placed carefully, and a gravel road was used instead of a wide new one to protect the trees.

Transport and daily life. Buses now run on cleaner fuel, and a shared bicycle plan encourages short trips. Drivers are asked to record their [[mileage|L7-0633]] on a phone app, which keeps a [[cache|L7-1925]] of past trips so that each family can see its own progress. Roads were repaired with a mix that uses less [[tar|L7-1034]], and one town replaced its old [[neon|L7-0665]] shop signs with low-energy lights. School canteens also added dishes made with [[soy|L7-1929]], such as tofu, because plant foods usually need less land and water. Some students complained at first, but after a month most had learned to enjoy the new menu.

The project is not perfect. At the beginning, a [[maze|L7-1909]] of rules slowed everything down, and each town had its own forms. Still, the mayors agree that cooperation was worth the effort. At the closing meeting, the head of the project stood at the [[podium|L7-1928]] and described the plan as a [[lever|L7-0580]] for change: a small tool that can move something heavy. The report recommends that the project continue for three more years.
zh: 過去三年來，阿爾卑斯山區的九個市鎮共同推動「綠色山谷計畫」。它的目標很簡單：在不讓一般家庭生活更辛苦的情況下減少污染。參與的地方有些是大城鎮，也有些是像石橋這樣的古老小村落。這份摘要說明了主要的行動，以及計畫到目前為止的心得。
能源。一座風力發電機建在山谷北側山腰的一座山丘頂上，那裡的風穩定地吹著。它長長的葉片是用一種輕盈的聚合物製成的，既堅固又容易沿著狹窄的道路運上山。規劃人員擔心附近的林地，所以風機的位置經過仔細安排，並且使用碎石路，而不是新闢一條寬闊的道路，以保護樹木。
交通與日常生活。公車現在使用較乾淨的燃料，共享單車計畫也鼓勵民眾短程移動。駕駛人被請求用手機應用程式記錄行駛里程，程式會把過去的行程存在快取中，讓每個家庭都能看到自己的進展。道路用瀝青用量較少的混合料修補，有一個城鎮則把老舊的霓虹商店招牌換成低耗能燈具。學校餐廳也增加了用大豆製成的菜色，例如豆腐，因為植物性食物通常需要較少的土地與水。有些學生一開始抱怨，但一個月後，大多數人已學會享受新菜單。
這個計畫並不完美。一開始，一團複雜的規定拖慢了所有事情，每個城鎮都有自己的表格。不過，市長們都同意，合作是值得的。在閉幕會議上，計畫負責人站在講台上，把這個計畫形容為促成改變的槓桿：一個能移動沉重物體的小工具。報告建議這個計畫再延續三年。

title: The Last Delivery Before the Snow
paragraphs: Nina had been a [[courier|L7-0252]] for only three months, but she already knew the [[alpine|L7-1931]] roads better than the old drivers. On the last day before the first heavy snow of the year, her boss gave her one more job: to carry medicine and bread to a [[hamlet|L7-1907]] high in the [[highland|L7-1862]]. "Be back before dark," he said. Nina pulled on thick [[trousers|L7-1867]], wrapped a [[scarlet|L7-1923]] scarf around her neck, and turned the key in the [[ignition|L7-1880]].

The first hours were easy. The road climbed through a quiet [[woodland|L7-1203]], where the air was cold and [[crisp|L7-1857]] and the only sound was the engine. Beyond the trees, the road turned into rough [[gravel|L7-1861]]. At the [[crest|L7-1901]] of a long hill, she stopped for a moment. A wide [[vista|L7-1855]] of white mountains lay before her.

Then the trouble began. Ahead, a huge [[boulder|L7-1848]] had fallen from the [[flank|L7-0404]] of the mountain and now blocked the whole road. There was no way around it. Nina studied the rock for a long time. Then she remembered the small [[cache|L7-1925]] of tools that road workers kept in a hut a few hundred meters back. She found a long iron bar and used it as a [[lever|L7-0580]]. It took an hour of hard work, and her hands were red with cold, but at last the great stone rolled slowly down into the valley.

By the time she reached the village, the sky was turning gray. A small dog ran out to meet her, followed by an old woman who thanked her again and again. "The other roads closed yesterday," the woman said. "You are the only one who could come." Nina handed over the box, drank a cup of hot tea, and looked at the bare [[willow|L7-1876]] beside the door, which already wore a thin coat of frost.

The ride home was colder. Snow began to fall, softly at first, then harder. When she finally returned to town, her boss was waiting at the door with a worried face. "I did not think you would make it," he said. Nina smiled, too tired to answer. She had learned that a good courier is not the fastest driver, but the one who finds a way.
zh: 妮娜當快遞員才三個月，但她對阿爾卑斯山區道路的熟悉程度，已經超過那些老司機。在今年第一場大雪前的最後一天，老闆又交給她一份工作：把藥品和麵包送到高地上的一個小村落。「天黑前要回來，」他說。妮娜穿上厚長褲，把一條緋紅色的圍巾繞在脖子上，轉動了點火開關的鑰匙。
最初幾個小時很輕鬆。道路穿過一片安靜的林地，空氣寒冷而清爽，唯一的聲音是引擎聲。出了樹林，路變成崎嶇的碎石路。在一座長長山坡的頂端，她停了一會兒。一片遼闊的白色群山景色展現在眼前。
接著麻煩來了。前方，一顆巨大的圓石從山腰滾落，把整條路擋住了。沒有任何辦法繞過去。妮娜盯著那塊石頭看了很久。然後她想起，後方幾百公尺外的一間小屋裡，修路工人存放著一小批工具。她找到一根長長的鐵棒，把它當成槓桿使用。花了一個小時的苦工，她的雙手凍得通紅，但最後那塊巨石終於緩緩滾進山谷。
當她抵達村莊時，天空正轉為灰色。一隻小狗跑出來迎接她，後面跟著一位老婦人，連聲向她道謝。「其他的路昨天就封了，」老婦人說，「只有你能來。」妮娜把箱子交出去，喝了一杯熱茶，看著門旁那棵光禿禿的柳樹，樹上已經蓋著一層薄薄的霜。
回程更冷了。雪開始下，起初很輕，後來越來越大。當她終於回到鎮上時，老闆正一臉擔心地站在門口等她。「我沒想到你能回來，」他說。妮娜微笑著，累得說不出話。她學到了，一位好的快遞員不是開最快的人，而是能找到辦法的人。

title: The Trip to Wildwood Park
paragraphs: When Mr. Wang's science class heard about the trip to Wildwood Park, nobody could sit still. The park was three hours away, so the school rented a small [[caravan|L7-1936]] of buses. On the way, students sang, traded snacks, and argued about which animal they most wanted to see. Mr. Wang had warned them to wear warm shoes and bring water, but half the class forgot at least one of the two.

The first stop was the [[pavilion|L7-1942]], a large open hall where a park worker greeted them with a wave. The park's [[mascot|L7-1940]], a person in a [[beaver|L7-1947]] costume, danced around the group, and even the shyest students laughed. The worker explained how a real beaver builds a dam from branches and mud, and why [[aquatic|L7-1932]] animals such as fish and frogs depend on the quiet pools behind it. He also asked each student to find one thing that the animals needed to survive.

After lunch, they rode an open truck across a dry [[savannah|L7-1944]], where long grass moved like waves. From a wooden [[lookout|L7-1951]] tower [[atop|L7-1924]] a rocky hill, they could see a large [[moose|L7-1952]] standing beside a lake. Then a [[gale|L7-1938]] pushed dark clouds across the sky. The guide told everyone to hurry down while she used the radio to [[dispatch|L7-1949]] a truck to meet them. In the dim light, she turned the handle of a small [[crank|L7-1948]] lamp, and the group followed its small yellow glow.

Back at the pavilion, the students ate hot soup and bread with a [[wedge|L7-1191]] of cheese. The wind outside was still strong, and far away a [[turbine|L7-1131]] turned slowly against the sky. Mr. Wang smiled. "One of the [[perks|L7-1943]] of a school trip," he said, "is that bad weather turns into a good story." On the way home, a girl showed everyone a photo of a baby animal as small as a [[kitten|L7-1918]], and the whole bus said "aww" together.
zh: 王老師的自然課全班聽說要去野林公園校外教學時，沒有人坐得住。公園距離三小時車程，所以學校租了一小列巴士車隊。一路上，學生們唱歌、交換零食，並爭論最想看到哪一種動物。王老師已經提醒他們要穿暖和的鞋子、帶水，但全班有一半的人至少忘了其中一樣。
第一站是涼亭展館，一個寬敞的開放式大廳，一位公園工作人員揮手歡迎他們。公園的吉祥物，一個穿著海狸服裝的人，繞著大家跳舞，連最害羞的學生也笑了。工作人員解釋真正的海狸如何用樹枝和泥巴築水壩，以及為什麼魚和青蛙這類水生動物要依靠水壩後方平靜的水池。他還請每位學生找出一樣動物生存所需要的東西。
午餐後，他們坐上一輛開放式卡車，穿越乾燥的熱帶草原，那裡的長草像波浪一樣搖動。從一座位於岩石山丘頂上的木造瞭望塔上，他們看見一隻大麋鹿站在湖邊。接著，一陣強風把烏雲吹過天空。導遊要大家趕快下來，同時她用無線電派一輛卡車來接他們。在昏暗的光線中，她轉動一盞小手搖燈的把手，一行人跟著那團小小的黃色光芒前進。
回到涼亭展館，學生們喝了熱湯，吃了配一塊楔形起司的麵包。外面的風仍然很強，遠處有一座風力發電機在天空下緩緩轉動。王老師微笑著說：「校外教學的好處之一，」他說，「就是壞天氣會變成一個好故事。」回家的路上，一個女孩給大家看一張小得像小貓一樣的幼獸照片，整車的人一起發出「哇」的一聲。

title: Flying Without Leaving the Ground
paragraphs: Forty years ago, a flight school might have trained its students in a dusty [[cellar|L7-0170]] with a wooden box and a simple handle. Today, much of that work happens in a [[simulator|L7-1954]], a room that copies the inside of an airplane [[cockpit|L7-0197]] almost perfectly. Screens show [[emerald|L7-1959]] fields, long runways, and dark clouds. When the student pulls back on the controls, the room tilts slightly, and the stomach drops as if the plane had really climbed.

At a recent [[symposium|L7-1015]] on flight safety, one speaker, a flying [[buff|L7-1966]] who now trains new pilots, explained why simulators matter. A [[rotary|L7-0877]] aircraft such as a helicopter is especially hard to learn, he said, because the pilot's hands and feet must work together every second. In a simulator, a mistake costs nothing. A [[crimson|L7-1958]] warning light flashes, the student tries again, and nobody is hurt.

Simulators also let students practice the worst moments of flying, such as engine failure or a sudden [[gale|L7-1938]], so that they know exactly what to do in a real emergency. Even the sound of a jet [[turbine|L7-1131]] is copied, rising and falling in the student's ears, while a voice from the [[dispatch|L7-1949]] office gives instructions over the radio. Behind the screens lies a great deal of mathematics. The motion of every wing and every cloud is described by [[calculus|L7-1956]], and engineers use the same machines to test new designs, from the shape of a wing to the way air moves through the cabin. One team studied [[ventilation|L7-1965]] by modeling the flow of air between rows of seats.

Not everyone is convinced. Some instructors worry that a game-like machine tempts students to [[binge|L7-1955]] on hours of easy practice and treat flying like a video game. No screen, they say, can copy the fear of a real storm, and staying calm takes a kind of mental [[gymnastics|L7-1960]] that only real flights can teach. Most experts therefore agree that a simulator should add to real flying, not replace it.
zh: 四十年前，飛行學校可能是在一間滿是灰塵的地下室裡訓練學員，用的只是一個木箱和一支簡單的操縱桿。如今，大部分的訓練都在模擬器裡進行，那是一個幾乎完美複製飛機駕駛艙內部的房間。螢幕上顯示著翠綠的田野、長長的跑道和烏黑的雲層。學員向後拉操縱桿時，整個房間會微微傾斜，胃也隨之一沉，彷彿飛機真的爬升了。
在最近一場關於飛航安全的研討會上，一位講者，也是現在負責訓練新飛行員的飛行迷，解釋了模擬器為何重要。他說，像直升機這類旋翼飛行器特別難學，因為飛行員的手和腳必須每一秒都協調運作。在模擬器裡，犯錯不會付出任何代價。一盞深紅色的警示燈閃爍，學員再試一次，沒有人會受傷。
模擬器也讓學員練習飛行中最糟的時刻，例如引擎故障或突然的強風，讓他們確實知道真正的緊急狀況時該怎麼做。連噴射渦輪機的聲音也被複製出來，在學員耳中時高時低，同時一個來自調度辦公室的聲音透過無線電下達指示。螢幕背後有大量的數學。每一片機翼、每一朵雲的運動都由微積分來描述，工程師也用同樣的機器測試新設計，從機翼的形狀到空氣在機艙內流動的方式。有一個團隊就曾模擬空氣在一排排座位之間的流動，來研究通風。
不是每個人都被說服。有些教官擔心，一台像遊戲的機器會誘使學員狂練大量輕鬆的練習，把飛行當成電玩。他們說，沒有任何螢幕能複製真實風暴的恐懼，而保持冷靜需要一種只有真正飛行才能教會的心理體操。因此，大多數專家都同意，模擬器應該是真實飛行的補充，而不是取代它。

title: The Science Behind Fireworks
paragraphs: Few things light up a night like fireworks. The story of how people learned to make them begins in China, [[circa|L7-1981]] the ninth century. Alchemists were searching for a medicine that would let people live forever, and they mixed many powders together. One mixture contained [[charcoal|L7-0175]] and a salt with [[potassium|L7-1979]] in it. Instead of a medicine, they got a black powder that burned with a sudden, [[fiery|L7-1988]] flash.

The science behind it is [[combustion|L7-1984]], the quick joining of a fuel with oxygen. In a firework, charcoal is the fuel, and the other chemicals supply extra oxygen, so the powder burns very fast and pushes hot gas outward. That push can send a small rocket high into the sky, where it reaches its [[apex|L7-1847]] and bursts open. This sudden release of energy is also why fireworks should be handled only by trained people.

The colors come from metals. Chemists add small amounts of different metals, because each one burns with its own color, from [[emerald|L7-1959]] green to deep [[crimson|L7-1958]] red. Light is a kind of [[electromagnetic|L7-1977]] wave, and its color depends on how quickly the wave moves up and down. Some of the light from a firework is not even visible: an [[infrared|L7-1849]] camera can see the heat that our eyes miss.

Today, fireworks mark many happy events, from New Year parties to the [[inauguration|L7-1991]] of a new bridge or stadium. In some cities, families gather on a [[bluff|L7-1971]] above the river, [[clad|L7-1974]] in thick coats, with oranges and other [[citrus|L7-1973]] fruit to share while they wait. A [[crescent|L7-1985]] moon hangs in the sky, and the dark night sits like a black [[cloak|L7-1983]] over the water. Then the first rocket rises, and for a few seconds, everyone forgets the cold. Children point at the sky, and even the sleepy ones forget to yawn.
zh: 很少有東西能像煙火一樣照亮夜空。人們學會製作煙火的故事，要從大約九世紀的中國說起。煉丹師當時在尋找一種能讓人長生不老的藥，他們把許多種粉末混在一起。其中一種混合物含有木炭和一種含鉀的鹽。他們沒有得到藥，卻得到一種黑色粉末，燃燒時會突然迸出火紅的閃光。
這背後的科學是燃燒，也就是燃料與氧氣的快速結合。在煙火中，木炭是燃料，其他化學物質提供額外的氧，所以粉末燃燒得非常快，並把熱氣向外推。那股推力可以把一枚小火箭送上高空，在最高點爆開。這種能量的突然釋放，也是為什麼煙火只應由受過訓練的人來處理。
顏色來自金屬。化學家加入少量不同的金屬，因為每一種金屬燃燒時都有自己的顏色，從翠綠色到深紅色都有。光是一種電磁波，它的顏色取決於這個波上下擺動得有多快。煙火發出的一些光甚至是看不見的：紅外線相機能看見我們的眼睛看不到的熱。
如今，煙火標記著許多快樂的場合，從新年派對到一座新橋或體育場的落成典禮。在一些城市，家人會聚在河邊的懸崖上，穿著厚外套，帶著柳橙和其他柑橘類水果一邊等待一邊分享。一彎新月掛在天上，漆黑的夜晚像一件黑色斗篷覆蓋在水面上。接著第一枚火箭升空，那幾秒鐘，每個人都忘了寒冷。孩子們指著天空，連昏昏欲睡的孩子也忘了打哈欠。

title: Rocks from Space
paragraphs: On the white ice of the [[Antarctic|L7-0048]], a dark stone is easy to spot. That is why scientists travel there to hunt for rocks from space. A bright streak across the night sky is called a [[meteor|L7-2009]], and if a piece of it survives the fall and lands on the ground, it is called a meteorite. Most of these stones come from an [[asteroid|L7-1997]], a rocky body that circles the sun, mostly between Mars and Jupiter.

On sand or in a forest, a meteorite looks like any other stone. On the ice, its dark color is a dead [[giveaway|L7-2008]]. The ice also moves slowly, and over thousands of years it carries stones to certain places where the wind clears away the snow. The researchers travel on snow vehicles, wearing thick helmets and goggles, because a fall on the ice can cause a [[concussion|L7-1999]]. Unlike a plain piece of [[sandstone|L7-1994]] from a river, a meteorite often holds tiny grains of metal.

Back in the lab, each rock is cut and studied under strong lights. Scientists compare it with other samples to learn how the [[planetary|L7-2003]] system formed about four and a half billion years ago, [[circa|L7-1981]] the time when Earth began. Some space missions bring back samples directly. A spacecraft carries an [[onboard|L7-2010]] [[processor|L7-2004]], a small computer that controls every move, and its batteries may use [[lithium|L7-2002]]. Not every mission succeeds, and a [[flop|L7-0410]] can mean years of work lost. At the end of their lives, old spacecraft are guided to a remote part of the ocean, a kind of [[graveyard|L7-2001]] far from any ship.

One night, in a cold tent, a young researcher said that she worked with "rock stars." The [[pun|L7-2011]] made everyone laugh, even though they were tired. Outside, a [[crescent|L7-1985]] moon hung above the snow. Far away, a mountain [[observatory|L7-1851]] was tracking the sky, and the team knew that tomorrow they might find the next stone.
zh: 在南極的白色冰面上，一顆深色的石頭很容易被看見。這就是科學家前往那裡尋找太空岩石的原因。夜空中一道明亮的光痕稱為流星，如果其中一小塊在墜落後倖存並落到地面，就稱為隕石。這些石頭大多來自小行星，一種繞著太陽運行的岩石天體，主要位於火星和木星之間。
在沙地或森林裡，隕石看起來和其他石頭沒有兩樣。但在冰上，它的深色就是一眼看穿的證據。冰也會緩慢移動，在數千年間把石頭帶到某些地方，那裡的風會吹走積雪。研究人員乘著雪地車，戴著厚頭盔和護目鏡，因為在冰上跌倒可能造成腦震盪。與河邊一塊普通的砂岩不同，隕石常常含有細小的金屬顆粒。
回到實驗室，每塊岩石都被切開，在強光下研究。科學家把它與其他樣本比較，以了解行星系大約在四十五億年前，也就是地球開始形成的那個時期，是如何形成的。有些太空任務會直接帶回樣本。太空船上裝有一個機載處理器，也就是控制一切動作的小型電腦，它的電池可能使用鋰。並非每個任務都成功，一次失敗可能意味著多年心血付諸流水。在生命結束時，老舊的太空船會被引導到遠離船隻的海洋偏遠區域，那是一種墓地。
某天夜裡，在寒冷的帳篷裡，一位年輕的研究員說她是和「搖滾巨星」（岩石明星）一起工作。這個雙關語讓所有人都笑了，即使他們都很累。外面，一彎新月掛在雪地上方。遠方，一座山上的天文台正在追蹤天空，而團隊知道，明天他們也許會找到下一顆石頭。

title: The Hidden City Under the Street
paragraphs: Every day, a modern city sends a huge amount of used water down its drains. This [[sewage|L7-2012]] flows through a hidden world of pipes before it reaches a plant that cleans it. Most of us never think about the system until something goes wrong, and when it does, the smell alone is enough to cause [[nausea|L7-2021]].

At the plant, cleaning begins when heavy solids settle to the bottom, and the water passes through beds of sand and [[gravel|L7-1861]]. Then tiny living things break down what remains. In some plants, this process produces [[methane|L7-2020]], a gas that can be burned to make electricity, so the city turns a problem into energy. Other plants grow [[algae|L7-2014]] in shallow ponds to take extra food out of the water. Care is needed, because too many nutrients can let algae and some kinds of [[fungus|L7-2033]] grow out of control.

Inspecting the pipes is dangerous work, so many cities now use [[robotic|L7-2024]] machines. A small robot travels through a pipe on wheels with strong [[bearings|L7-2016]], and its body is made of light [[titanium|L7-2013]], which does not rust. Some old pipes contain [[asbestos|L7-2015]], a material once common but now known to be harmful, so the robots keep people out of danger. A cracked metal pipe may be repaired by [[welding|L7-2029]], or workers may dig a [[trench|L7-1120]] in the road and lay a new pipe beneath the [[asphalt|L7-2030]]. Air must also move through the system, so the engineers plan every [[duct|L7-1976]] and [[ventilation|L7-1965]] opening with care.

Cities in earthquake zones face another challenge. During a [[seismic|L7-2026]] shock, the ground can move [[sideways|L7-0936]] as well as up and down, and stiff pipes may break. Engineers therefore design flexible joints that bend instead of crack. Because these systems are hidden, people seldom thank the workers who build and protect them. Yet every clean glass of water and every flush of a toilet depends on the hidden city under the street.
zh: 每一天，現代城市都會把大量的用過的水送進排水管。這些污水在一個隱藏的管線世界中流動，然後抵達淨化它的處理廠。我們大多數人從不去想這套系統，直到出了問題，那時光是氣味就足以令人作嘔。
在處理廠，清潔工作從沉重的固體沉到底部開始，水接著通過一層層的沙和碎石。然後，微小的生物會分解剩下的東西。在一些處理廠，這個過程會產生甲烷，這是一種可以燃燒來發電的氣體，所以城市把一個問題變成了能源。其他處理廠則在淺水池中養藻類，吸走水中多餘的養分。必須小心，因為太多養分會讓藻類和某些真菌失控生長。
檢查管線是危險的工作，所以許多城市現在使用機器人。一台小機器人靠裝有堅固軸承的輪子在管子裡行進，機身由不會生鏽的輕質鈦製成。有些老舊管線含有石棉，這種材料曾經很常見，但現在已知有害，所以機器人讓人們遠離危險。破裂的金屬管可能用焊接修復，或者工人會在路上挖一條壕溝，在柏油路面下鋪設新管。空氣也必須在系統中流動，所以工程師會仔細規劃每一條管道和通風口。
位於地震帶的城市面臨另一項挑戰。在地震衝擊時，地面除了上下移動，也會橫向移動，僵硬的管子可能斷裂。因此，工程師設計了能彎曲而不會破裂的彈性接頭。因為這些系統隱藏在地下，人們很少感謝建造與保護它們的工人。然而，每一杯乾淨的水、每一次沖水，都仰賴著這座藏在街道下的城市。

questions.stem: What is the best title for the passage?
options: The Hidden System That Cleans Our Used Water

title: What a Mummy Can Tell Us
paragraphs: A [[mummy|L7-1992]] is more than a strange object in a museum. It is a letter from the past, written in bone, hair, and cloth. In ancient Egypt, people preserved the bodies of important persons so that they could continue their journey after death. Today, scientists use these same bodies to learn how those people lived, what they ate, and what made them sick.

Doctors who study the remains have found signs of illnesses that we think of as modern. Some mummies show [[arthritis|L7-1946]] in their joints, and a few carry the marks of [[tuberculosis|L7-1129]] in their bones. This tells us that disease is very old. The people of that time had no modern medicine, yet they suffered from many of the same problems that we do.

The tombs themselves also speak. Many were built with blocks of [[sandstone|L7-1994]] cut from a [[quarry|L7-1963]] near the river, and workers moved the heavy stones on wooden sleds. Wood was rare in Egypt, so builders bought good [[lumber|L7-0604]] from distant lands, which arrived with trading [[caravans|L7-1936]] and boats. Their tools were made of copper mixed with tin, a strong [[alloy|L7-0038]] that we call bronze. The first great pyramids rose [[circa|L7-1981]] 2500 BCE, and no machines were used to build them.

Art on the walls adds more clues. Painters mixed bright colors from minerals and earth, including a deep [[crimson|L7-1958]] red. Many tombs are covered with [[inscriptions|L7-2019]] that tell the name and the story of the dead person. The ceilings are sometimes painted with [[celestial|L7-2032]] scenes, a dark blue sky filled with golden stars, because the Egyptians believed that the sky was part of the journey after death. Jewelry found in tombs may contain a green [[emerald|L7-1959]] from mines in the eastern desert, showing that these people loved beauty as we do.

Of course, studying the dead must be done with respect. Modern scientists often use scans and tiny samples instead of opening the cloth, so that the mummy stays whole. In this way, they can hear the voices of the past without silencing them again.
zh: 木乃伊不只是博物館裡一件奇怪的物品。它是一封來自過去的信，用骨頭、頭髮和布料寫成。在古埃及，人們會保存重要人物的遺體，讓他們在死後能繼續自己的旅程。如今，科學家用這些遺體來了解那些人如何生活、吃些什麼，以及什麼使他們生病。
研究這些遺骸的醫生發現了一些我們以為是現代才有的疾病徵兆。有些木乃伊的關節顯示出關節炎，少數則在骨頭上留有肺結核的痕跡。這告訴我們，疾病非常古老。那時的人沒有現代醫學，卻也承受著許多和我們相同的困擾。
墓葬本身也會說話。許多墓是用從河邊採石場切下來的砂岩塊建成的，工人用木橇搬運沉重的石頭。埃及的木材稀少，所以建造者從遠方購買優質木材，隨著商隊和船隻運來。他們的工具是用銅混合錫製成的，一種堅固的合金，我們稱之為青銅。最早的大金字塔大約在西元前 2500 年興建，而且建造時沒有使用任何機器。
牆上的藝術帶來更多線索。畫家用礦物和泥土調出鮮豔的顏色，包括深紅色。許多墓裡佈滿銘文，記載死者的名字與故事。天花板有時畫著天體的景象，一片深藍的天空佈滿金色星星，因為埃及人相信天空是死後旅程的一部分。墓中出土的珠寶可能含有來自東部沙漠礦坑的綠寶石，顯示這些人和我們一樣熱愛美。
當然，研究逝者必須帶著尊重。現代科學家常使用掃描和微小的樣本，而不是打開包裹的布，讓木乃伊保持完整。這樣，他們就能聆聽過去的聲音，而不必再次令它們沉默。
